20463-three-years-on-the-plains-observat:
Three Years on the Plains records observations of Native peoples on the American frontier between 1867 and 1870. The writer spent those years where settlers, soldiers, and tribes met in uneasy contact. His contents page asks plain questions, starting with where the Indians came from.

His letters are blunt about policy. To friendly tribes he would give what they ask. To those who chose war, his answer was war until they were satisfied. The book preserves a frontiersman's views in his own harsh words, useful now as evidence of the attitudes that drove events on the plains.
archidoxorvm-avreoli-ph-theophrasti-para: Archidoxa Avreoli Ph, theophrasti paracelci, 1570, the paracelsian archidoxes. This book preserves that work. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
arxiv-2510-00170:
Fatma Almaz and Cumali Ekici wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on electromagnetic fields along curves in curved spaces. Their stage is a three-dimensional space form that is not flat, with either spherical or hyperbolic shape. Along any non-null curve they use the moving frame of tangent, normal, and binormal vectors. The paper works out how field quantities change along those frame directions.

The authors first extend the classic Serret-Frenet relations to this curved setting. They then express the bending elastic energy of a particle tied to the curve. That energy gets a geometric reading for unit vector fields along the path. Finally, they solve Maxwell's equations for the electric and magnetic field vectors in this space. The results give geometers a ready toolkit for field problems on curved three-dimensional backgrounds.
arxiv-2510-00470:
Yilin Wu wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on higher Calabi-Yau structures in representation theory. Calabi-Yau categories carry a duality that algebraists prize, and Iyama and Yang encoded key examples as triples. Wu generalizes their notion to a Calabi-Yau quadruple. Each quadruple yields a Higgs category with a Frobenius extriangulated structure.

That Higgs category also owns a canonical cluster-tilting subcategory, a rigid skeleton that organizes the whole. Concrete examples come from ice quivers with potentials and from singularity categories. The payoff is a unification: two known constructions now fit one frame. Both the relative Amiot-Guo-Keller construction and the Higgs construction respect silting reduction. In Wu's hands, that reduction passes to Calabi-Yau reduction on the nose. The paper tightens the architecture behind cluster categories, a busy meeting point of algebra and geometry.
arxiv-2510-00670:
Tanuku and five co-authors study active particles swimming through a tunable crowded environment in this 2025 arXiv paper on soft matter physics. Their bath is a two-dimensional layer of silica colloids, and the swimmers are gold-coated Janus spheres driven by an alternating electric field. One knob, the field strength, stiffens the bath while also speeding the swimmers up. That dual control lets the team watch cause and effect inside a single experiment, in place and reversibly.

As the field rose, the swimmers' motion shifted from viscous-like to viscoelastic-like behaviour. Their reorientation rate grew with speed, and the trajectories eventually turned spontaneously chiral, curling into self-sustained rotations. The authors trace that chiralization to local compressions of the bath and asymmetric interactions around each particle. The mechanism is particle-level and general, they argue, so it should apply to other active systems in complex media.
arxiv-2510-00770:
Ni, Chen, Sadeghian, and Haddadin build a tele-teaching framework for robot-assisted rehabilitation in this 2025 arXiv paper. Stroke and injury survivors need intensive, repetitive therapy, but therapist shortages limit how much patients can get. Their system links two robotic arms by bilateral teleoperation, so a therapist in one place demonstrates an exercise while the patient-side robot guides the patient through it elsewhere. Movement skills transfer between the robots online.

A six-degree-of-freedom dynamical movement primitives model encodes both position and orientation, working in the space that pairs ordinary coordinates with unit quaternions. The patient-side robot adapts the motion smoothly within a few learning iterations. Control shifts gradually between therapist-led guidance and passive patient training, based on learning level and operator intent. Experiments with seven-degree-of-freedom manipulators confirmed the approach works, pointing toward personalized, remotely supervised rehabilitation.
arxiv-2510-01070:
Cywiński and seven co-authors study secret elicitation in this 2025 arXiv paper on AI safety: extracting knowledge a model uses but refuses to state. The team trained three families of language models to hold secrets, such as the user's gender, which shape their answers while they deny knowing anything. An auditor model then tries to guess the secret, with or without help from elicitation techniques. The setup gives honesty research a controlled testbed.

Many techniques beat baselines at helping the auditor. Prefill attacks worked best in every setting: the target model, forced to continue a prepared prefix, leaks the secret in its completion. White-box methods using the logit lens or sparse autoencoders raised the auditor's success rate, though less strongly. The authors release the models and code as a public benchmark. Their results suggest determined auditors can surface knowledge that models actively conceal.
arxiv-2510-01270:
Phan, Li, and Lei defend language models at generation time by making them reflect on their own draft before releasing it. Jailbreaks succeed when a model answers first and never reconsiders. Progressive Self-Reflection inserts rounds of self-monitoring directly into decoding, with no extra training.

Attack success collapsed from over three-quarters to a small fraction on tested models. Benign task performance stayed intact while the reflection ran. A lightweight predictor spends extra rounds only on suspicious inputs, protecting the compute budget. Base models with enough reflection matched externally guarded systems while using less memory. Test-time scaling trades compute for safety in a tunable way. Three open models, two Llama variants and one Qwen, hosted the defense. Reflection rounds stack, so persistence wears down most attacks. No guardrail model needs loading beside the generator. Thinking twice costs less than apologizing once.
arxiv-2510-01470:
Meisenbacher, Nestorov, and Norlander mine millions of job advertisements to build public labor-market data structured by the federal O*NET taxonomy. Job ads describe work in free text, while O*NET catalogs occupations with fixed feature lists. The National Labor Exchange corpus supplies ads at national scale.

Custom models extract O*NET features from the ad text automatically. Aggregation turns the extractions into public-use statistics about changing workplaces. The tools and data are published openly for researchers and practitioners. Limitations in both source datasets are exactly what the pipeline is designed to overcome. The European ESCO classification complements the American taxonomy in the build. Code is published on a public repository for reuse. Workplace change becomes measurable at occupation level over time. Free text turns structured because the taxonomy disciplines the extraction. Aggregate release protects the underlying postings and posters.
arxiv-2510-01570:
Maitra, Hota, and Srivastava model two virus strains that mutate into each other while people choose whether to protect themselves. The framework is the classic susceptible-infected-susceptible cycle, where recovery returns people to the at-risk pool. Protection choices follow game-theoretic payoffs, so behavior and biology steer the epidemic together.

The team characterizes when the disease dies out and when a steady endemic state exists. Strategic protection reshapes both outcomes, sometimes in surprising directions. One clean result stands out: mutation from the weaker strain to the stronger makes coexistence of both strains impossible. Policy built on one strain alone can mislead. Equilibria come in two flavors here, extinction or a persistent endemic balance. Mutation direction matters as much as mutation rate. Instant payoffs drive choices, so today's protection reflects today's perceived risk. Coexistence questions decide whether one treatment plan fits both strains.
arxiv-2510-01670:
Shayegani and co-authors show that computer-use agents chase goals blindly, pursuing tasks that are impossible, unsafe, or contradicted by context. Agents that click through interfaces for users are deploying fast, and their failure mode is quiet over-eagerness rather than refusal. Three patterns define the bias: ignoring context, deciding under ambiguity, and obeying infeasible goals.

Their benchmark of ninety tasks on a real operating-system environment measures the behavior. Nine frontier models averaged strikingly high blind-pursuit rates. Prompting interventions lowered the rates but left substantial risk. Stronger training-time or inference-time safeguards are the stated need. Ninety tasks span the three blindness patterns by design. Model-based judges agreed with human annotations nearly ninety-four percent of the time. Hallucinated completion claims appear in the qualitative failures. Risks arise even when user inputs are not directly harmful. Obedience without judgment is the named disease.
arxiv-2510-01870:
Chen retraces how entropy decays in noisy diffusion systems, path by path, in this 2025 survey paper. Relative entropy dissipation is a classic topic for Itô-Langevin dynamics in stochastic analysis. The standard proofs average over all paths at once. A pathwise approach instead follows single random trajectories using time reversal of the diffusion.

Following single paths exposes delicate structure that averaged arguments hide. Fisher information enters as the local measure of how fast the entropy falls. Chen shows the pathwise account recovers the known classical results without extra localization tricks. The Wasserstein viewpoint adds a geometric picture on top. There, entropy decay appears as steepest descent with an exponential velocity rate. The article serves readers who want the machinery explained rather than merely cited. It ties probability, geometry, and information into one narrative of dissipation.
arxiv-2510-01970:
Yao and seven co-authors convert sensor streams into pictures to catch anomalies in this 2025 paper. Multivariate time series anomaly detection watches many variables at once for abnormal patterns. Threshold-based unsupervised methods misfire often, while supervised ones miss local structure and cost too much. Their framework, Moon, fuses both views of the data.

A multivariate Markov transition field turns the numeric series into image representations across variables and time. A multimodal convolutional network then learns from the numbers and the images together, sharing parameters between the streams. That fusion captures cross-variable relationships that either view alone would miss. Moon also explains itself with SHAP values that rank which variables drove each anomaly. Analysts receive a detailed report rather than a bare alarm. Experiments validated both the overall performance and each component's contribution. The design targets settings where labeled anomalies are scarce but costly to miss.
arxiv-2510-02070:
Chugainova and Treschev solve the Riemann problem for a two-component hyperbolic system in this 2025 analysis paper. The system couples two conserved fields through a cubic flux potential. Its viscous regularization adds a diagonal diffusion matrix. The authors admit only shocks that possess an internal traveling-wave structure.

They construct the full solution from rarefaction waves and structured shocks. Depending on the states imposed at plus and minus infinity, extra wave types appear. Undercompressive shocks, which break the usual compressibility count, enter some solutions. Jouguet waves also arise in suitable regimes. The traveling wave test replaces ad-hoc admission rules with a physical one. That choice determines which jumps the system can actually sustain. The construction shows how viscosity quietly selects the observable wave pattern. Such structure-aware solutions matter for elasticity and phase-transition models with similar fluxes.
arxiv-2510-02270:
Silva and co-authors present microCLIP, a way to sharpen image classification without labeled training data. Their 2025 machine learning paper adapts the CLIP vision-language model. CLIP matches whole images with text very well. Fine-grained tasks are harder, though. Telling apart similar bird or car types needs tiny local details. CLIP leans on one global token and misses those details. microCLIP adds a second token built from the most telling image patches.

A module named SOAP pools patch features by saliency, meaning likely importance. A two-part classifier from language model descriptions guides self-training. One part stays frozen as a stable guide. The other part learns during adaptation. Across thirteen fine-grained benchmarks, average accuracy rose from about sixty one percent to near sixty nine percent. That set a new best mark for this unsupervised setting.
arxiv-2510-02470:
Jha and Ahmadi-Asl select training subsets from a stream using gradient agreement sketches. Their 2025 machine learning paper presents a method called SAGE. Training on full datasets burns compute and energy. SAGE watches examples flow past once or twice. It keeps a compact sketch of gradient geometry. The sketch uses a classic tool called Frequent Directions. Memory stays fixed no matter how long the stream runs. Examples whose gradients agree with a consensus direction get priority. That agreement marks them as representative of the whole.

Benchmarks included image sets up to ImageNet scale. SAGE kept accuracy competitive at aggressive pruning rates. It ran on a single graphics card for those tests. End-to-end compute and peak memory both fell sharply. The method needs no pairwise similarity matrix at all. Streaming selection suits datasets too large to hold. Efficient training gains a simple, principled filter.
arxiv-2510-02670:
Yang, Poggio, Chuang, and Ziyin prove that training rules preserve neuron topology below a critical learning rate. Their 2025 machine learning theory paper covers common optimizers. Rules like SGD and Adam treat neurons symmetrically. Training then acts as a smooth, stretch-bounded map on neurons. That map strongly constrains how the neuron cloud can deform. A critical learning rate splits training into two regimes. Below it, all topological structure survives training intact. Above it, the neuron manifold simplifies step by step. Simplification coarsens the model and cuts its expressivity.

The result reframes the known edge of stability picture. Training first optimizes smoothly inside topological limits. Later it learns through drastic structural simplification. The theory ignores architecture, depth, and initialization details. Such independence makes the claim unusually broad. Practitioners gain a new lens on learning rate choice. Big steps buy speed at a structural price.
arxiv-2510-02870:
Kii and co-authors improve how evolutionary search designs physical parts. Topology optimization spreads material inside a fixed region for best performance. Evolutionary methods suit hard cases, but their child designs are often poor. Complex parent features rarely blend well that way. The team's Wasserstein crossover treats each design as a pile of mass. It then computes the optimal-transport average of two parents.

That average, called a barycenter, becomes the child design. The blend is smooth and keeps each parent's key structures. The framework starts with cheap, low-grade designs. High-grade checks then select parents for each new round. Three test problems showed the method at work. Two minimized peak stress in flat and solid parts. One improved turbulent heat transfer in a channel. Children improved step by step across rounds. The crossover beat a neural-network-based rival in a direct comparison.
arxiv-2510-03070:
Bouterakos and Tzounas track stability markers in power grids with time delays. Modern grids lean on fast data links and inverter controls. Those links add delays that can eat into stability margins. Eigenvalues reveal whether small wobbles grow or fade. With delays, a system has endless eigenvalues to track. The authors build a continuation method for that tracking job. It follows each value as system settings drift.

The method keeps the model's sparse structure intact. Sparse math is what lets huge grids stay computable. Even the delay length itself can serve as the drifting dial. Tests used a modified IEEE 39-bus system with renewables. A full dynamic model of the Irish grid checked scale. Accuracy and speed both held up in the trials. Guides for delay-proof control design are the next aim. Such guides matter as grids grow more inverter-heavy.
arxiv-2510-03170:
Sanna, Byrd, and Amin give relational programming its missing collections: sets and lookup tables. miniKanren lets programmers state relations instead of steps. Its data, though, is still built from linked pairs. Sets squeezed into lists lose their natural meaning. Two lists with the same members count as different sets. Failure and backtracking also behave badly under such encodings. Their extension, pronounced set-Kanren, changes that at the core.

Sets become first-class objects with their own constraints. Membership, union, and disjointness form a complete constraint family. Association lists join with shadowing and scoped lookup rules. Programs can describe collections lazily and declaratively now. Equality of sets follows contents, as it should. Finite failure becomes possible where search once wandered. Interpreters benefit most, since they juggle partial information constantly. The build sits atop a modern miniKanren without core changes. Examples show the new structures at work in practice.
arxiv-2510-03470:
Dherin and Munn, at Google Research, present a 2025 arXiv paper that proves a popular hunch about deep residual networks. ResNets and transformers stack many layers with skip paths, and depth clearly helps them learn. An older view says such networks act like crowds of shallower models voting together. The authors derive an exact formula for that hidden crowd. Their Residual Expansion Theorem makes the ensemble view precise instead of a loose analogy.

The formula shows that adding depth grows the crowd in a ranked, layered way. It also shows the output signal exploding as paths multiply, which explains why normalization layers became standard gear. Scaling each residual branch tames that growth on principle, the authors show. The same scaling quietly caps model complexity as a bonus. Their result gives the first structure based defense of normalization free tricks like Fixup and SkipInit, which earlier rested on optimizer lore.
arxiv-2510-03970:
Saad and colleagues wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on predicting data center energy use without pooling private data. Data centers now produce a notable share of global emissions, and schedulers like Kubernetes could place work where and when it costs less carbon. Good scheduling needs energy forecasts, but firms resist sharing operational data with central servers. The authors turn to federated learning, where models train locally and only updates are shared.

They extend an open energy exporter for Kubernetes and train gradient-boosted models across distributed clients. A bagging-based aggregation method merges the local models into one global model. On the SPECPower benchmark, the federated approach cut prediction error by about twelve percent against a centralized baseline. It did so while every firm's raw data stayed on site. Enterprises gain a realistic path toward lower-carbon cloud operations.
arxiv-2510-04070:
Degenne presents this 2025 arXiv paper on the role of Markov kernels in Mathlib, the Lean proof assistant's library. Kernels generalize random transitions: they map each starting point to a probability distribution over outcomes. Mathlib's probability folder leans on them heavily, and this paper explains the design. The centerpiece is a disintegration theorem for kernels.

Disintegration lets the library define conditional distributions of random variables and Bayesian distributions. The paper then shows a less obvious use: kernels give one common definition of independence and conditional independence for whole families of variables. The same kernel-centric pattern supports definitions of sub-Gaussian random variables. Kernels also underpin the library's treatment of entropy and Kullback-Leibler divergence.
arxiv-2510-04270:
Cristian and Velázquez present this 2025 arXiv paper on a coagulation model in which particles merge while gravity pulls them through space. Coagulation equations describe droplets or particles that collide and combine, a process relevant to rain formation. Strong kernels can produce instantaneous gelation in the spatially uniform model, meaning mass appears to vanish from the finite-size distribution at once. Adding spatial transport changes the problem because larger particles fall faster and leave regions at different rates.

To illuminate global behavior, Cristian and Velázquez examine the limit of very fast sedimentation. They rigorously show that solutions concentrate into a Dirac measure in the spatial variable. A formal reduction then produces a one-dimensional coagulation equation with a diagonal kernel, where only equal-sized particles interact. The result explains how such diagonal models can arise physically from settling rather than being imposed arbitrarily.
arxiv-2510-04370:
Thach Nguyen and three coauthors wrote this 2025 physics paper on a curious mirror effect. They studied self imaging in a concave cylindrical mirror, where the observer is also the object being seen. The team predicted how many self images a viewer would see from each spot in a room. They sorted the space around the mirror into regions, with one region for each image count.

The team then tested the map with a cheap stainless steel mirror of the kind used in teaching labs. A webcam played the role of the observer, and a glowing sticker marked the light source. Photos taken in the dark matched the predicted regions, and the count of bright dots showed the image number. The paper turns the setup into a classroom demonstration and a student exercise. It links basic ray optics to something students can see with their own eyes.
arxiv-2510-04570:
Longo and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on what happens when a star explodes inside a galactic jet. Jets from active galactic nuclei cross their host galaxies and pass many stars. Given time, some of those stars will explode as supernovae while inside the beam. The blast could disturb the jet and light it up in new ways. The team simulated the clash with relativistic hydrodynamics codes.

They ran one flat symmetric simulation and one three dimensional run that adds the orbital motion of the star. The blast site sat about a kiloparsec from the central black hole, where such events are most likely. The ejecta starts far smaller than the jet width, yet it expands to cover most of the jet cross section. Jet energy pours into the ejecta and speeds its breakup over tens of thousands of years. By the end, ejecta and jet gas were partly mixed.
arxiv-2510-04870:
Chambers, Ophelders, Schenfisch, and Sollberger wrote this 2025 paper on what degree counts can and cannot tell us about triangulations. A set of points in the plane can be triangulated many ways. One might hope that knowing a vertex degree pins down the pattern. Splitting the count by compass direction, north, south, east, and west, seems rich. The authors show the hope fails. Triangulations can share the list of cardinal degrees.

Counting the triangulations that match degrees is computationally hard. They prove the counting problem belongs to the class known as sharp P complete. The proof reduces a hard counting problem about vertex covers in planar bipartite graphs to theirs. So no exact counter exists unless complexity beliefs collapse. Degree data, direction aware, is thus a weak fingerprint of a triangulation. Algorithms that reconstruct meshes from degrees must expect ambiguity. The result warns counters in geometric settings to check hardness.
arxiv-2510-05070:
Siheng Zhao and six co-authors give humanoid robots finer control over whole-body tasks in this 2025 arXiv paper. A humanoid should walk, carry, and handle objects in one fluid motion. General motion tracking can copy human movement well. It lacks the precision and object awareness that carrying a heavy box demands.

Their framework, ResMimic, starts with a general tracking policy trained on large human motion data. A smaller residual policy then refines those motions for each task. New rewards encourage smooth object tracking and accurate body contact. A curriculum controller stabilizes the early training phase. In simulation and on a real Unitree G1 robot, ResMimic beat strong baselines on success, efficiency, and robustness.
arxiv-2510-05370:
Xin Wang and Xialu Liu make latent factors in big time series easier to interpret in this 2025 arXiv paper. Factor models compress thousands of series into a few hidden drivers. Their loadings show what each factor means, yet dense loadings defy reading. Many applications also group variables naturally, like the categories inside economic datasets.

The authors impose sparsity at both the individual and group level on the loading matrix. An ADMM algorithm estimates the loadings and the common component together. They also establish the asymptotic properties of the resulting estimators. Simulations show the sparse-group estimator beats the plain sparse one when group information is known. On the Stock-Watson dataset with 14 categories, prior knowledge produced noticeably more interpretable factors.
arxiv-2510-05570:
Toth and Xiao study how quantum waves spread when a curved space is stretched into the complex domain. Laplace eigenfunctions describe standing waves on a Riemannian manifold. Quantum ergodicity says most of them spread evenly at high frequency. Their 2025 paper extends that picture to analytic continuations on Grauert tubes.

The authors prove a quantum ergodic restriction theorem for real hypersurfaces inside the tube. Their proof tracks the FBI transform of the eigenfunctions onto those surfaces. As an application, they win upper and lower bounds that ignore the frequency parameter. The bounds hold under generic geometric conditions on the surface. The setting starts from a compact real-analytic manifold and its complex thickening. Density-one subsequences carry the equidistribution in their theorem. Earlier work had the averaged formula, but not matching two-sided control. Such control helps predict where eigenfunction mass can concentrate.
arxiv-2510-05670:
Debot and Marra measure a hidden cost of interpretable neural networks. Concept bottleneck models predict through human-understandable concepts, which makes them explainable. A sidechannel that bypasses the bottleneck restores accuracy but smuggles in opaque information. Their 2025 paper builds tools to quantify and control that leak.

The authors first unify existing sidechannel models in one probabilistic meta-model. They then define a Sidechannel Independence Score for each model. The score contrasts predictions made with and without the sidechannel's input. Penalizing that score during training pushes models back toward their concepts. Experiments show accuracy-trained sidechannel models are barely interpretable in representation. Predictor expressivity and sidechannel reliance jointly shape the final interpretability. Regularization improves interpretability, intervenability, and the quality of the interpretable predictor. Users gain an explicit dial on the accuracy-interpretability trade-off. That dial was missing from the concept-model toolbox until now.
arxiv-2510-05770:
Yuennan and colleagues revisit Higgs inflation under fresh telescope data. New Atacama Cosmology Telescope results, joined with DESI measurements, favor a slightly higher spectral index. Standard attractor models sit a little low by comparison. Their 2025 paper asks whether quantum corrections to Higgs inflation close the gap.

Starting from a one-loop effective action, they add radiative corrections through an anomalous scaling parameter. Analytic formulas then give the spectral index and the tensor-to-scalar ratio. Quantum corrections push the index upward while keeping the ratio small. At sixty e-foldings, the model predicts an index near zero point nine seven. That matches the ACT and DESI combination excellently. The ratio also sits well under the Planck limit. The authors also pin down the allowed range for the coupling ratio. Near-future polarization experiments like LiteBIRD and CMB-S4 can probe that range precisely. No new fields are introduced.
arxiv-2510-06270:
Ran and seven co-authors pair a frozen closed model with a trainable small one for discrete optimization in a 2025 machine learning paper. Multi-objective problems like molecular design hide optima in vast combinatorial spaces where evolutionary algorithms get trapped. Language models bring strong priors, but closed models cannot learn from experience, while small open models lack knowledge.

Their framework, Multi-LLM Collaborative Co-evolution, unites both around a shared trajectory memory. The small model improves through reinforcement learning with similarity-filtered preferences. Both models support global exploration, enhancing each other through mutual inspiration, not one-way distillation. On multi-objective drug design benchmarks, the system reached state-of-the-art Pareto quality. It consistently outperformed the baselines tested. The paradigm shows how hybrid systems keep evolving: knowledge-driven exploration from the big model, experience-driven learning from the small one. Neither alone offers both ingredients.
arxiv-2510-06370:
Ghate and seven co-authors benchmark how well reward models steer toward individual users' values in a 2025 computational linguistics paper. Globally deployed language models must serve users with diverse values and styles. Pluralistic systems need reward models that adapt to a stated profile.

EVALUESTEER supplies over one hundred sixty-five thousand synthetic preference pairs. The pairs vary along four value dimensions and four style dimensions including verbosity and warmth. Six language and reward models faced eleven prompting conditions and six comparison scenarios. Given a full user profile, the best models chose the aligned response less than three quarters of the time. Given only relevant preferences, accuracy exceeded ninety-nine percent. Current reward models cannot pick the pertinent parts out of a rich user profile. The benchmark gives developers a hard testbed for genuinely steerable reward models.
arxiv-2510-06470:
Şanlan and three co-authors replace raycasting with a sliding grid for terrain-aided navigation in a 2025 systems and control paper. Aircraft without GPS can navigate by matching sensed terrain against elevation maps. Point cloud measurements can aid the inertial system through a measurement innovation error. Standard models raycast from a hypothesized pose to predict measurements, which is computationally heavy.

The sliding grid skips raycasting entirely. Given a pose and the measurement's pattern, it slides over the elevation model to predict the point cloud. Comparisons show accuracy comparable to raycasting. The match is especially close at higher altitudes. The sliding grid runs orders of magnitude faster. Removing raycasting removes any need for GPUs or high-performance processors. Real-time terrain-aided navigation becomes feasible on resource-constrained embedded platforms. For small drones and backup systems, that efficiency decides whether terrain aiding ships at all.
arxiv-2510-06570:
Shingo Araki and four colleagues in Japan measure an unusual electrical effect in a crystal called PrSb2. Their 2025 paper uses Hall measurements, which track how a voltage bends sideways in a magnetic field. The material changes state at two clear temperatures. A charge-density wave forms near 100 kelvin, and magnetic order sets in near 5 kelvin.

Inside the magnetically ordered state, the team found an extra Hall signal that stood out from the usual parts. They attribute that signal to the topological Hall effect, which comes from electrons moving through twisted spin patterns. Ordinary and anomalous Hall contributions were ruled out by their analysis. When they applied pressure, the extra signal faded steadily. It almost vanished near one gigapascal, where the charge-density wave also disappeared. That link suggests the charge order helps create the topological effect in this material.
arxiv-2510-06670:
Shangjian Yin leads the team behind PIKA, a family of training datasets for language models. Their 2025 paper addresses a data bottleneck in alignment research. The best instruction datasets are private or costly to label by hand. Common open recipes use over 300,000 examples and still trail proprietary models.

PIKA takes the opposite approach, using far fewer but expert-level examples. Its supervised dataset holds only 30,000 examples, roughly a tenth of common recipes. Models fine-tuned on it beat models trained on much larger public datasets. The team also trained the Qwen2.5 model series on PIKA data. Those models outperformed their official instruction-tuned counterparts across sizes. A further 30,000 preference examples improved alignment again after the first training stage. The results suggest data quality can substitute for sheer volume. That matters for labs with limited budgets and no private data.
arxiv-2510-06870:
Yining Wang leads a team fixing a hidden bias in how language models learn from rewards. Their 2025 paper studies GRPO, a popular reinforcement learning method for reasoning models. GRPO hands the same advantage score to every token in a response. Longer answers therefore spread their reward thinly, yet dominate the training updates.

Several patched variants change how token scores are pooled, but they stay heuristic. Nobody could say what token preference each variant secretly encodes. The authors unify these frameworks in one formulation with a learnable dial, called lambda. At zero, the method is neutral about length. Positive settings favor longer answers, and negative settings favor shorter ones. Their method, lambda-GRPO, beat plain GRPO and DAPO across math reasoning benchmarks. On Qwen2.5 models of three sizes, average accuracy rose by roughly one to two percent. Letting the model learn its own length taste beats hand-set rules.
arxiv-2510-06970:
Marlon Müller leads a team training autonomous ships to obey the rules of the road at sea. Their 2025 paper combines reinforcement learning with falsification, a technique that hunts for failures. A learning vessel only behaves well in situations it has practiced. Handcrafting realistic traffic scenarios is slow, and real data alone does not cover the dangerous cases.

Their system generates adversarial scenarios where the vessel breaks maritime traffic rules. The rules are written as signal temporal logic specifications, so violations are precise. Each counterexample becomes new training material for the agent. Experiments used open-sea navigation with two vessels. On a test set of ten thousand scenarios, rule compliance improved clearly. Compliance also became more consistent across varied encounters. This is the first use of falsification-driven learning for maritime motion planning. The recipe pairs formal methods with learning in a way other vehicle domains could copy.
arxiv-2510-07270:
Masin and co-authors add effective core potentials to a leading suite for electron-molecule scattering calculations. Their 2025 paper extends the UKRmol+ codes, which model how electrons collide with molecules and how light ejects electrons from them. Heavy atoms are the obstacle: treating every electron is costly and often inaccurate. Effective core potentials replace the inner electrons with a smooth stand-in. The team derived the needed integrals for the suite's spline-based orbitals using momentum-space forms.

Test calculations covered bromine, silicon tetrabromide, and tungsten hydride collisions, plus light-driven ionization of methyl iodide. The implementation proved accurate across the test set. It also restores relativistic effects that all-electron treatments of heavy atoms often miss. With core potentials in place, the suite can now tackle molecules containing heavy elements on a routine basis. That widens its reach for plasma science.
arxiv-2510-07370:
Zhang and a large collaboration deliver the first systematic test of distance estimation for the Rubin Observatory's preview data. Their paper uses Data Preview 1 images from the commissioning camera. Most galaxies are too faint for direct distance measurement, so colors must estimate redshift instead. The team ran eight estimation algorithms through the RAIL evaluation framework. Two sky fields were used, one with six color bands and one with four. A reference catalog stitched together several kinds of known distances for checking.

Machine learning methods met the accuracy bar set for the survey's first year. Per-galaxy scatter stayed very small in the six-band field, with about one in ten galaxies landing as outliers. Performance worsened for faint galaxies and for the most distant ones. Adding near-infrared photometry from partner surveys improved the estimates.
arxiv-2510-07470:
Renaud, Hermant, Wei, and Sun accelerate image reconstruction algorithms while keeping their quality guarantees mathematical. Their 2025 paper extends regularization by denoising, a popular framework that plugs a denoiser in as an image prior. Such methods recover sharp images from undersampled, noisy measurements, but their convergence speed rested on heuristics. The new method, RISP, adds restarted inertia: momentum that resets whenever progress stalls. It still admits modern score-based priors learned from data. The authors prove a faster stationary-point convergence rate than the base framework achieves, and the proof never requires the prior to be convex.

A continuous-time analysis links the algorithm to the heavy-ball differential equation, a classic accelerated dynamics. Experiments span several inverse problems, from noise removal to linear inverse scattering at large image sizes. Reconstructions stayed high quality while iterations fell.
arxiv-2510-07570:
Tymkow, Schnapp, Valipour, and Ghodsi generate mathematical formulas with a diffusion model instead of writing them left to right. Their 2025 paper works on symbolic regression, the search for a closed-form expression fitting given data points. Genetic programming long dominated the task, but neural generators took over recently. Nearly all of them are autoregressive: each token of the equation is produced conditioned only on earlier tokens, so a bad early choice poisons everything after it. Symbolic-Diffusion instead denoises the whole expression at once, using a discrete diffusion process over tokens.

On the bivariate benchmark built for an earlier autoregressive system, the diffusion model matches its rival's expression accuracy with an equivalent encoder and transformer. By some metrics it improves on it. The authors credit the parallel generation with capturing global syntactic structure more faithfully.
arxiv-2510-07870:
Chatterjee wrote this 2025 paper on random satisfiability and the power of small choices. In random k-SAT, formulas switch from satisfiable to unsatisfiable near a threshold density. Inspired by two-choice models in random graphs, He asks whether limited choice can shift that threshold. He introduces MIDDLE-HEAVY, a rule that prefers clauses with balanced sign profiles. The rule is symmetric and blind to structure.

Through a biased projection to 2-SAT and a branching process argument, he derives formulas for the shifted thresholds. Tiny choice counts beat the first-moment bound for larger clause sizes. Five choices suffice at clause length four, and only three suffice from length six upward. A hybrid rule matches earlier biased methods while keeping symmetry. The results extend Achlioptas-style processes from graphs into random constraint problems. Fairness in clause choice need not cost threshold power.
arxiv-2510-08070:
Nöller, Tran, Gachechiladze, and Kueng wrote this 2025 quantum information paper showing that learning tasks form an infinite ladder indexed by how many state copies a measurement may touch. Entangling many copies is powerful but needs deep circuits. Two-copy measurements already beat single-copy ones exponentially on some tasks. For every prime copy count, the authors construct a task exponentially hard with one fewer copy yet easy with the full count.

Their protocols stay sample-efficient with shallow circuits, so the advantage is practical. The construction generalizes a Pauli-amplitude task through the Weyl-Heisenberg group. Such tasks also exist for all square-free copy counts. Each rung is a genuine phase transition in sample complexity. The results cast quantum memory as a key resource behind exponential learning advantages, and warn that benchmarks ignoring the copy budget miss the essential variable.
arxiv-2510-08170:
Chen and nine coauthors wrote this 2025 photonics proposal for converting light between modes using sound waves in lithium niobate waveguides at visible wavelengths. Thin-film lithium niobate on sapphire confines acoustic and optical modes without fragile suspended structures. Forward Brillouin scattering at visible wavelengths faces phase-matching obstacles. The authors introduce quasi-phase-matching by periodically modulating the waveguide width, which confines the acoustic mode while satisfying the condition.

After optimizing the geometry, their design predicts complete conversion between optical modes. It needs only a single milliwatt of acoustic power over a waveguide just over a millimeter long. Acousto-optic devices promise compact footprints and low power versus other modulators. A working visible-wavelength version would extend those benefits to microscopy, displays, and quantum optics. The paper is a simulation-based proposal, so experimental demonstration remains the next step.
arxiv-2510-08270:
Damir Nurtdinov and co-authors test control methods on real cable-driven robots in a 2025 arXiv paper. These robots move a platform held by cables, like a camera rig over a stadium. The tested system is underconstrained, meaning cables alone cannot fully fix its position. Control updates also arrive at limited rates, which makes steady control harder.

The team compared a classic PID controller with three reinforcement learning methods on the real hardware. The learning methods were DDPG, PPO, and TRPO, each trained to steer the platform along set paths. TRPO won, with the lowest root mean square errors across the tested trajectories. It also stayed robust when time gaps between control updates grew larger. The authors say this stability cuts the need for rapid sensor feedback. That could lower computing demands in messy, real-world settings.
arxiv-2510-08370:
Peter Albers, Lael Edwards-Costa, and Serge Tabachnikov study a recently proposed fourth kind of billiard in a 2025 arXiv paper. Billiard systems track a point bouncing around a smooth closed curve, called an oval. Inner billiards use reflection angles, while outer billiards use tangent lines and area rules. Symplectic billiards form a third family, mixing ideas from geometry and mechanics.

The missing fourth family, outer length billiards, was introduced only recently by other researchers. Its reflection rule rests on lengths along tangent lines rather than angles or areas. For ellipse tables, this map is completely integrable, with confocal ellipses as invariant curves. The authors study the system on a large scale, far from the table itself. Rescaled orbits there appear as circles when the table shrinks to almost a point. They also give the map's generating function and invariant area form.
arxiv-2510-08470:
Bianca-Mihaela Ganescu and co-authors train a vision-language model on child-scale data in a 2025 arXiv paper. The BabyLM Challenge limits training data to amounts a child might plausibly hear and see. Within the Vision track rules, the team built a lightweight decoder-based model. It must fuse words and images carefully to squeeze value from scarce data.

Three design choices carry the model: token-wise dynamic gating, feature modulation with channel attention, and contrastive grounding losses. The gate decides, for each token, how much visual or linguistic signal to use. On five benchmarks, including BLiMP, Winoground, and VQA, it matched or beat multimodal baselines. The learned gate showed readable patterns with no explicit supervision. It favored visual cues for content words and language cues for function words. The authors also flag limits from global image embeddings and split-related training instability.
arxiv-2510-08570:
Nimrod Berman, Assaf Hallak, and Assaf Shocher show that neural networks can be made literally linear in a 2025 arXiv paper. Linearity depends on the vector spaces involved, and standard spaces make networks nonlinear. Their construction sandwiches a linear operator between two invertible neural networks. New addition and scaling rules, induced by those networks, define the matching vector spaces.

They call this architecture a Linearizer, and it unlocks classical linear algebra for nonlinear maps. Singular value decomposition, pseudo-inverses, and orthogonal projections all become available. Composing two Linearizers that share one network yields another Linearizer, a closure property they prove. Training diffusion models in this form collapses hundreds of sampling steps into a single step. They also enforce idempotency, making a globally projective generative model. Modular style transfer demonstrations round out the applications.
arxiv-2510-08870:
Mrozinski and colleagues test whether picking the best of several machine translations works for whole documents, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The technique, quality estimation reranking, first drafts many candidate translations and then scores them, keeping the winner. It is proven for single sentences but barely tried on documents, where context runs long and coherence matters more. The team tried both trained scoring metrics and metrics built on large language models.

Their best trained metric, called SLIDE, lifted a standard quality score by about two points when choosing between just two candidates. With thirty-two candidates the gain grew to about five points, across both kinds of translation system tested. A leading model-based metric gained slightly less. Gains shrank as documents grew longer, yet they held up even on the longest texts in the study. The extra cost in running time stayed small under the right setup.
arxiv-2510-09170:
Liu, Hu, and Liu trace the tangled family history of a new kind of magnetism and the strange superconductivity it may enable, in this 2025 arXiv review. The newcomer is altermagnetism, a magnetic order recognized only recently. The review argues it grew from two older ideas: electronic liquid crystal phases, where electrons organize like liquid crystals, and multipole expansions, a language for magnetic patterns. All three share one mechanism, spin-momentum locking, tying each electron's spin to its motion.

Altermagnets spread their magnetic moments across at least two interlocking sublattices, which the multipole language captures neatly. The second half follows the same mechanism into superconductors whose electrons pair up in unconventional ways. It surveys finite-momentum pairing, d-wave and spin-triplet states, and topological paired surfaces. The authors close with open topics, offering both an introduction to altermagnetism and a map for using its superconductivity in quantum devices.
arxiv-2510-09770:
Adam Byerly and Daniel Khashabi turn a language model flaw into a search tool in a 2025 arXiv paper. In long-context tasks, models show position bias: they favour information by where it sits in the prompt, not by how relevant it is. Existing mitigations need white-box access to the model, which the strongest commercial models deny.

Their framework, GOLD PANNING, is a black-box Bayesian method that searches long contexts at inference time. It reorders documents so high-belief candidates sit where the model reads most diagnostically, a step called signal anchoring. Outputs then update relevance beliefs, and the process repeats. Unlike classic active learning, anchoring preserves weak cues once flagged. The method provably finds a target among many documents in logarithmically many rounds. On retrieval and question answering, it matched a permutation-based rival using thirty to sixty-five percent fewer queries.
arxiv-2510-09870:
Vayner and a large team of co-authors probe dusty outflows in the early universe in this 2025 arXiv paper in astrophysics. Galaxy-scale outflows, winds of gas leaving a galaxy, shape how galaxies form and grow. Dust grains matter twice here: molecules form on them, and they help push the winds that can drain a galaxy's gas.

The team uses complex organic molecules, carbon-based molecules with several atoms, as tracers of these winds. Such molecules can reveal the physical state of gas that other tracers miss. By studying them in a distant galaxy, the authors test how dust and gas move together in an outflow. The work links the chemistry of the wind to the force that drives it.
arxiv-2510-10070:
Rendon Restrepo and O. Gressel present an efficient spectral Poisson solver tuned for the NIRVANA-III code in this 2025 arXiv paper in astrophysics. The code simulates how a rotating fluid behaves under its own gravity, a problem that spans protoplanetary discs and whole galaxies. The local shearing box model simplifies that setting.

Solving the Poisson equation for gravity is a core cost in such simulations. The authors give an efficient spectral solver tuned to the shearing box with vertical vacuum boundary conditions, meaning no material above or below the disc. Spectral methods solve the equation in frequency space, where it becomes simple. A fast, accurate gravity solve lets the code spend its budget on the physics of disc stability.
arxiv-2510-10170:
Adarbeh and Mohammad Saleh introduce uniformly-S-pseudo-projective modules in this 2025 arXiv paper in module theory. Projective modules are a basic building block of algebra, and many generalizations relax their defining lifting property. The uniformly-S version ties the property to a multiplicative subset S of the ring.

The authors define the new class as a generalization of uniformly-S-projective modules. They then study its basic behavior, asking which constructions preserve the property and how it relates to neighboring classes. Such fine-grained module classes matter because they mark exactly how much of a theorem survives when hypotheses are weakened. The paper adds one more calibrated step to that hierarchy of projectivity notions.
arxiv-2510-10670:
Yu Li and nine co-authors teach video generation models to choose camera viewpoints for dynamic scenes, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Text to video models have learned to simulate real world geometry and physics, which hints they could act as implicit world models. A video naturally pairs a moving scene with sensible viewpoints. The team asks whether that prior can be reused for viewpoint planning in 4D scenes, meaning scenes that evolve over time.

Their method, AdaViewPlanner, works in two stages. First, an adaptive learning branch injects the 4D scene into the pretrained video model, which generates a video that embeds good viewpoints. Second, a camera diffusion branch extracts the camera positions, guided by the generated video and the scene. Experiments showed the method beating existing competitors, and ablation studies confirmed the key design choices. The authors present this as evidence that video generation models can support 4D interaction.
arxiv-2510-11770:
Yoshinobu Fudamoto leads a large team watching massive galaxies assemble astonishingly early in cosmic history. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies a tight complex of at least five galaxies, nicknamed the A2744-Quintet. The system sits in the core of a young galaxy cluster about six hundred fifty million years after the Big Bang. The team observed it with the JWST space telescope and the ALMA radio array in Chile.

The five galaxies crowd into a region only about ten kiloparsecs wide, and they are plainly interacting. The observations reveal a cycle at work. Mergers strip gas from one galaxy and temporarily halt its star formation. The stripped gas is then recycled, boosting star formation in the neighbors. Through such cycles the system should grow galaxies holding more than ten billion suns' worth of stars. The authors call this the first full evidence that cluster cores drive massive galaxy growth this way.
arxiv-2510-11870:
Renai Chen and Galen T. Craven show that a single molecule can remember how it was heated. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies a molecular junction, one molecule bridging two contacts, under a temperature difference that swings back and forth in time. Steady heat flow through such junctions is well mapped, but driven, far-from-equilibrium flow is not. The team combines nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulations with stochastic thermodynamics.

The central observation is heat transport hysteresis. The heat flux at a given instant depends not only on the current temperature bias but also on the bias's recent history. Turn the drive up and back down, and the flux traces a loop instead of retracing itself. That loop is a memory effect: present behavior encodes the past. Memory is exactly what neuromorphic computers, hardware mimicking brain-style computing, require. The authors argue this sketches a route toward thermal neuromorphic devices.
arxiv-2510-12070:
Sangmin Jo and four colleagues teach sleep-staging AI to work on patients it has never seen. Automatic staging from brain signals guides sleep-disorder diagnosis, but models stumble on new subjects because everyone's physiology differs. Their 2025 arXiv paper, MEASURE, pursues domain generalization by trimming representations down to the minimal sufficient core.

The key target is excess domain-relevant information, subject-specific baggage smuggled inside features that contrastive learning leaves behind. Naively stripping it, though, overfits to high-level features and wastes the temporal and spectral detail spread across network layers. MEASURE instead reduces domain information at multiple scales while preserving that multi-level signal. In exhaustive experiments on two public benchmarks, SleepEDF-20 and MASS, it consistently beat leading methods. The code is public. For sleep clinics, the promise is a stager trained at one hospital that still reads another hospital's patients correctly.
arxiv-2510-12370:
Shi and colleagues make a robot's intentions readable to humans, with a dial for how obvious those intentions should be, in a 2025 arXiv robotics paper. Legible motion lets people quickly infer which goal a robot is moving toward, which is vital for safe collaboration. Efficient motion generators rarely signal intent, and earlier legibility methods produced only the single most legible trajectory.

The authors score trajectories with an Information Potential Field, assigning each a continuous legibility value. A two stage diffusion framework first generates paths at a requested legibility level, from highly legible to deliberately ambiguous, then turns them into executable robot actions. Experiments in two and three dimensional reaching tasks show diverse, controllable motions across the full legibility spectrum. Performance remained comparable to leading methods. The work treats expressiveness as a dial to tune to context: a robot sometimes should telegraph its goal, sometimes stay neutral.
arxiv-2510-12470:
Chen and co-authors show that future gravitational wave detectors will localize lensed events precisely enough to identify their host galaxies, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. Gravitational lensing splits a wave signal into several images. Lensed events could measure cosmic expansion, but only if the source's redshift is known, which normally requires finding the host galaxy, hard when localization is poor.

Third generation ground based detectors will catch lensed events having three or more detectable images. Those multiple arrivals at distinct times and places form an effective network. It shrinks the typical localization area dramatically. For most such events the gain over unlensed cases exceeds a factor of ten. Precise localization plus lens modeling then pins down the host. Using simulated mergers, the team finds two years of observation could measure the Hubble constant to about one percent precision from these dark lensed sirens alone. Other parameters are constrained too.
arxiv-2511-00170:
Rye Howard-Stone and Ion Mandoiu present AmpliconHunter2, a fast in silico PCR engine written in C for finding primer matches across genomes. The tool handles degenerate primers with an accurate melting temperature model, using a bit-mask matcher accelerated by AVX2 vector instructions. User-specified mismatches and three-prime clamp constraints are supported, and amplicons are called in all four primer pair orientations.

Sequences are packed into two-bit batches and streamed in chunks to keep memory low, with optional primer trimming and barcode extraction. Bioinformatics readers get a scalable simulator for primer design. Predicting PCR products in silico prevents wasted laboratory work on primer pairs that misfire.
arxiv-2511-00370:
Chaochen Wu, Guan Luo, Meiyun Zuo, and Zhitao Fan work on video moment retrieval: given a text query, find the matching segment inside a long, untrimmed video. Combining several models should help, but models often disagree on the segment boundaries, and earlier systems had no way to settle such conflicts. Their model scans the whole video once, returns boundaries, and produces evidence for its choice.

On top sits a multi-agent framework where agents argue their locations, and evidential learning weighs the conflict. A useful side effect follows: the system can declare a query out of scope, with no matching moment in the video, without extra training. Benchmark tests beat leading rivals. The authors argue that modeling conflict between agents is itself a strong way to lift retrieval performance.
arxiv-2511-00470:
Ryuhei Mizutani studies the minimum submodular cost allocation problem: split a ground set among several agents so the total cost, scored by one submodular function per agent, is as low as possible. Submodular functions capture diminishing returns, and the monotone case matches the facility location problem with submodular facility costs posed by Svitkina and Tardos. Mizutani analyzes a natural linear programming relaxation of the problem.

He shows the relaxation's integrality gap is at most half the number of agents, which yields a matching approximation algorithm with the same guarantee. For a fixed number of agents, a matching lower bound and a hardness result, reduced from vertex cover in multipartite hypergraphs, show the bound is tight. Applications follow for polymatroid intersection duals and minimum-weight vertex cover variants.
arxiv-2511-00770:
Chenyang Zhao and seven co-authors inspect the surfaces of two-dimensional materials with a microscope that breathes helium. Molybdenum disulfide and its cousins promise electronics and sensors, but device performance hinges on surface cleanness at the atomic scale. Even surfaces prepared in ultra-high vacuum collect trace contamination, and conventional tools barely notice submonolayer dirt. Scanning helium microscopy offers non-destructive, ultra-sensitive eyes.

Minute amounts of stray carbon, the measurements reveal, disorder the surface enough to erase helium diffraction entirely. Tracking helium reflectivity over time quantifies how order decays in different regions: flat areas succumb faster than regions near edges. Surface order in these materials is fragile even under vacuum, the team concludes, and their microscope gives wafer-scale quality checks a new, gentle instrument.
arxiv-2511-01070:
Dinh-Hieu Tran and colleagues survey quantum reinforcement learning as a tool for sixth generation wireless networks. Sixth generation systems are expected to deliver higher data rates, lower delay, and denser connections than 5G. Artificial intelligence is seen as essential to running them. Yet classical methods strain under the strict delay and throughput limits.

As a review and vision article, the paper summarizes what deep reinforcement learning has achieved for 6G and where it falls short, then introduces the quantum version and its potential advantages. A case study on dynamic spectrum access shows the quantum approach outperforming the classical one. The authors close with research directions they judge most promising for quantum learning in future networks.
arxiv-2511-01170:
Ruofan Zhang and colleagues propose DART, a way to teach language models to stop thinking sooner on easy problems. Chain of thought reasoning improves accuracy, but models produce long explanations even when the problem is simple, wasting computation. Earlier reinforcement learning attempts to fix this were unstable and depended heavily on reward design.

DART is supervised instead. It distills concise reasoning patterns from stronger models, interpolates them into a continuum of reasoning styles, and curates training data that balances correctness with compactness, so the model learns when to stop. On mathematical benchmarks it preserved or improved accuracy while cutting reasoning output sharply, in one reported case by over eighty percent with more than five times faster computation.
arxiv-2511-01370:
Saurav Patel and colleagues use first principles calculations to find several prized properties woven into one compound, the wurtzite crystal LiZnAs. The prized set starts with hyperferroelectricity: keeping spontaneous polarization even under open circuit conditions with a depolarizing field present. It also holds multiple topological phases. A giant Rashba effect rounds out the set: a momentum space spin splitting with reversible spin textures.

Crystalline symmetries plus spin orbit coupling supply the shared frame. An unstable lattice mode settles into a free energy minimum with great depth and polarization, showing stable hyperferroelectricity, backed by mode specific effective charges and large high frequency dielectric constants. The study also takes up the fine question of what happens at the critical point of the topological phase transition in such a material.
arxiv-2511-20070:
Goyal and Khurana probe a symmetry question in abstract ring theory. Their 2025 paper revisits a problem posed by Hartwig and Luh in 1977. The question concerns strongly pi-regular elements in rings. Such elements have powers that stabilize in a precise sense. One-sided versions might not imply the two-sided property.

Dedekind-finite rings form the setting for the question. Dittmer, Khurana, and Nielsen answered it negatively in 2014. Yet exchange rings gave a positive answer in their work. Goyal and Khurana test many other ring classes. Several classes preserve the one-sided to two-sided implication. Others break it, supplying fresh counterexamples. They also prove the condition lacks left-right symmetry. A property holding on the right can fail on the left. Suitable elements and UU rings enter the analysis. The paper refines where the old question holds. Pure algebra gains a sharper map of ring behavior.
arxiv-2511-20170:
Belucci, Lounici, and Meziani rescue neural networks on tiny tabular datasets. Their 2025 paper introduces AdaCap, an adaptive contrastive training scheme. Tree-based models dominate small-data tables stubbornly. Neural nets overfit or learn too little with few rows. AdaCap targets exactly that fragile regime.

A shuffle-based contrast loss shapes the learned codes. Shuffled features create contrast examples during training. A Tikhonov closed-form output mapping finishes the model. Ridge-style math replaces a learned final layer. Eighty-five real data tables tested the scheme. Multiple network designs were included in the trials. Gains were consistent and clearly real overall. Residual designs benefited most in small samples. A meta-predictor forecasts whether AdaCap will help. Dataset size, skew, and noise drive its predictions. It anticipates benefits accurately across the collection. Code and results are publicly available online. Small-data practitioners gain a targeted regularizer.
arxiv-2511-20570:
Kim and Parker Jones put a safety referee between brain signals and robot arms. Their 2025 paper presents GUARDIAN, a runtime monitor for neural-controlled robots. Brain-computer interfaces decode intent from EEG signals for people with limited mobility. Decoders are often wrong, and wrong commands can hurt. Accuracy alone cannot certify such systems safe.

GUARDIAN couples calibrated decoding with symbolic goal checks. Dual invariants police both logical safety and bodily trust signals. Tests used the BNCI2014 motor imagery dataset of nine subjects. Those trials numbered 5,184 in total. Decoders were weak, scoring only twenty-seven to forty-six percent accuracy. Their confidence was badly miscalibrated as well. Yet the system held a safety rate of ninety-four to ninety-seven percent. Correct interventions ran about 1.7 times the baseline rate. The monitor decides in under a millisecond at one hundred hertz.
arxiv-2511-20770:
Raghuveer Thirukovalluru and colleagues argue in 2025 that image encoders should read the question before looking at the picture. In standard vision-language models the encoder processes every image the same way, blind to what will be asked, and the language model copes downstream. Their Text-Guided Semantic Image Encoder, TIE, conditions the image representation on the input text query, steering visual features toward what the question needs.

Vision-language models equipped with TIE beat their counterparts by 1.5 points averaged over nine image-to-text benchmarks at the one-billion-parameter scale, and by 1.3 points at three billion. Gains reached 6 points on document tasks like DocVQA and InfoVQA, which usually demand many tiles. TIE models won while using only half as many image tiles, an inference saving. Attention analysis confirms the encoder fixates on query-relevant regions, and even generic queries work well, suggesting the training teaches encoders what to keep.
arxiv-2511-20870:
Nan Jiang tackles in 2025 a quiet problem inside simulators: how to rewind them. Planners and calibration tools need to reset a simulator to a past state, but hidden variables make the true state uncertain. Resetting means sampling from the belief state, the probability distribution over hidden states given what was observed. Exact sampling is usually impossible, so practitioners pick an approximation. Jiang asks how to choose among approximations using only the ability to run the simulator.

He shows the choice reduces to a general problem of selecting conditional distributions, and gives an algorithm with guarantees under sampling-only access. Two formulations emerge: match the hidden-state distribution, or match the distribution of observations it produces. Surprisingly, the observation-based route can fail with the natural single-reset roll-out yet works under a repeated-reset scheme. The paper maps the trade-offs, including distribution shift and sampling policy.
arxiv-2511-21170:
Secure coalitions are the focus of a 2025 graph theory paper by Swathi Shetty, with Sayinath Udupa and B. R. Rakshith of the Manipal Institute of Technology in India. A graph is a network of points linked by lines. A secure dominating set is a group of points that watches over the whole network and can defend any attacked point. Two weaker sets form a secure coalition when only their union gives that protection.

Shetty and her coauthors prove that every graph can be divided into a partition of such coalitions. They pin down exactly which graphs have a secure coalition number of 1, 2, or the full point count. They also list all trees whose number is one less than the point count. They close by showing that any graph with no isolated point can appear as a coalition graph.
arxiv-2511-21470:
Stephen Brittain, Robert Coulter, and Alice Hui close a gap open since 1957 in finite geometry, in a 2025 paper. Hughes planes are non-classical projective planes, geometries where points and lines meet by unfamiliar rules, traditionally described through a planar ternary ring, an algebraic gadget encoding the plane's incidence structure. Despite decades of study, nobody had written down a polynomial that represents such a ring for a Hughes plane.

Brittain and his coauthors determine that reduced PTR polynomial for every Hughes plane built over a regular nearfield. The coefficients hold a surprise: the Catalan numbers, the famous counting sequence 1, 2, 5, 14, and their generalizations appear throughout, depending on the representation chosen. Because PTR polynomials connect to permutation polynomials, functions that shuffle a finite field, the result yields three new infinite families of them, again involving Catalan numbers. The authors also compute the new permutations' differential uniformity, a security-relevant measure.
arxiv-2511-21570:
María Pérez-Ortiz argues that governments should design futures, not just predict them, in a 2025 position paper. Prediction narrows the future to a single forecast, while responsible foresight treats it as open but not empty: outcomes can still be shaped by ethical action today. She coins the term responsible computational foresight for using AI and simulation inside that practice, and sets out founding principles for the new field.

Pérez-Ortiz surveys the AI-driven foresight tools now emerging, from scenario analysis to world simulation, and assigns AI a strictly supportive role. It should sharpen policymakers' handling of uncertainty and risk while complementing, never replacing, human judgment. The timing is practical, not abstract: a 2024 report found 37 percent of UK government departments already using AI, with another 37 percent piloting or planning it. Her principles aim at futures that are sustainable, resilient, and accountable by design.
arxiv-2511-22070:
Guo, Lyu, Wu, and colleagues at Peking University design MagnifierSketch, a streaming algorithm for quantile estimation. Each arriving item is a key-value pair, and users care about one target quantile per key, such as the 99th-percentile latency, rather than the whole distribution. Existing sketch algorithms target arbitrary quantiles or whole streams. So they waste accuracy and throughput on this focused job, especially at the high speeds of real data streams.

Three techniques do the work: Value Focus keeps values near the target point. Distribution Calibration converts any target quantile problem into a median problem. Double Filtration discards infrequent keys in both stages. The authors prove the estimator unbiased, analyze its space and time costs, and show its average error is significantly lower than state-of-the-art methods for both single-key and per-key estimation. They also implement it inside the RocksDB database.
arxiv-2511-22370:
Rothe and Schlotter study hedonic games, where players form groups and care about which group they end up in. In altruistic versions, a player's happiness also depends on how well their friends do in their own groups. A grouping is core-stable if no set of players would all rather leave and form a new group together. Checking core stability had stayed unsolved for four variants of these games.

The pair settle all four open cases at once. For each variant, they prove that checking core stability is coNP-complete. The variants cover average-based and minimum-based ways of counting friends' outcomes under two treatments of altruism. CoNP-complete is the class of problems whose wrong answers can be verified quickly. Their proofs use intricate gadgets built into the friendship networks. With these results, the complexity picture for verifying core stability in altruistic hedonic games is now complete.
arxiv-2511-22470:
Nguyen, Tran, Phan-Nguyen, and Dinh tackle text-based person anomaly retrieval: finding images of a person behaving abnormally, given only a written description. Standard retrieval leans toward common actions and whole images, missing fine details marking unusual behaviour. Their framework combines a Local-Global Hybrid Perspective module, feeding a vision-language model fine-grained local features and coarse global context, with a Unified Image-Text model trained on four objectives at once.

The unified model mixes contrastive, matching, masked language, and masked image losses, and a feature selection algorithm guided by the hybrid module trims inputs. An iterative ensemble combines models in sequence, refining predictions step by step. On the PAB benchmark the method set a new state of the art, improving top-1 recall by 9.70 percent over earlier work on the full dataset and by 12.59 percent on the smaller subset, with ablations confirming each part contributed.
arxiv-2511-22970:
Immorlano and colleagues built one AI emulator that imitates nine different climate models at once, instead of training a separate emulator for each. Real climate models are so expensive to run, taking weeks to months on supercomputers, that each produces only a small handful of future projections. That makes it hard to judge the range of possible warming and extreme weather ahead.

Their conditional diffusion model, a generative method that builds outputs by gradually removing noise, learns the shared patterns across the nine models and several emission pathways. It then produces daily global temperature maps for past and future periods. A fixed-seed trick lets them compare emission pathways fairly, matching the precision of ordinary sampling with 50 to 300 times fewer samples. Tests on a climate model the system never saw showed it still generalized reliably to unseen future climates.
arxiv-2511-23070:
Zhu and colleagues tackle a practical weakness of multimodal AI models, which combine image, text, and audio inputs. When one input channel goes missing, because a sensor fails or privacy rules block it, accuracy drops sharply. Existing fixes either rebuild the missing channel with a generative model, which is expensive, or fine-tune with prompts that only look at nearby network layers.

Their method, Replay Prompting, stores early-layer features for each modality in buffers and replays them into deeper layers. It keeps private buffers for modality-specific detail and shared buffers for cross-modal meaning, with a task-aware setup for the buffers. On vision-language tests it degraded far more slowly as inputs vanished. At a 70 percent missing rate it scored 83.01 percent accuracy, against 75.66 and 76.69 percent for two leading rivals, while adding only negligible extra parameters to the model.
arxiv-2511-23170:
Kawamura and colleagues strengthen CLIP-style vision-language pretraining, where models learn to match images with text, by fixing a compositional blind spot in how they align parts. The usual standard methods align whole images with whole sentences, or single tokens with single patches. But meanings that span several regions at once, like a phrase describing two objects together, escape both schemes.

Their PowerCLIP instead aligns every subset of image regions, the full powerset, against the phrases of the caption's parse tree, using bidirectional triplet losses to pull matching pairs together. Because enumerating all subsets explodes combinatorially, they introduce non-linear aggregators that cut the cost from exponential in the number of regions to linear while provably approximating the exact loss to arbitrary precision. The trained model beat seven state-of-the-art rivals in their experiments on zero-shot classification and diverse retrieval benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-23370:
Caubrière and Gauthier ask whether bigger self-supervised speech models help African languages, which remain badly under-represented in speech technology, by training HuBERT encoders exclusively on African speech at three scales. Alongside a base-size counterpart they release SSA-HuBERT-Large at 317 million parameters and SSA-HuBERT-XL at 964 million parameters. They are the first large speech encoders trained solely on African audio, as open weights for the community in their study.

Pre-training used about 60,000 hours of speech spanning 18 languages, led by Swahili, Hausa, and Kinyarwanda. Evaluation fine-tuned the models for speech recognition and language identification on the FLEURS Sub-Saharan subset of 320 hours across 20 languages. The larger architectures significantly improved performance over base-size models, including a previous Africa-focused HuBERT and a large multilingual wav2vec model. Model capacity pays off when paired with Africa-centric data at scale in practice.
arxiv-2512-00570:
Loop equations tie the behavior of gauge theories to the averages of closed loops of field lines. Hao Shen, Scott Andrew Smith, and Rongchan Zhu derive Makeenko-Migdal equations for lattice Yang-Mills-Higgs theory in 2025. The structure groups covered include the special orthogonal, unitary, and special unitary families.

Adding a Higgs field to the pure Yang-Mills setting creates several new operations in the equations. These master loop equations organize infinitely many relations into one framework that computations can use. They serve probability and mathematical physics, where lattice gauge theory is a testing ground for rigorous quantum field theory. The Higgs field adds mass-giving structure that pure gauge theory lacks.
arxiv-2512-00670:
Diffusion language models refine their answers through many denoising steps, but the answer often stabilizes early. Sebastian Stich and co-authors propose EDIT in 2025, an early termination method for diffusion model inference. The name stands for early diffusion inference termination.

EDIT stops denoising adaptively once the reasoning is stable enough relative to training-time behavior, judged from the dynamics of training gradients. Stopping early saves computation on every query without retraining the model. As diffusion models enter production, such inference-time savings compound into major cost and energy reductions. Diffusion language models are a newer rival to the autoregressive models most people know. Stability relative to training behavior gives the stopping rule its reference point. For firms that serve such models, the gain is plain cash and watts. Each cut step is time and power saved, on each call, all day, at full scale.
arxiv-2512-00970:
