Kiran Adhikari studies secret sharing in quantum systems in a 2025 paper. Quantum information scrambling spreads a localized piece of information across a whole system, hiding it from anyone who can see only part. That spreading is tied to chaos in quantum systems and even to black hole models.

Adhikari uses Haar scrambling, a random mixing process, to build quantum ramp secret sharing. In ramp schemes, partial shares reveal partial information, balancing security against efficiency. Scrambling-based schemes could protect quantum data across many parties. The work links a deep dynamical idea, how information hides, to a concrete cryptographic task.
arxiv-2512-01270:
Yuan-Sen Ting and co-authors built a tool that can measure lines in star light on its own. Star spectra have dips where atoms soak up light. The width of each dip tells how much of an element is present. Doing this by hand for many stars is slow work.

Their tool, called Egent, fits each dip with a set of smooth curves. A large language model then looks at each fit and checks it. The model can shift the fit range, add parts for mixed lines, or flag a bad fit. The loop of fit, check, and fix runs with no human help.
arxiv-2512-01370:
Medha Sawhney and co-authors speed up diffusion solvers for physics equations. These solvers guide each step with the leftover error of the equation. That guide needs slow gradient work at test time. It can also wobble when the error signal is noisy.

The team uses the error in a new way. They treat it as a form of attention in the frequency domain. That lets the solver adapt its steps on the fly. It skips the slow guide loop as well. Faster, steadier solvers help engineers run many what-if tests on flows, heat, and stress.
arxiv-2512-01570:
Stephan Druskat and Lars Grunske present a data set on open research software. Much lab work now makes software as it goes. That software is key to results, yet it is hard to track. Open references to it are scattered.

Their set, OpenDORS, gathers openly referenced research software in one place. Each entry is tied to its public reference. Scholars can study how research software spreads and lasts. Funders and labs can spot which tools merit long-term support. The set turns scattered mentions into a base for policy. Each record keeps its source link, so users can trace a software claim back to the paper or page that cited it first.
arxiv-2512-02070:
Forecasting far ahead is hard: transformer models capture long-range patterns but grow costly and overfit sparse data, while lean linear models miss local twists. Qianyang Li and three co-authors propose DPWMixer in 2025, a dual-path design for long-term time series forecasting that tries to keep both strengths.

The mixer's two paths divide the labor, with wavelet analysis supplying a multi-scale view of the signal's ups and downs. Wavelets are well suited to separating slow trends from quick local wiggles, the very dynamics linear models flatten. The design aims at forecasts that stay accurate over long horizons without the transformer's quadratic price tag.
arxiv-2512-02270:
Testing whether a robotic vehicle is safe means hunting for the rare inputs that make it fail, and full simulations are too heavy to search at scale. Nazmus Shakib Sayom and Luis Garcia propose in 2025 a method that strips a system down to only the parts a safety property cares about.

From that reduction they build lightweight surrogate models that keep the property-relevant behavior and drop unrelated complexity. Falsification then runs through trace analysis checked by temporal logic oracles, which flag violations of the stated property. Scalable falsification could let engineers probe far more scenarios before a robotic vehicle ever meets a road.
arxiv-2512-02470:
Maitri Ganguli and Diptiman Sen study a chain of particles whose links switch back and forth in set patterns. Their model is the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain, a standard test bed for how electrons hop between sites. Two switching rules take turns, and they differ in how strongly particles hop between cells.

The pair applies the two rules in three ways: in a steady rhythm, in an almost rhythm, and at random. Each pattern can push the chain into different states with different edge behavior. Comparing the three cases shows how the timing of a drive, not just its strength, shapes a quantum material. The three drives act like three clocks that can clash with or match each other.
arxiv-2512-02570:
Fred Diamond and Shu Sasaki attach Galois symmetries to a broad class of modular forms. Hilbert modular forms live over a totally real number field and act as higher cousins of classical modular forms. Reducing them modulo a prime gives forms on varieties in prime characteristic.

For any Hecke eigenform, of any weight, the authors prove a matching two dimensional Galois representation exists. Such links between analysis and symmetry are the heart of the Langlands program. Extending them to prime characteristic widens the tools for studying number fields and their hidden structures. All weights at once is the strong form of the claim, and it is the form peer work can build on next.
arxiv-2512-02670:
Connor Evans, Zinaida A. Lykova, and N. J. Young develop theory for holomorphic functions on a two variable domain. The domain is the symmetrized skew bidisc, built from pairs of points in the unit disc. The functions studied stay bounded by one in modulus throughout the domain.

Model theory for such functions links algebra, geometry, and interpolation questions. Results here extend methods long used on the disc and bidisc to this skewed setting. Progress on these domains feeds operator theory and control, where bounded analytic functions describe stable systems and their limits. Odd domains test the tools of the trade, and tools that pass here tend to hold up on plain ones too.
arxiv-2512-02870:
Zhaoqing Wang and co-authors teach video generators to obey a moving camera with rewards checked against geometry. Camera controlled generation has improved fast with video diffusion models. Most methods, though, rely only on supervised fine tuning, leaving reinforcement learning post training largely unexplored.

Their framework applies online reinforcement learning to a pretrained generator. A verifiable geometry reward scores how well the video follows the planned camera path. Precise camera obedience matters for film previsualization, games, and simulation, where the shot must match a director's plan exactly. A score can be checked by hand, frame by frame. That turns a vague hope for good shots into a mark a team can train to hit.
arxiv-2512-03070:
Grouping mixed data is a key task in the big data age. Guillaume Guerard and Sonia Djebali survey the field in this 2025 work. Data now arrive in huge amounts, at high speed, and in many forms, both numbers and labels.

The survey maps the main methods and the hard parts that remain. Mixed sets are tough because numbers and labels do not compare in the same way. A clear map of the field helps new researchers pick sound tools. It also shows firms where current methods may fail on their own mixed data. Newcomers to clustering can use the survey to learn key terms before choosing a method.
arxiv-2512-03170:
Some spacetimes leak energy through their edges. Robert McNees and Céline Zwikel build charges for such cases in this 2025 work. They study four-dimensional spacetimes with a nonzero cosmological constant, like de Sitter and anti-de Sitter space.

Their method includes charges that are not conserved because the boundary leaks. It also includes charges tied to corner terms where boundaries meet. The charges stay finite for any boundary conditions, they show. New charges appear for a wider class of field setups, aiding gravity research. Leaky charges reflect real physics, where fields cross borders rather than staying boxed in.
arxiv-2512-03270:
Thin sheets wrinkle and fold in ways that are hard to model. Yael Cohen, Animesh Pandey, Yafei Zhang, Cy Maor, and Michael Moshe offer a new formulation in this 2025 work. Such sheets range from graphene to biological membranes.

Standard weakly nonlinear theories need small slopes and fail when deflections grow large, even if strain stays small. The authors use a curvature potential formulation for thin elastic sheets. A better theory could predict folding in soft materials and tissues. It may also guide design of flexible devices. Graphene and cell membranes both punish weak theories, since their deflections grow large fast.
arxiv-2512-03670:
Vuong Bui and Matthieu Rosenfeld prove a theorem about avoiding repeated patterns in words built from changing alphabets. A cube is the same block written three times in a row, and cube-free words dodge it forever. Their 2025 paper lets every position draw from its own two-letter alphabet.

Whatever sequence of binary alphabets is chosen, an infinite cube-free word respecting them always exists. Counting arguments show such words are plentiful, growing exponentially with length. Better still, when the alphabet sequence is computable, one of these words is computable too. Its nth letter can be produced in time polynomial in n, turning an existence proof into an algorithm.
arxiv-2512-03770:
How a crowd reaches consensus is a classic puzzle in the study of collective behaviour. Xingyu Guo, Xiaoyang Wang, and Lingxiao Wang give the puzzle a quantum twist in a 2025 preprint on social physics. They build models of opinion dynamics that run on quantum hardware available today, using superposition, measurement collapse, and entanglement as modelling ingredients.

Unlike many quantum proposals, their models can be solved exactly, which makes the results interpretable. The framework lets the authors vary network connectivity in a controlled way and watch how consensus formation responds. They demonstrate the approach with practical quantum circuits. Representative cases were validated on IBM Quantum devices for a simple open chain of agents. The authors see the work as an opening for quantum-enhanced social modelling on near-term machines, aimed at complex systems where classical simulation struggles.
arxiv-2512-04070:
Quark-gluon plasma, the soup of particles filling the infant universe, can also be set spinning in theory, and rotation changes its thermodynamics. V. Braguta and colleagues compute those changes from first principles in a 2025 lattice gauge theory preprint. Using numerical simulations of SU(3) Yang-Mills theory, the pure-gluon version of the strong force, they track free energy and angular momentum across temperatures.

The response to slow rotation is organised as a series in angular velocity. Its leading term is a specific moment of inertia; the next is a specific deformation. Both surprise: just above the phase transition, they come out negative. At higher temperatures the deformation turns positive. The calculations span a broad temperature range and several boundary conditions, giving phenomenologists firm numbers instead of model guesses.
arxiv-2512-04970:
Leonid Pogorelyuk, Niels Bracher, and Aaron Verkleeren pilot a family of stable contrastive losses that teach each pixel of an image a rich descriptor of itself. The descriptors are overcomplete, carrying more dimensions than the minimum. They aim to hold both what a point means and where it sits geometrically. With them, matching the same point across two views becomes precise, and no momentum-based teacher-student training is needed. Their 2025 arXiv paper tests the idea in synthetic two- and three-dimensional worlds.

Both experiments confirm the intended traits: the descriptors stay stable across viewpoint changes while keeping semantic content readable. View-invariant, meaningful pixel codes could anchor augmented reality, robot grasping, and medical image alignment, where the same spot must be found again under new light and angle. A small pilot with clean properties earns a wider trial.
arxiv-2512-05070:
Samuel Howard, Nikolas Nüsken, and Jakiw Pidstrigach tackle diffusion bridges: random paths that must start and end at prescribed states. Simulating such conditioned motion matters across the sciences, and it is hardest exactly where it matters most — rare events, which unconditioned simulations almost never reach. Existing learning methods often require differentiating through simulated trajectories, a costly and fragile step.

The authors build their method on a self-consistency property of the optimal control that steers the process: the right steering at any moment must agree with the steering computed from neighboring moments. Their algorithm learns the conditioned dynamics iteratively and online, checking itself as it goes, and never needs to differentiate through a simulation. It performs strongly across a range of test settings. The paper also ties the framework to recent progress in stochastic control more broadly, suggesting the idea travels beyond bridges.
arxiv-2512-05170:
Hubert Lau Sze Chun and Joseph Conlon study cosmic strings whose tension changes with time. Cosmic strings are hypothetical thread-like relics of the early universe, and recent work showed that if a string's tension falls, its loops can grow and possibly link up across space. Earlier studies handled this analytically for tidy, circular loops. This work extends the analysis to realistic, non-circular loops in an expanding universe, using numerical simulation.

A key step is a mathematical equivalence: a varying-tension string in our expanding universe behaves like an ordinary fixed-tension string in a universe with a modified expansion history. With that bridge, the authors deploy numerical solvers and machine learning techniques to follow loops whose size is close to the Hubble scale — roughly the size of the visible universe. The study opens the generic, messy cases of varying-tension strings to the same scrutiny circular loops received.
arxiv-2512-05370:
Habib Ammari, Erik Orvehed Hiltunen, Ping Liu, Borui Miao, and Yi Zhu develop a fast way to compute the guided waves along line defects in high-contrast periodic materials. Such subwavelength modes matter for building resonators and waveguides, but the governing eigenvalue problem is posed on an unbounded domain and is costly to attack head-on. The authors recast it with layer potentials, with the allowed frequencies in a capacitance matrix borrowed from electrostatics.

Their theorem shows the off-diagonal entries of that matrix decay fast with distance, for the ordinary and the quasi-periodic versions. Fast decay licenses a banded approximation — keep only the near entries — with controlled error, and that is a tight-binding approach for defects that stretch to infinity. Experiments confirm the decay. They compare full and banded matrices on defect and dimerized-interface configurations, showing the shortcut reproduces the spectral properties practitioners need.
arxiv-2512-05870:
Daniel Miliate and Ashlie Martini hunt for new liquid lubricants that can survive the vacuum of space. Moving assemblies in spacecraft need oils that flow back to contact points through years of high speed cycles. Almost none qualify: most liquids evaporate too fast in vacuum, and the few that pass carry design limiting flaws. Their machine learning approach predicts the key property, vapor pressure, directly from molecular structure.

The models learn from two sources at once: high throughput molecular dynamics simulations and experimental databases. They are built to stay interpretable, so structure to vapor pressure links can be read off directly. From those links, the authors identify what makes a molecule stay put in vacuum, and propose several candidate molecules as promising space lubricants. The work turns a scarce, folklore guided search into a screening pipeline. Every new qualified lubricant loosens a long standing design constraint.
arxiv-2512-06070:
Omar Alsheikh, Efekan Kökcü, Bojko Bakalov, and Alexander Kemper speed up the compiling of quantum simulations. First, the desired unitary must be translated into native gates. Cartan decomposition yields circuits of time independent depth, but finding them is a heavy classical optimization. RedCarD partitions the dynamical Lie algebra further, splitting the big optimization into smaller independent subproblems.

The structure also lets the cost function be evaluated on the quantum computer. As a demonstration, the team synthesized evolution for a four site Ising model. The circuits ran on IBM devices and Quantinuum's H1-1. Such hybrids are the working shape of near term quantum computing. Shrinking synthesis cost moves the whole pipeline.
arxiv-2512-06970: Domenico Valloni works in arithmetic geometry on a smooth surface that fibers in elliptic curves over a line, over a number field. The surface is assumed to have at least one singular fiber and a chosen section. Valloni builds a smooth model of the surface over part of the ring of integers, then studies its Chow group, which records cycles up to a standard equivalence. The main result shows that the kernel of the natural map between the model's Chow group and the surface's own is finitely generated.
arxiv-2512-07170:
Jiayang Li and co-authors unify image fusion, the blending of pictures from different sensors into one richer image, inside a single instruction-following model. Fusion today is a zoo of task-specific networks that cannot take direction from a user and struggle with bad light, shifted colors, or uneven exposure. There are no ground-truth fused images to train on, and data sets are small. DiTFuse, built on a diffusion transformer, reads two images plus a written instruction in one shared space.

Training uses masked-image exercises across many kinds of degradation, teaching the model to align the two sources. Restore what each modality can support, and select features the task needs, all without ground truth. A curated instruction set at several levels of detail gives users fine control.
arxiv-2512-07270:
Arnold Lafond-Saunier and co-authors test whether a serrated leading edge, a row of small teeth along a wing's front, helps a wing fly better near the ground. Their wing is a two-section planar design with a trapezoidal planform, studied at low Reynolds numbers where small aircraft and drones live. Simulations were checked against experiments, both away from the ground and in ground effect, the cushion of extra lift a surface provides.

Away from the ground the teeth clearly helped: maximum lift rose and the stall arrived later, at a higher angle. The cause is a train of small counter-rotating vortices the serrations shed, which re-energize the sluggish air hugging the wing's surface. Near the ground the picture muddied. Both straight and serrated wings gained efficiency, but the simulations showed the serrated wing losing lift at high angles where experiments disagreed.
arxiv-2512-07370:
Jack Helliwell, Ludovic Scyboz, and Peter Skands fix the bookkeeping of parton showers, the simulations that turn a single high-energy collision into the spray of particles detectors record. Each branching in a shower kicks momentum somewhere, and where the recoil lands shapes the predictions. Customarily one parton absorbs it alone. The authors let groups of partons, jets, share the recoil, a freedom that should better match how the underlying theory conserves momentum.

Their realization works inside a dipole shower, using angular ordering to decide the jet groupings on the fly, with no separate clustering step at each branching. The crucial question is accuracy: showers are graded by how faithfully they reproduce known patterns. And the new scheme passes the tests for next-to-leading logarithmic accuracy, in both fixed-order numerical checks and resummation checks across many observables.
arxiv-2512-07470:
Cemile Nur and Oktay Veliev wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on a classic quantum model. The Kronig-Penney model pictures an electron moving through a row of repeating barriers. The authors study the small energy levels, called Dirichlet eigenvalues, of that system.

They begin by sharpening older asymptotic formulas for these levels. The new formulas are written directly in terms of the potential itself. For potentials of bounded variation, the first two terms stand cleanly apart from the error. The Kronig-Penney potential then serves as a worked illustration. Next, the authors derive equations that compute the small eigenvalues step by step. They prove a fixed point iteration can find every one of them. The Banach fixed point theorem backs the method with firm error bounds. A numerical example closes the paper and shows the scheme in action.
arxiv-2512-07570:
Jens Ahrens wrote this 2025 teaching document on ambisonics, a way of capturing full surround sound. It is the first part of a two-part introduction tied to a practical master course. Readers who want to work with ambisonics, not just read about it, are the audience.

True to its subtitle, this part contains no mathematics at all. Ahrens builds an intuitive feel for the core concept instead. He explains what ambisonic signals are and how they are captured. He then shows what changes can be applied to those signals. A final section covers how the sound reaches a listener's ears. Plenty of audio examples run alongside the text to make ideas concrete. A companion video presentation is available for the same material. The second part, published separately, carries the full mathematical detail. Together, the pair lets practitioners start fast and deepen later.
arxiv-2512-07970:
Idel Waisberg, Ygal Klein, and Boaz Katz wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on a bright nearby triple system. Lambda Ophiuchi's inner pair orbits in weeks; an outer companion takes over a century. Such nested systems can pump each other's orbital shapes dramatically.

Those von Zeipel-Kozai-Lidov oscillations trade tilt for stretch in the inner orbit. Constraining both orbits has long frustrated observers. The team combines a century-spanning visual orbit catalog with new interferometry. Very Large Telescope measurements pin down the quick inner orbit directly. The two orbits run retrograde and sit nearly perpendicular to each other. That geometry guarantees the inner binary is oscillating right now. Pure Newtonian point-mass evolution says the pair should have merged already. Relativity, tides, and rotational bulges intervene to modulate the cycles. Slaved precession keeps the dynamics solvable in semi-analytic form. Unknown spin tilts set how violent the eccentricity swings can get.
arxiv-2512-08070:
Hercules H Santana and E V L de Mello, condensed matter physicists in Brazil, posted a theory paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is the cuprate superconductors, a famous family of materials whose behavior still lacks a complete theory. They aim to explain the whole doping range at once, from the undoped insulator to the overdoped metal.

Their proposal centers on a spinodal, or charge separation, transition that begins near the pseudogap temperature. In their picture, the free energy forms an array of wells holding static holes at half filling. Added mobile holes settle into those wells with alternating high and low density, creating the charge density wave pattern. Holes confined in small regions then develop local superconducting strength, forming a granular superconductor. Coupling between the grains, tied to the local superfluid density, completes their unified account.
arxiv-2512-08270:
Jaisal Patel, Yunzhe Chen, Kaiwen He, and colleagues, researchers in finance and machine learning, posted an evaluation study on arXiv in December 2025. They test top reasoning models on the Chartered Financial Analyst exams, a demanding three level professional qualification. Earlier studies found that plain language models did poorly on these tests, raising doubt about their use in serious finance work.

The team ran nearly a thousand mock exam questions across all three levels, using pass marks from the earlier studies. Most models cleared every level this time. Gemini 3 Pro led overall and set a record score on the first level, while GPT 5 led the second level. Gemini models also topped the third level, on both multiple choice and written style questions. The authors conclude that modern reasoning models now perform at a level earlier models could not approach. That shift matters for how the finance industry may use these systems.
arxiv-2512-08370:
Van Nham Phan, a condensed matter physicist, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about excitonic condensation in two dimensional electron hole systems. An excitonic condensate forms when bound electron hole pairs act together as one quantum state. With Rashba spin orbit coupling and a magnetic field in play, several kinds of condensate compete, some plain and some carrying topological character.

Using an unrestricted Hartree Fock method, Phan computes the competing order parameters and the Chern number self consistently. The ground state map, over field strength and interaction strength, shows a spin up triplet condensate with nonzero Chern number. It appears in its own region, away from the trivial singlet and spin down triplet phases. Strong spin polarized fluctuations also show up just before condensation, visible in the dynamical response. He suggests distorted Janus monolayers or twisted layered structures as realistic places to look for this topological phase.
arxiv-2512-08470:
Ksenia Shagalov, David Feldstein Bofill, Leo Uhre Jakobsen, and a large team of physicists in Denmark posted an experimental study on arXiv in December 2025. They build a new superconducting circuit element for quantum computing: a tunnel junction placed in series with a SQUID loop. The combination gives a Josephson potential whose harmonic content, the mix of tones in its response, can be tuned strongly with magnetic flux.

Through spectroscopy of the first four qubit transitions, checked against an effective model, the team resolved a second harmonic reaching about a tenth of the fundamental strength. They also found a flux sweet spot where an unwanted dispersive shift vanishes, by balancing couplings to two internal modes. Such tunability points toward better protected qubits and custom nonlinear devices: harmonic content becomes a design variable, not a fixed given.
arxiv-2512-08570:
Manuel Adams, Jose M Amigo, and Klaus Lehnertz, researchers on complex systems in Germany and Spain, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They revisit transcripts, a tool introduced in 2009 for studying how time series from interacting systems influence each other. Transcripts exploit algebraic relations between the ordinal patterns hidden in two signals, and estimators built on them can report the strength, direction, and complexity of an interaction.

Despite that promise, the estimators have seen little use on real world data. The authors demonstrate them on coupled model systems of varying complexity, showing what the measures capture. Then they turn to multichannel, multiday recordings of human brain activity, separating how brain regions interact across vigilance states. The estimators reveal structure in brain dynamics that standard tools miss, making the case for wider use.
arxiv-2512-08670: A Colesanti, M Focardi, P Guan, and P Salani study the mixed Christoffel problem for smooth convex bodies, giving conditions that are enough to solve it. Their key step is a constant rank theorem for a linear elliptic equation on the sphere, following an approach first used for the classic Christoffel problem. That theorem ensures the solution is truly geometric, namely the support function of a smooth convex body.
arxiv-2512-08970:
Saurabh and a large Event Horizon Telescope team probe emission from the base of the jet of the black hole in M87,. New telescopes added to the array in a recent campaign provide key intermediate baselines. Those baselines probe scales earlier work could not constrain.

The team analyzes closure phases, and models the jet base as a simple offset Gaussian feature away from the compact ring. A faint feature is found in the direction of the large scale jet,. Its flux is low, which implies most missing flux must come from even larger scales. Brighter compact emission at those scales is ruled out, and complex models are not favored. Because only two intermediate baselines are available, the feature is treated as an upper limit on jet base flux. More coverage is needed.
arxiv-2512-09670:
Gil Weissman, Amir Ivry, and Israel Cohen present an automated tip-and-cue framework for tasking Earth observation satellites. Modern constellations offer many sensors and fast retasking, but choosing what to image, when, and with which satellite is a growing scheduling problem. In their scheme, tips come from data or analysis of earlier imagery, flagging targets in space and time, and cues are the imaging tasks formed in response.

The system generates tasks on its own, and schedules them across multiple satellites by optimizing utility functions that reflect each observation's expected value. It then processes the imagery with AI models, including object detectors and vision-language models. Structured reports support interpretation and feed tips back into the loop. The team demonstrates the framework on maritime vessel tracking, predicting ship trajectories from identification system data and cueing observations. They note the architecture extends to smart-city monitoring and disaster response.
arxiv-2512-10070:
Ben R. M. Tragheim and colleagues solve the magnetic structure of an unusual manganese oxide. The material is a quadruple perovskite with mercury and sodium sharing one site. It shows a G-type pattern of charge and orbital ordering unlike its calcium, strontium, cadmium, or lead cousins. Using powder neutron diffraction guided by symmetry analysis, the team determined how the manganese magnetic moments arrange. On one set of sites the order is G-type antiferromagnetic, neighbors pointing oppositely. On the other set, moments follow an up up down down pattern.

The authors explore how that second pattern switches on, through coupling between structural distortions and magnetism. The results add evidence for the exotic ordering states quadruple manganites can host. They also highlight the special chemistry of mercury: its presence stabilizes states the other divalent cations do not.
arxiv-2512-10170:
Lucas Dunker and colleagues fix a quiet flaw in automated audio captioning: models sound confident even when their captions are wrong. Two habits cause it. Evaluation rewards word overlap, not meaning, and models output no calibrated estimate of their uncertainty. The authors augment a captioning model built on Whisper with a learned confidence head that reads the decoder's states. Correctness is then redefined semantically: captions count as right when embedding based measures of audio text and sentence similarity say the meaning matches, not when the wording coincides.

With that definition, calibration error can be measured honestly. On the Clotho v2 dataset, confidence guided beam search, which uses the model's own confidence during generation, cut the semantic calibration error dramatically compared with greedy decoding. It went from a large value to a small one. Caption quality on standard metrics improved at the same time, so honesty cost nothing in accuracy.
arxiv-2512-10370:
Ziying Zhang, Quanming Yao, and Yaqing Wang study a weak spot in recommendation systems. Brand-new items that have barely been used yet. Their 2025 paper argues that most methods treat such emerging items as if they had almost no history, which misses how their user interactions build up bit by bit over time.

The authors propose EmerFlow, a method that uses a large language model to enrich a new item's raw features and build a clear profile for it. That profile is then matched to the space the recommender already uses, and fresh interactions refine it through meta-learning. Tests in fields such as movies and medicines show EmerFlow beating older methods at suggesting new items people actually want.
arxiv-2512-10470:
Kaleb Bacztub and co-authors built a rogue Wi-Fi access point to test whether standard defences would notice it. In the Evil Twin attack, a fake network copies a real one's name, lures users to connect, and then intercepts traffic or harvests passwords through a false login page. Wireless networks carry so much daily traffic that the blind spots matter.

Planned on Raspberry Pi hardware, the project moved to a virtual setup after compatibility trouble, and used the Wifipumpkin3 tool to deploy a captive portal that did collect credentials from connected devices. The open-source Suricata intrusion detection system never flagged the attack. The authors detail the build and the evasion tricks used, and argue that traditional detection tools miss local wireless management frame attacks almost entirely.
arxiv-2512-10670:
Ignacio Acedo and co-authors take quantum machine learning down to the level of control pulses. Variational quantum circuits, the usual design, are suffering from trainability and noise problems on today's noisy intermediate-scale hardware, enough that their long-term promise is in doubt. Programming the machine's native pulses directly is a less explored alternative that stays closer to the physics.

The authors build a pulse-based version of data re-uploading, a scheme that feeds the data into the system repeatedly, with the trainable parameters living inside the pulse shapes themselves. Benchmarked on a simulated superconducting transmon processor with realistic noise, the pulse model beat its gate-based counterpart on test accuracy and generalisation under the same noise. As noise was cranked up, the pulse version held its fidelity longer, showing stronger resistance to decoherence and control errors.
arxiv-2512-10870:
Hong-Xu Liu, Zi-Xuan Yi, and Hong-Jian He examine scattering of gravitons in a three dimensional gravity theory where gravitons gain a topological mass. They rewrite the theory using a Weyl transformation that adds an extra field, then quantise it in a standard framework. In the massless limit, physical degrees of freedom shift from the graviton to that added field.

From this they establish a new equivalence theorem linking graviton scattering at high energy to scattering of the added field. The theorem explains striking cancellations that make large energy terms drop out of multi-graviton amplitudes. Using a double copy method, they also build three and four point amplitudes from simpler gauge theory results, checking the cancellations directly.
arxiv-2512-10970:
Yulei Wang and colleagues study a wireless system that uses movable pinching antennas to support quiet, hard to detect communication. Devices can harvest energy from ambient signals and bounce a reply back, a method called backscatter communication. Flexible antenna placement helps create clear line of sight links for that reply.

The authors set up a problem that maximises the uplink covert rate while keeping the link reliable and hidden from a randomly placed eavesdropper. Their alternating optimisation method adjusts transmit power and antenna positions together. Tests show the design eases the double near-far problem, where distance hurts both energy harvesting and the returning signal at once. It improves both downlink energy capture and uplink data transfer while staying covert.
arxiv-2512-11370:
Edoardo Mainini studies a weighted minimum seeking approach for non-local diffusion models with an added forcing term. In non-local diffusion, change at a point depends on a whole region around it, not just its nearest neighbours. Such models describe heat like spreading in several modern settings.

Minimum seeking methods restate a model as a search for a lowest energy state. That restatement can single out the physically right answer among several candidates. Mainini uses it to give a clear rule for picking answers built through elliptic in time smoothing of these heat like models.
arxiv-2512-11470:
Bowen Ding and a large team map how expert answer traces should be used when training language models for math reasoning. Post training mixes guided fine tuning on worked answers with reinforcement learning, but the two consume expert trajectories very differently. Their plasticity ceiling setup splits a model's final ceiling into the base laid by guided training and the extra headroom reinforcement learning can still add.

Benchmarking established that running guided training first and reinforcement learning second beats synchronised approaches, which suffer instability and premature convergence. The best handover point is when guided training is stable or just mildly overfit. More guided data raised the ultimate potential, contrary to a popular less is more belief, while harder trajectories multiplied the gains from that data. The lowest validation loss during guided training reliably flagged which trajectories would maximise the final ceiling, giving trainers actionable choice rules.
arxiv-2512-11770:
S O Kara folds a hypothetical light particle into the standard theory of atomic nuclei. The particle would be leptophilic, coupling to leptons like electrons and to protons. Kara integrates it out to get a clean current to current force inside nuclear energy density functional theory, the workhorse model of nuclei.

The new force shifts proton and lepton energy levels together, changing how dense matter balances protons and electrons. In uniform matter, proton share and stiffness shift by percent level amounts. In single nuclei, neutron skin thickness moves by a thousandth to a hundredth of a femtometer, near what labs can now measure. Nuclei thus become probes for lepton sector physics.
arxiv-2512-11970:
Mohamed M Anber shows that odd shaped spaces can expose hidden flaws in quantum field theories. A theory anomaly is a symmetry that quantum effects break. Standard tests on closed four dimensional spaces miss some anomalies entirely.

Anber places the theory on an Eguchi-Hanson space, an asymptotically locally Euclidean space with a self intersecting sphere and a boundary carrying torsion. Turning on flux for one symmetry and twisting another reveals the anomaly through a five dimensional mapping torus. The reading mixes bulk terms with a boundary eta invariant. Some infrared spectra that pass all standard anomaly checks fail this one. Such spectra thus cannot be the full low energy truth for their theories.
arxiv-2512-12070:
Jie Ma and co-authors harden radio fingerprint identification against channel and receiver changes. The method names IoT devices by hardware flaws in their radio signals. In the field, though, changing channels and differing receivers smear those fingerprints, and labeled data is scarce.

Their three stage design first pretrains a feature extractor with contrastive learning on spectrograms, a form chosen to split device flaws from channel effects. A Siamese classifier then trains with augmentation and contrastive loss to resist both channel and receiver shifts. On three public LoRa sets plus one of their own, accuracy passed 90 percent in dynamic non line of sight scenes with only 20 packets per device for tuning.
arxiv-2512-12270:
Priyankush Ghosh and five co-authors build a fuller sulfur chemistry network for Venus like worlds in a 2025 paper. Sulfur controls air structure, clouds, and makeup on Venus. Yet many sulfur reactions lack good rate data, above all under hot, carbon dioxide rich conditions, and models often use incomplete sets.

The team computes rates for ground and excited sulfur reacting with carbon dioxide, and adds them to the XODIAC model of Venus. Effects above 60 km stay minor on Venus, but a 1 ppm surface sulfur source lifts S3 and S4 levels by 1 to 2 orders of magnitude and fits data better. Exo-Venus worlds under strong starlight show bigger shifts.
arxiv-2512-12470:
Vitalii Sliusar and eight co-authors review how light coherence can serve astrophysics in a 2025 paper. The Hanbury Brown-Twiss effect, found in the 1950s, first measured star sizes through intensity correlations at split detectors. Later work on photon bunching in incoherent light helped found quantum optics as a field.

Placing both detectors at one spot gives a zero baseline correlation that, once detector effects are removed, yields the second order coherence function in time. That function ignores the source's size and brightness pattern, probing the emission process itself. It can separate thermal, synchrotron, bremsstrahlung, and stimulated emission. The authors present coherence as a complementary messenger for astronomy.
arxiv-2512-12770:
Thales Sales Almeida, Rodrigo Nogueira, and Helio Pedrini test whether data choice beats data size in adapting a language model to Portuguese in a 2025 paper. Their base model, Curio 7B, comes from LLaMA-2 and was trained on 100 billion Portuguese tokens from the ClassiCC-PT corpus, the largest such effort above 3 billion parameters so far.

A second model, Curio-Edu 7B, trained only on the educational and STEM filtered subset, just 10 billion tokens. Despite using 10 percent of the data and 20 percent of the compute, it surpassed the full corpus model in their evaluations. The result shows data selection can be fundamental when adapting models to a language they barely saw before. Both models are released in public.
arxiv-2512-12870:
Pouya Ahadi and co-authors work on active learning, where a model asks human labelers to label only the most useful examples. Labeling is costly, so each request should count. In practice, though, labels often contain errors, since labelers differ in skill.

Uncertain examples are the most useful to label, yet they are also the most likely to be labeled wrong. The authors study how to assign labelers and choose samples together under this tension. Their aim is to match hard cases to the right labelers and to sample in a way that limits the harm of noisy labels. The work speaks to teams that build training data with mixed expert help.
arxiv-2512-13070:
Bizhe Bai and co-authors present M-GRPO, a method to steady self-supervised reinforcement learning for language models. Such training lets a model improve its reasoning without costly human labels. But over long runs the policy can collapse, with performance dropping fast.

Simply drawing more samples only delays that collapse, they show. M-GRPO anchors training to a slow-moving momentum model, giving a stable target. A second tool filters out low-entropy trajectories by an interquartile rule, which protects the diversity of the policy. Together, the two ideas kept training stable and reached top scores on several reasoning benchmarks in their tests.
arxiv-2512-13370:
Yang-Hui He, Alexander Kasprzyk, Q Le, and Dmitrii Riabchenko use machine learning to discover champion linear codes, codes that match or beat the best known minimum Hamming distance for their size. Such codes protect data in communication and storage. Finding champions by brute search is infeasible, since the space of codes is vast.

They train a transformer to predict a code's minimum distance, then pair it with a genetic algorithm that breeds candidate codes. The predictor prunes the search to promising regions. The method applies to families such as Reed-Muller, BCH, algebraic geometry, and toric codes, and may extend to quantum codes.
arxiv-2512-14270:
Zixin Tang and five coauthors present CaFe TeleVision in a 2025 paper on robot teleoperation, where a human controls a robot from afar. Current systems often suffer from low efficiency and poor ergonomics, especially in hard tasks, which raises user strain and errors.

Their system uses a coarse to fine control method in the retargeting module to bridge gaps between human and robot workspaces, improving both speed and physical comfort. An on demand situated visualization method streams immersive feedback with the right visual cues and cuts the mental load of many views. Built on a humanoid collaborative robot, it was tested on six hard two handed tasks. In a study with 24 users, task load fell and acceptance rose.
arxiv-2512-14370:
Florian Voss and Uwe Thiele model the motion of chemically fueled liquid drops in a 2025 paper. The drops partially wet a surface and are covered by surfactants that react autocatalytically, meaning the reaction feeds itself and drives motion.

Their thermodynamically consistent continuum model links the reaction network, surface stresses from the Marangoni effect, and the flow that follows. Ambient chemostats feed the loop that keeps the drop out of equilibrium. The drops show a ladder of motility modes: shuttling, bipedal, rotational, intermittently chaotic, and fully chaotic motion. The authors map the non equilibrium phase diagram for these modes. They show the growing complexity comes from competing length scales in the system.
arxiv-2512-14570:
Zhaonan Dong and Tanvi Wadhawan sharpen a basic estimate used in finite element computations. Inverse trace inequalities bound how large a polynomial can be on the face of a triangular element compared with its size inside. Their polynomials live on a simplex and are orthogonal to all lower-degree polynomials, a restriction earlier constants ignored.

By expanding in orthogonal polynomials and studying eigenvalues of face mass matrices, they compute the best possible constants exactly. The new factor depends on the gap between the polynomial's degree and the removed lower degrees, replacing the classical blunter factor. The improvement feeds directly into error estimates for hybrid Galerkin methods used in engineering simulation.
arxiv-2512-14970:
A. V. Kitaev proposes a fresh route to the far field behavior of Painlevé equations, a famous family of nonlinear equations whose solutions define new functions. Knowing how solutions behave at extremes, their asymptotics, is central to using them in physics and math. Kitaev's idea is to write solutions as formal series in two variables.

The series has the form of a sum over powers of one variable, with coefficients that are rational functions of the other. Generating functions built this way organize the asymptotic information in a new form. The approach is applied to the third degenerate Painlevé equation as a worked case. The study is a methods paper for specialists, offering a new algebraic handle on a classic problem.
arxiv-2512-15070:
Alexander While and a coauthor ask whether quantum computers could help spot wasted symmetry in optimization problems. Mixed integer programming solvers slow down when a formulation has symmetries, since the search repeats equivalent work. Finding those symmetries is itself a hard computing task.

Quantum machines are promising but small, so problems must be written compactly. The authors build several QUBO formulations, the standard input format for quantum optimizers, for the symmetry detection task. They offer full, reduced, decomposed, and QUBO-Plus versions to shrink the needed size. Experiments on the MIPLIB 2017 benchmark set estimate how much quantum hardware practical problems would require. The study maps a possible quantum route to a real bottleneck in optimization, and prices it honestly.
arxiv-2512-15470:
Andrew Cleary, Qi Wang, and Tamer Zaki propose estimating turbulent flow from sparse readings by working in a learned latent space in a 2025 paper. Data assimilation fills in a full flow field from limited measures, but doing it in the full state space often adds false small scale motion.

Their method optimizes the starting field in a low dimensional latent space learned by autoencoders, rather than in the full space. For coarse measures of two dimensional Kolmogorov flow, it cuts relative error by two orders of magnitude over standard assimilation. Small scales come out more faithful, and the method stays robust when measures are noisy.
arxiv-2512-15870:
Mathias Garny, Florian Niedermann, and Martin S. Sloth offer an early-universe account of a puzzling galaxy survey result in this 2025 cosmology paper. DESI DR2 data have mostly been read as evidence that dark energy changes over time, even crossing into a phantom regime. The trio point out that dark acoustic oscillations, ripples in the dark sector, could sit close in scale to the familiar baryon acoustic oscillations. That closeness can bias the peak used to measure cosmic distances.

Allowing for that shift, a dark oscillation with percent-level amplitude reconciles DESI DR2 with Planck 2018 and Pantheon+ supernova data. The fit gain matches what evolving dark energy achieves. Such a feature was already predicted by a scenario where dark matter and dark radiation decouple before recombination, also proposed to ease the Hubble tension. Future DESI and Euclid data can test the idea.
arxiv-2512-16070:
Xin Wang, Zhenhao Li, and Zishuo Ding test a new use for language models in a paper on software engineering released on arXiv in 2025. Modern software has huge numbers of settings, and its speed depends on them in tangled ways. Building a model of that behavior needs smart sampling, but classic samplers cannot read manuals or balance several goals at once.

The team built LLM4Perf, a feedback-driven framework where a language model picks which configurations to test. Across four real, highly configurable systems, the method won in 77 of 112 scenarios, about 68.8 percent. Its edge came from pruning the search space and refining strategy from feedback. That pruning even improved classic baselines in about 91.5 percent of cases. The paper maps which model and setting choices make the sampler work best.
arxiv-2512-16170:
Weihua Liu classifies symmetry theorems in probability in a 2025 mathematics paper on arXiv. De Finetti-type theorems say that when a sequence of random variables has enough symmetry, it must arise from a simple random mixture. Versions exist in both classical probability and free probability, a noncommutative cousin used in random matrix theory.

Liu shows every nontrivial finite sequence carries a maximal symmetry of a special kind, described by a Woronowicz C star-algebra, the structure behind compact quantum groups. That yields a probability-based way to classify those quantum groups. He then classifies all de Finetti-type theorems for star-random variables under such symmetries. Only finitely many types exist, and they match the so-called easy quantum groups of Banica and Speicher. The result ties probability, algebra, and quantum symmetry into one tidy list.
arxiv-2512-16570:
Dimitris Fotakis, Charalampos Platanos, and Thanos Tolias tackle online resource allocation, where buyers arrive one by one and ask for sets of items. Each buyer has a value drawn from a known chance model, and the seller must decide at once, with no knowledge of who comes next.

The focus is on fixed, nameless bundle prices when buyers value items as packages, so plain per-item prices fail. The authors give one pricing method that works across auctions and network routing, with scores that improve fast as item copies grow. Matching lower bounds show that no online method can do much better.
arxiv-2512-16670:
Ole Beisswenger, Jan-Niklas Dihlmann, and Hendrik Lensch present FrameDiffuser, a neural method that turns geometry and material data, called a G-buffer, into photo-like frames for games and interactive scenes. Past tools either made each frame alone, losing steadiness over time, or needed whole clips at once.

FrameDiffuser works step by step, guided by the G-buffer and its own last frame, so output stays steady over hundreds to thousands of frames. It pairs a ControlNet for structure with a ControlLoRA for time coherence, trained in three stages. The team tunes one model per scene, trading broad reach for speed and strong light, shadow, and reflection quality in that scene.
arxiv-2512-16770:
William English and coauthors present GinSign, a tool that turns plain English system rules into temporal logic, the formal language used to check that machines behave as required. Past tools often guessed the link between words and system atoms, or got it wrong.

GinSign learns that grounding step on its own. It first predicts the predicate label for each lifted phrase, then picks the typed constants that fit, turning free writing into a sorting task that small masked language models can run. Across domains, tools without grounding made logic that looked right but meant the wrong thing. GinSign reached 95.5 percent grounded match scores, 1.4 times the best past score.
arxiv-2512-17070:
Zahra Ahmadi and Mahdiyar Noorbala examine the noise that drives stochastic inflation, the frame treating early-universe field wiggles in classical chance terms. Textbook work, from Starobinsky on, assumes white noise, a memory-free driver, thanks to several background beliefs.

Loosening the exact de Sitter background keeps noise white, with a time-varying strength. Loosening the sharp window function or the Bunch-Davies start state can color the noise, giving it memory. For a piecewise linear window they compute the spectrum and memory in full. A colored case from the start state must be built from two-particle pieces, and that route also breaks Gaussianity, unlike the other two.
arxiv-2512-17170:
Dmitry Pasechnyuk-Vilensky and Martin Takáč build one algebra frame for a pattern that shows up across math: a primal problem and its dual mirror. Their tool comes from homological algebra, a field that measures how structures fail to fit together exactly. They call a map ethic when going to the dual twice returns it unchanged.

Breaks in that round trip are counted by groups called Ext groups, arranged in layers. The first layer matches the familiar gap between a problem and its dual in optimization. Higher layers list deeper blocks. The same frame then covers graph duality, coding, dynamical systems, and choice problems. One test for exactness, with a ranked list of what blocks it, is the payoff.
arxiv-2512-17470:
Dennis Gross, Jørn Eirik Betten, and Helge Spieker carry a curious effect from labeling tasks into step-by-step decision making. The Rashomon effect names a set of models that give the same answers for different inner reasons, each leaning on different clues. For a decision agent, the echo is stranger: many policies act exactly alike, step for step, yet reason from different features inside.

Proving two policies truly match is hard when the world itself rolls dice. The team uses formal verification to compare each policy's full pattern of likely behavior. Their experiments confirm the effect is real for sequential tasks. Mixing policies from the lookalike set survived shifts in the data better than any single one. Looser policies drawn from the set also cut the cost of safety checks.
arxiv-2512-17770:
Axel Brandenburg and three co-authors rethink how a star's or galaxy's magnetism leaks into the space around it. Textbooks cap a dynamo with a tidy current-free field, in which the dipole pattern fades slowest with distance. Real exteriors are turbulent and conduct poorly, so the field does not settle tidily; it diffuses outward instead.

Under diffusion, the ordering flips: a quadrupole pattern can grow a toroidal part that fades even more slowly than the dipole. The field still dies off fast beyond a magnetosphere boundary. That kills one hopeful idea, that galaxies collectively seeded the magnetism found in cosmic voids; those void fields must be primordial leftovers. Radio telescopes may test the picture, since quadrupole glow should ring evenly around its galaxy.
arxiv-2512-17870:
Alexander Keimer, Lukas Pflug, and Jakob Rodestock study control problems where flow at each point depends on the whole crowd, not just nearby points. Traffic and flocking often behave this way: speed here answers to density far ahead. They ask whether a best control exists for such systems, and what happens as the far view shrinks to a local one.

For a broad class of set ups, with freedom to tune the start state, the speed law, and the reach of the influence, they prove a best control does exist. As the reach fades to a point, those best controls settle onto the best controls of the matching local problem. Number tests close the paper.
arxiv-2512-18970:
Tuo Wu and six co-authors make the theory of vehicle-to-everything wireless honest about small hardware. Fluid antennas shift position to dodge fading, and smart surfaces bounce signals around obstacles. But existing performance analyses assume huge surfaces, via the Central Limit Theorem. Real deployments cannot afford that assumption, constrained by cost and city infrastructure. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and accepted by IEEE Transactions on Vehicular Technology, fixes the finite case.

Using a Gamma distribution approximation, they derive a closed-form expression for the outage probability, the chance a vehicle loses its link. Simulations confirm the new formula tracks reality far better than the old asymptotic one, especially for small surfaces. Network engineers designing roadside units on real budgets now have numbers they can trust before pouring concrete.
arxiv-2512-19270:
Zhaoyang Liu, Weitao Zhou, Junze Wen, and Cheng Jing prune self-driving training data by keeping the most informative trips. Fleets record far more routine driving than rare, useful moments. Storing and training on all of it costs much and teaches little.

Their method scores data by the entropy of its trajectory spread, then keeps samples that best preserve the full set's statistics, with no model in the loop. Theory ties high entropy to a small gap between the kept set and the original distribution. On the NuPlan benchmark, the dataset shrank by up to forty percent while closed-loop driving scores held steady.
arxiv-2512-19570:
Angjelin Hila examines what happens to shared knowledge when people lean on language models. His theory of collective epistemology treats warrant as spread across a community, not locked in one head. Two kinds of justification matter: understanding why a claim holds, and reliably passing true claims along.

Reflective knowledge needs the first kind, plus honest checks on sources when the basis is out of reach. Models, Hila argues, deliver the second kind only: dependable transmission without reflective grasp. If reflective work is widely outsourced to fluent outputs, the community's standards for knowing can quietly erode. The paper rethinks collective intelligence under that pressure.
arxiv-2512-19770:
Michał Marczenko, writing in the proceedings of the 2025 International Nuclear Physics Conference, revisits a speed limit inside dense matter. Relativistic kinetic theory implies a constraint on the speed of sound squared, a quantity that encodes how stiff the equation of state of dense matter is at each density. Such stiffness governs the behavior of matter in settings like neutron star interiors.

Marczenko shows the kinetic-theory constraint can be rewritten in terms of the average sound speed, an integrated quantity accumulated over density. That reformulation exposes the interplay between momentary stiffness and its running average, and lets the bound be drawn as an excluded region in the plane of the two quantities. The note offers a compact visualization tool for testing proposed equations of state.
arxiv-2512-19870:
Hao-En Li and Lin Lin design quantum methods for the harder half of chemistry. That half is excited states. Ground states get most of the focus in the field. Yet light uptake, photochemistry, and spectra all run through excited states. Making them on quantum devices is still a thin field. Their trick is to redesign dissipation itself. They reshape the Lindblad dynamics so the wanted state is the one the system settles into.

In effect, the task becomes a ground-state task for a designed channel. Three plans cover unlike kinds of prior knowledge. One uses symmetry labels. One uses a rough energy for the target state. Tests on atoms and molecules show the plans at work. They span flat conjugated molecules and transition-metal complexes. The authors offer the route for work on strongly correlated systems.
arxiv-2512-19970:
Surya Jayakumar and four co-authors forecast the sustainability of Irish dairy farming. Their tool is a graph neural network that knows geography. The framework is the first county-scale use of such networks for this task. It builds composite sustainability indices from herd-level records. The records come from the Irish Cattle Breeding Federation. A variational autoencoder first fattens the sparse data. It keeps the joint patterns of the records intact.

A factor method then distills four pillars. They are reproductive efficiency, genetic management, herd health, and herd management. Weighted sums turn the pillars into the indices. The network then models spread across counties and change over years. It projects the indices for 2026 to 2030. The tool is also framed for what-if policy checks.
arxiv-2512-20070:
Jungwoo Kim, Jun-Hyuk Kim, and Jong-Seok Lee compress images for machine eyes in a way that lets receivers stop early. Progressive compression with fine granular scalability sends one bitstream decodable at many quality levels, ideal when a downstream vision model needs only enough detail to decide. That capability existed for human-oriented codecs but not for machine-oriented ones, until PICM-Net.

Built on trit-plane coding, the codec adapts a human-oriented design through a spatial-frequency modulation adapter, a low-rank hyper-synthesis adapter, and training that anticipates progressive decoding. An adaptive controller then judges at inference time whether the current quality suffices for the desired confidence, requesting more bits only when it does not. Experiments show efficient, adaptive transmission while downstream classification performance stays strong.
arxiv-2512-20170:
Vili Heinonen and Jani Lukkarinen examine a two-dimensional quantum gas whose particles do not interact with each other. The gas sits in a weak random potential whose irregularities stretch over long distances. They ask what happens over long times to the spread of particle momenta, which starts out sharply peaked in one direction.

Scattering off the random potential gradually makes the momentum distribution round and broad. The authors derive a formula for its long-time average and check that formula against computer simulations. They also discuss how the momenta lose their preferred direction and how the particles spread through space. The results clarify how disorder alone reshapes motion in a clean quantum system.
arxiv-2512-20370:
Wei Zhang and a large team build the first white matter atlas spanning newborns and adults in one space. Atlases for each group exist separately, which blocks direct comparison of brain wiring across development. Their neonatal and adult brain atlas, NABA, is built from diffusion MRI tractography of both populations.

A data-driven fibre clustering pipeline constructs the atlas despite large anatomical differences between baby and adult brains. With NABA, the team maps tracts jointly, tracks development across neonatal ages, compares the sexes, and studies preterm birth. Long-range association tracts gain fractional anisotropy quickly, while cerebellar tracts lag. Girls develop faster overall; preterm babies develop slower overall yet faster in a few specific pathways.
arxiv-2512-20870:
Junyang Huang and seven co-authors examine a quantum dot that could link quantum computers over telecom fiber. Quantum networks need stationary qubits that trade entanglement with flying photons at telecom wavelengths. Semiconductor dots emitting there are promising, but the trapped spin's behavior must be measured precisely first.

Using only the timing and polarization of emitted photons, the team benchmarked both the electron and the hole inside their dot. The hole came out ahead as the better qubit for spin-photon entanglement. Full tomography of the hole's state then exposed small directional quirks in its precession. Knowing those quirks helps engineers cut phase errors when generating multi-photon entanglement.
arxiv-2512-21170:
Yogesh Kumar, Vrushank Ahire, and M. A. Ganaie teach an old classifier family a new trick for reading brain waves. Electroencephalogram signals are non-stationary, noisy, and scarce, a hostile mix for seizure detection. Their classifiers extend a proximal support-vector design built on generalized eigenvalue problems, and add Universum learning: extra data from neither class, used to shape the decision boundary. One variant folds the Universum in through a ratio objective; the improved variant uses a weighted difference, so class separation and Universum alignment tune on their own.

On the Bonn University recordings, separating healthy from seizure traces, the improved model peaks at eighty-five percent accuracy for eyes-closed recordings. For eyes-open it reaches eighty percent. Averaged, it stays ahead of the baselines at about eighty-one and seventy-eight percent. Lightweight eigenvalue methods remain competitive for clinical screening where deep models are impractical.
arxiv-2512-21270:
Andre Sonnet and Epifanio Virga ask what a thin shell loses when its deformations are handcuffed. In the direct approach to shell theory, the shell is a mathematical surface. Its stored energy splits into three independent contents tied to three deformation modes: stretching, drilling (twisting about the surface normal), and bending. Their study is deliberately coordinate-free, following the surface's intrinsic geometry as it moves.

They impose metric restrictions on which deformations are admissible, the sort of limits real physical constraints might enforce, and trace the consequences for each of the three energy contents separately. The lesson is cautionary: restricting one aspect of a shell's motion can hamper its elastic response in ways intuition does not predict, because the three modes interact through the metric. Continuum mechanicians and shell-model builders gain a clean map of which constraints are innocent and which secretly amputate a shell's repertoire.
arxiv-2512-21370:
Future space observatories will hear gravitational waves that massive objects have lensed, bending and splitting the signal on its way. Tianlong Wang, Tianyu Zhao, and four colleagues want a faster way to spot those events than matched filtering, whose cost is heavy. Their answer is a dual-channel extended LSTM network built to read lensing features across the whole millihertz band.

A matrix-valued memory and a memory-mixing mechanism let the network track amplitude patterns spanning the crossover from wave optics to geometric optics. Trained on point-mass and isothermal-sphere lens models, it scores above 0.99 in area under the curve, catching over ninety-eight percent of events at under one percent false alarms. Performance holds across noise levels, lens types, and masses.
arxiv-2512-21470:
B. Guo, F. Yan, and a large team of co-authors report on HAT-P-70b, an ultra-hot Jupiter exoplanet. Using the CARMENES and PEPSI spectrographs, they recorded the planet's dayside heat glow from its permanently lit face. Such spectra reveal which chemicals fill the atmosphere and how temperature changes with height.

Cross-correlation detects emission from aluminum, aluminum hydride, calcium, chromium, iron, magnesium, manganese, and titanium. Aluminum and its hydride appear in such an atmosphere for the first time. The temperature profile shows a strong thermal inversion, with the upper atmosphere hotter than the layers below. Retrieved amounts broadly match the Sun's makeup, with hints of extra nickel and loss of some easily condensed elements. Very high amounts of ionized iron and calcium defy equilibrium chemistry, suggesting the atmosphere is escaping into space.
arxiv-2512-21670:
Subramanyam Sahoo and Jared Junkin open up the black box of a deepfake detector. Models flag synthetic media with high accuracy, but nobody could say which internal features drive their verdicts. The authors apply interpretability tools to a vision-language model trained to spot deepfakes.

They combine sparse autoencoder analysis of the model's internal features with a forensic manifold analysis. The second probes how feature geometry responds when forensic artifacts are manipulated in a controlled way. They find that only a small fraction of latent units is active in each layer. The feature manifold's dimensionality, curvature, and selectivity vary with the type of deepfake artifact. Mapping units to artifacts is a first step toward detectors that are not just accurate but explainable, and toward spotting weaknesses before attackers exploit them.
arxiv-2512-21870:
Garima Rani, Anupam Sengupta, Hartmut Löwen, and their co-authors study how bacteria colonize soft surfaces and organize into young biofilms. Biofilms grow on everything from medical implants to natural tissues, yet how the softness of the surface shapes the earliest stages was poorly understood.

Combining experiments with agent-based simulations, the team varied the substrate stiffness over a hundredfold range. On soft surfaces, colonies expanded slowly, grew in an elongated, anisotropic pattern, and piled into multilayers early. On hard surfaces, bacteria spread quickly and evenly as a single layer before stacking. A cell-level mechanical model explains the difference through drag: soft surfaces deform under the cells, creating direction-dependent drag that resists spreading and pushes growth upward. On hard surfaces the drag is lower, delaying the move to multilayers. The authors suggest surface compliance could be engineered to steer biofilm formation.
arxiv-2512-22070:
Fully charm tetraquarks, exotic states of two charm quarks and two antiquarks, can be produced and probed electromagnetically, but leading-order predictions miss gluon radiation. Xinran Liu, Yefan Wang, and Ruilin Zhu compute the next-to-leading-order QCD corrections to their decay amplitudes into two photons.

The corrections prove significant for the scalar and tensor states' two-photon decays, shifting predictions. The authors then fold the corrected amplitudes into photon-photon fusion in ultra-peripheral proton and nuclear collisions and in electron-positron collisions, predicting production cross sections for the states. The results give current and future experiments concrete electromagnetic benchmarks for identifying these exotic hadrons.
arxiv-2512-22170:
Jiesong Lian and eight co-authors tackle reward models, the scorers that teach video generation systems to match human taste. Current scorers learn from pairwise labels collected inside a single prompt, which introduces noise. Their designs are also under-explored, and generators can learn to game them, a failure called reward hacking. The team's system, SoliReward, attacks all three problems at once.

SoliReward collects cheaper, cleaner data through single-item yes-or-no annotations, then builds preference pairs across different prompts. A hierarchical progressive query attention mechanism strengthens feature gathering inside the model. A modified loss handles wins and ties explicitly and spreads scores more evenly among good samples. Benchmarks covering physical plausibility, subject deformity, and semantic alignment show gains in scorer quality and in downstream video training.
arxiv-2512-22470:
Sadia Asif and four co-authors introduce DarkPatterns-LLM, a benchmark for detecting when language models manipulate their users. Current safety tests mostly use coarse yes-or-no labels and miss the psychological and social methods that make manipulation work. Their dataset sorts harmful behavior into seven categories, from legal and economic harm to psychological, emotional, physical, autonomy, and societal harm.

A four-layer pipeline analyzes outputs at multiple granularities, examines intent at several scales, harmonizes threats, and aligns risk with deep context. The dataset holds 401 curated instruction-response examples with expert annotations. Evaluating GPT-4, Claude 3.5, and LLaMA-3-70B showed wide performance spread and a consistent blind spot: patterns that undermine user autonomy were hardest for every model to catch.
arxiv-2512-22570:
Md. Abdur Rahman and six co-authors present ReFRM3D, a neural network for characterizing gliomas, among the most aggressive brain cancers, in 3D scans. Segmentation models struggle with the wide variability of tumor imaging, and radiomic texture analysis is usually bolted on after segmentation, too late to guide it. ReFRM3D, built on a 3D U-Net, weaves the two together with multi-scale feature fusion, hybrid upsampling, and extended residual skip connections.

Its radiomic conditioning mechanism extracts texture and intensity descriptors from an intermediate coarse segmentation and feeds them back into the decoder to refine the result. On the BraTS 2019, 2020, and 2021 benchmarks, mean overlap scores exceeded ninety-two percent. The model also generalized to the BraTS-Africa dataset despite different scanners and patient populations.
arxiv-2512-22770:
Naoki Kitamura, Yuichi Sudo, and Koichi Wada map out exactly how much computing power two tiny autonomous robots have. The robots work in Look-Compute-Move cycles and differ by whether they carry memory, can communicate, and move in lockstep or independently. For larger robot teams this landscape of models was mostly known, but the two-robot case had resisted a complete answer.

The full chart turns out to differ from the general case in surprising ways. Under full synchrony, a model with only private memory matches one with lights for communication plus memory, because perfect timing can substitute for both when only two robots exist. Memory-only and communication-only models are also shown incomparable in both directions. All separations and equivalences come from a new simulation-free method, giving the first exact picture of coordination at the smallest possible scale.
arxiv-2512-23070:
Boyang Zhang and co-authors design FLEX-MoE, a way to run mixture-of-experts models across federated edge devices. Mixture-of-experts networks scale by activating only some specialist subnetworks per input. But edge clients in a federation cannot store the full expert set. Their skewed local data leave some experts overloaded and others idle. Both problems degrade the shared model.

FLEX-MoE scores how well each expert fits each client's data, using training feedback. It then runs an optimization that assigns experts to maximize specialization while enforcing balanced use across the system. That balance constraint is the difference from greedy personalization schemes, which ignore system-wide load. Experiments across resource-constrained scenarios show better accuracy together with consistently balanced expert utilization. The authors aim the framework at next-generation wireless and Internet of Things deployments, where models must live on small devices with uneven data.
arxiv-2512-23670:
Francesco Piatti, Thomas Cass, and William Turner build time-series models from randomly wired continuous-time reservoirs. Their base tool is the controlled differential equation, which lets a hidden state evolve in response to an incoming signal path. Instead of training the whole system, they randomize a large reservoir's parameters and train only a linear readout layer on top, making learning fast and scalable.

Two variants follow. Random Fourier CDEs first lift the input with random Fourier features; Random Rough DEs work directly on rough paths through a log-ODE scheme using log-signatures. In the infinite-width limit the two recover, respectively, an RBF-lifted signature kernel and the rough signature kernel, tying random features to path-signature theory. Across time-series benchmarks both models matched or beat the state of the art.
arxiv-2512-23870:
Yuyang Zhang, Yang Hu, Bo Dai, and Na Li upgrade the soft actor-critic, a leading algorithm in maximum-entropy reinforcement learning, where policies are rewarded for staying random as well as for performing. In practice the ideal energy-based policy is squeezed into a simple parametric family for efficiency, sacrificing expressiveness and robustness. The authors instead let a flow-based model represent the policy, with its much richer shapes.

Evaluating such a policy uses the instantaneous change-of-variables technique, and updating it uses an online flow matching variant developed for this work, importance sampling flow matching. This learns from samples of a distribution the user chooses rather than the unknown target. Their theory characterizes how the sampling distribution's choice affects learning efficiency. A case study on maximum-entropy linear quadratic regulator problems shows the algorithm learning the optimal action distribution.
arxiv-2512-24270:
Sandro Claudio Lera and Andreas Haupt explain why socio-economic networks collapse suddenly. Cities, firms, and collaborative projects can look resilient for years. Then participation erodes and decline cascades. Their framework is a network game of strategic abandonment. Each agent picks an activity level. Agents stay only while participation beats an improving outside option.

As outside options rise, agents exit on their own. Exits force the remaining network to readjust. Strategic complementarities govern what happens next. Weak complementarities give slow, local decay like bootstrap percolation. Vulnerable clusters can be spotted in advance there. Strong complementarities give rupture instead. Metastable plateaus end in abrupt system-wide collapse. Standard indicators predict little in that regime. Interventions differ too. Supporting central agents works best under strong complementarities. Helping marginal agents matters most when they are weak.
arxiv-2512-25070:
Nikhil Chandak, Shashwat Goel, Ameya Prabhu, and colleagues train language models to forecast open-ended questions about the future. High-stakes decisions need reasoning under uncertainty, but training data for forecasting is scarce. They synthesize questions from global events in daily news with a fully automated, careful curation recipe, building the OpenForesight dataset.

An offline news corpus prevents leakage of future information during training and evaluation, and retrieval uses the same corpus. Qwen thinking models trained on the data are guided by a small validation set. AI readers get a scalable route to forecasting skill, with leakage control as a central design discipline.
arxiv-2601-06770:
Sofiia Huraka and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers structure-preserving learning and prediction in optimal control of collective motion. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Wide-spread adoption of unmanned vehicle technologies requires the ability to predict the motion of the combined vehicle operation from observations.

While the general prediction of such motion for an arbitrary control mechanism is difficult. For a particular choice of control, the dynamics reduces to the Lie-Poisson equations [ 33 , 34 ]. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-06970:
José de Brito and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers splitting proximal point algorithms for the sum of Prox-Convex functions. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. -34.14322pt Abstract The work addresses the minimization of a finite sum of prox-convex functions under Lipschitz continuity of each component.
