Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136770: This Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers is dated only to 1960 in the catalog, with the date marked as estimated. An earlier summary described war planning for Europe and invasion options; that is material from another war and is not supported by this record, so it is dropped. What stands is a Spanish document of the exile brigade from its training year, released in the CIA's declassified files.
cia-0000136870: Should the agency back a labor bulletin? This March 1954 cable debates the question. The agency does not want a sounding board for exiles on a lasting basis. But a broader bulletin might be worthwhile. It would stress the communist menace. It would also preach free trade unionism. A growing gap between two labor figures offers a chance. A new labor project could grow from it. The present backstop is too weak for a long run, though. A new one must be built.
cia-0000136970: Do not use an air strike against the referenced target, headquarters tells LINCOLN in this June 1954 cable. Despite full accord with the field's purpose, careful examination and expert opinion concluded the target is difficult and unprofitable for air because it is extremely isolated. Air power should be restricted to targets vulnerable to it. The referenced target is most vulnerable to sabotage, so every effort should be made by that means instead. Restraint here is tactical, not political.
cia-0000137470: Venezuela's Communist Party now aims to take over the government. These December 1961 field reports warn of it before Kennedy's visit. European technicians help the party train groups in sabotage materials. Party splits would aid the communist cause. A heated argument was overheard between President Betancourt and COPEI head Caldera. Betancourt said he did not need COPEI in the coalition. Caldera apparently agreed to go along in the end. The party plans disturbances in eastern Venezuela. Sabotage around Cabimas and a power plant is planned. Agitators will be brought in.
cia-0000139170: Excerpts from a daily record, catalogued under the spelling Daily Dairy, make up document 0000139170, dated 1978 in the CIA files. The odd spelling is the archive's own and runs through this whole series. Excerpt form means the reader gets chosen slices of a running diary rather than the full run of days. Whose days they were, the record here does not say, and that gap should be kept in mind while reading the declassified pages.
cia-0000139370: Terms of reference for NIE 10-61 are forwarded in this January 1961 memorandum. Chester Cooper signed it. The estimate covers authority and control in the communist movement. Representatives are asked to meet on 3 February. Room 115 of the Administration Building is the place. Distribution is the standard B list. The sample holds only the forwarding paperwork. The estimate's analysis of Moscow-Peking authority is not here. That split stood at its height in 1961. The title and meeting record are what this excerpt supports.
cia-06774470: AGENCY SECURITY CLASSIFICATION MANAGEMENT PROGRAM DATA, fiscal year covered 200, a CIA document. The data file. This file preserves that declassified paper. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
columbus-select-letters-major-1870:
Select Letters of Christopher Columbus gathers the admiral's own reports from 1493 to 1503, edited and translated by R H Major for the Hakluyt Society in 1870. Related documents stand with the letters to fill out the record. Columbus wrote to Spain's rulers and patrons as the first European reporter of lands across the Atlantic.

The famous letter on the islands he had found, De Insulis Inventis, announced the discovery to all Europe. In these pages Columbus describes coasts, peoples, and wonders in the first flush of encounter. Later letters show strain, dispute, and a man fighting for his honors. Together they form the first European descriptions of the New World, in its finder's own words.
cox-mythology-aryan-nations-vol-1-1870:
George William Cox was an English scribe on myths and old tales. His Mythology of the Aryan Nations came out in two books from 1870. Book One starts the vast work. Cox was a keen fan of the new school that read myths as tales of sun and storm.

He traces the gods and heroes of India, Persia, Greece, and the North to one root. Dawn, sun, and night form the core of his scheme for each tale. Cox writes with verve and a store of tales from all the Aryan tongues. The set is a chief work of the myth school of its age.
das-geheimniss-der-hermetischen-philosop: The secret of hermetic philosophy got a German airing in 1770. The author laid bare the hidden doctrine. The esoteric enlightenment. Its pages add to the record of the past. This book preserves that rare work for future readers.
dircks-perpetuum-mobile-second-series-18:
Henry Dircks brought out this second series of his perpetual motion survey in 1870. It picks up where his 1861 book left off. New claimants kept coming forth with wheels and weights, and Dircks kept track of them all. Some were cranks, and some were sharp men led astray by hope.

The new part adds fresh schemes, fresh claims, and the men who made them. Dircks tests each claim with the same cool care as in the first book. Bound with the first, the two parts form the full record of three hundred years of vain work.
emerson-society-and-solitude-1870:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published Society and Solitude in 1870, his late essay collection of summing-up. The set holds Society and Solitude, Civilization, Art, and Eloquence among its twelve grave pieces in print. Age had mellowed the prophet into a counselor, and the voice here is genial and wise.

The title essay balances the need for company with the soul's need to be alone and think. Eloquence praises the speaker who masters himself before he tries to move a crowd of hearers in earnest. Farming, Books, and Old Age weigh a life's tools and seasons with humor and calm acceptance in age. Emerson's fire burns lower here, but the light is steady and the counsel kind to young readers. It is a fitting last word from America's sage in his full maturity.
europmc-pmc10367370:
Li and co-authors reviewed in 2023 how fuel use shapes immune cells inside tumours. The cells are macrophages, white blood cells that eat germs and debris. Near a tumour they often switch sides and help the tumour grow. They also blunt the immune attack and foster drug resistance.

Macrophages come in two broad states with distinct fuel habits. Li notes that one state burns sugar fast, while the other relies on oxygen-based fuel use. Small chemicals in the tumour zone can push cells from one state to the next. The review asks how that switch might be reset on purpose. Such a reset could form part of future cancer care.
europmc-pmc10371870:
Kanemaru and a large team charted the cell zones of the human heart in 2023. A cell's job depends on its traits and on its niche, the tissue spot where it lives. The team joined single-cell gene reads with maps that keep each cell's place. They covered eight heart regions, plus the wiring that sets the beat.

The beat core, the sinoatrial node, held a mix of pacemaker cells, support cells, and nerve-like glial cells. Kanemaru flagged a gene, FOXP2, as a mark of the pacemaker type. A new tool, drug2cell, used the cell data to predict how drugs shift heart rate. In the heart's outer layer, the team found immune zones rich in antibody-making cells.
europmc-pmc10474270:
Zhang and a large team found in 2023 a chemical tag on a heart muscle protein that keeps the heart strong. The protein, alpha-myosin heavy chain, forms part of the heart's contractile unit. It grips a giant partner protein, Titin, as the heart squeezes. Lactate, a fuel made from sugar, supplies the tag.

The tag, called lactylation, sits at one spot on the protein, lysine 1897. Zhang found less of this tag in failing hearts of mice and patients. Mice built to lack the tag showed weak grip and poor heart shape. Raising lactate in heart cells restored the tag and eased failure. Two enzymes add and strip the tag: p300 and Sirtuin 1.
europmc-pmc10504070:
Bowe, Xie, and Al-Aly followed Covid patients for two full years in 2023 to map lasting harm. Infection with SARS-CoV-2 can leave sequelae, health problems that linger in many organs. Most past proof stopped at one year. The team used US Veterans Affairs records for 138,818 infected people and near 6 million controls.

They tracked death plus 80 named after-effects. Bowe found that extra death risk faded after six months for people who were never in hospital. For hospital cases, the risk stayed high through year two. Most after-effects eased with time, yet the total health loss stayed large. Hospital cases lost 642.8 healthy years per 1,000 people over the two years.
europmc-pmc12035670:
Chan and many co-authors updated guidance for trial protocols in 2025. A protocol is the full plan for a randomized trial. It guides setup, conduct, reporting, and outside review. Many protocols leave out key design details.

The SPIRIT statement first set minimum protocol items in 2013. The update draws on a broad evidence review. Input also came from harms, outcomes, and reporting guide teams. Items were tested against current best practice. Chan aims for protocols complete enough to judge before trials start. Clear plans protect patients and research funds. The statement updates the 2013 SPIRIT version.
europmc-pmc1240370:
Rubin and co-authors tested low-dose bisphenol A in rats in 2001. Bisphenol A, or BPA, is a building block of hard plastics. It can leak from can linings, dental sealants, and bottles. Though weakly estrogen-like, low doses were assumed safe.

Pregnant rats drank water with low or higher BPA doses. Exposure ran through pregnancy and nursing. Pups exposed early gained more weight from birth into adulthood. Females on the higher dose showed altered cycles. Their levels of a key reproductive hormone also dropped. Rubin shows early low-dose exposure can leave lasting marks.
europmc-pmc1325270:
Lassmann and Sonnhammer built a fast sequence alignment program called Kalign in 2005. Aligning many protein sequences underpins family and structure studies. Existing methods were either inaccurate or too slow for genome-scale data. Kalign uses a fast string-matching algorithm to speed the work.

Tests ran on three benchmark collections against popular rivals. On small alignments Kalign matched the best accuracy. On large, distant sequence sets it was significantly more accurate. It ran about ten times faster than ClustalW. Against iterative methods it ran up to fifty times faster. Speed plus accuracy suits large comparative genomics.
europmc-pmc1447670:
Fungi hide a loud alarm signal under a coat of proteins. Wheeler and Fink studied that masking trick in 2006. The signal is beta-glucan, a sugar chain in the fungal wall that stirs immune attack. A mild dose of an antifungal drug stripped the coat and exposed it.

Exposed fungi drew a much stronger response from immune cells. Using yeast mutants, Wheeler mapped a gene network that keeps the signal buried. Breaking parts of that network in a harmful fungus also exposed the sugar. Mouse immune cells then released more attack signals. The team suggests drugs that strip the mask could fight many fungi at once.
europmc-pmc1550270:
Bacteria silence foreign genes they pick up from other germs. Lucchini and co-authors showed how in 2006, studying Salmonella. A protein called H-NS wraps the bacterial DNA. They mapped where it binds across the genome.

H-NS shunned active genes and the enzyme that reads them. It bound most where DNA was rich in the letters A and T, a mark of foreign DNA. Many genes gained by sideways transfer sat under its grip, including whole disease islands. Removing H-NS unleashed those genes and hurt the germ's fitness. Lucchini frames H-NS as a gatekeeper that lets bacteria take in new genes without being swamped by them.
europmc-pmc1594570:
Viruses may be as old as cells themselves. Koonin, Senkevich, and Dolja proposed an ancient Virus World in 2006, built from genome evidence. Many RNA and DNA virus groups share key genes for copying and shell building that no cell carries.

The trio infer a lasting pool of viral genes running through life's whole history. Main virus lineages sprang from a primordial soup of genetic elements, the same pool that seeded cellular genes. RNA viruses came first, then retro-like elements, then DNA viruses. Later gene swapping blurred but never erased that ancient split.
europmc-pmc1766370:
Making sense of a genome-wide expression experiment needs a map, not a list. Usadel and co-authors built PageMan in 2006, a tool that drapes expression data over functional categories. Early programs handled only pairwise comparisons, while modern studies span many conditions.

PageMan condenses data into overview graphs organized by ontology, the hierarchy of gene functions. It runs over-representation and Wilcoxon tests and exports graphics ready for papers. Users can compare stress responses across time points, mutants, or species on one display. Usadel designed it as a stand-alone, user-friendly program for plant and general profiling work.
europmc-pmc1947970:
Arora, Kapoor and co-authors cataloged in 2007 the complete MADS-box gene family in rice and tracked its activity through flower development and stress. These transcription factors, proteins that control other genes, specify floral organs and shape many growth processes. A full family portrait existed for the model plant Arabidopsis but not for rice, a world staple crop.

Careful annotation found 75 MADS-box genes in the rice genome. Family tree analysis sorted them into five groups, named MIKCc, MIKC-star, M-alpha, M-beta, and M-gamma. The team mapped each gene's chromosome position and structure. Microarray profiling then measured activity across reproductive development stages and stress conditions. Comparing rice with Arabidopsis highlights which family roles are ancient and shared, and which shifted as the two plant lines diverged.
europmc-pmc2125070: A medical paper with further studies on the identity of precipitins and protein sensitizers. The clumping proteins. This article preserves that immunology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2125370: A medical paper with a further study of the bactericidal action of ethylhydrocuprein on pneumococci. The germ-killing drug. This article preserves that pharmacology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2126270: A medical paper on modifications of culture media for isolating typhoid bacteria. The improved plates. This article preserves that bacteriology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it.
europmc-pmc2131270: A medical paper with experimental epidemiology of tuberculosis. The TB's spread. This article preserves that epidemiology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2131470: A medical paper on the effect of oxidation of filtrates of a chicken sarcoma. The oxidized tumor juice. This article preserves that oncology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2131770: A medical paper on the viscosity of the blood of the dog after obstruction of the upper gastrointestinal tract. The thick dog blood. This article preserves that hematology. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2140370: A biology paper on the free energy of biological processes, preliminary. The life's energy. This article preserves that biophysics. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2140670: A biology paper on the relation between the initial rise and subsequent decline of milk secretion. The milk's curve. This article preserves that physiology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2180270: A medical paper on the relative reaction within living mammalian tissues, on the tissue reaction. The tissues again. This article preserves that physiology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2233670:
Miller and co-workers showed in 2008 that dengue virus enters macrophages through the mannose receptor. Macrophages are major targets of this mosquito-borne virus, which can cause haemorrhagic fever. The receptor normally binds sugars on microbes and host molecules. Using binding assays, sugar analysis and antibody blocking, the team tested all four dengue serotypes against the receptor on human cells.

The receptor bound all four serotypes, specifically to the viral envelope glycoprotein. Stripping sugars from that protein abolished binding. Adding the receptor to normally resistant cells made them bind virus. Antibodies against the receptor blocked infection of primary human macrophages. Pre-treating blood cells with type 2 cytokines such as IL-4 or IL-13 raised receptor levels and made infection more productive. The finding assigns the mannose receptor a new role in dengue disease.
europmc-pmc2265470:
Tokuriki, Stricher, Serrano and Tawfik tested in 2008 whether gaining a new enzyme function usually costs protein stability. Many studies had noted that trade-off, but most random mutations also destabilise proteins, so the comparison baseline was unclear. Using the FoldX computation tool, they analysed 548 mutations from directed evolution of 22 enzymes. They compared those function-changing mutations with every possible single mutation in the same enzymes.

Function-changing mutations were mostly destabilising. They added on average 0.9 kilocalories per mole of instability, close to the average mutation's 1.3 on the same scale. Mutations reshaping the substrate-binding pocket carried a larger stability burden than surface mutations behind neutral change. Such pocket changes create new specificities. The analysis also found many extra mutations in evolved enzymes were stabilising. Those silent compensations appear to balance the costly functional changes, enabling adaptation.
europmc-pmc2568870:
Maier and colleagues hunted in 2008 for the parasite proteins that make malaria-infected red blood cells stiff and sticky. Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria parasite, exports its own proteins into the red cells it invades, rebuilding them so they cling to vessel walls. The team knocked out genes one by one on a large scale and screened the mutants for lost remodelling.

Eight genes proved essential for exporting the parasite's main adhesin, PfEMP1, and for building the knobs, small bumps on the cell surface that anchor it. Other proteins contributed to the infected cell's rigidity. Together the exported set works like a secretion system borrowed from bacteria. Because these proteins drive the disease's lethality, the authors flag them as targets for antivirulence therapies, drugs that disarm rather than kill the parasite.
europmc-pmc261870:
Wang and colleagues described in 2003 a DNA microarray platform that can identify entirely new viruses, and proved it on the SARS outbreak. Existing tests only find pathogens already known, leaving emerging diseases hard to name. Their chip carried the most conserved stretches from every fully sequenced virus genome in GenBank, designed to light up for known viruses and novel relatives alike.

In March 2003 the array flagged a previously uncharacterised coronavirus in a sample cultured from a SARS patient. The team then physically recovered about 1,000 DNA letters of the unknown virus from the array spots and sequenced them. The fragments confirmed a new member of the coronavirus family, later known as the SARS virus. The authors present array screening plus sequence recovery as a general strategy for emerging infections.
europmc-pmc2661770:
Nagy and co-authors explained in 2009 why the blood vessels inside tumors are so badly built, and why the details matter for treatment. Tumor vessels leak, twist, and carry blood poorly, unlike the tidy vessels of healthy tissue. Doctors had long lumped them together as one abnormal kind.

The team argues there are at least six distinct vessel types in tumors, each forming by its own route. A growth signal called VEGF-A drives some of them, and drugs that block it can prune those types. Other types have outgrown their need for that signal, so the same drugs leave them untouched. Naming the types apart, the authors say, points to which vessels a treatment must hit. Future therapy should aim at the stubborn subsets, not just the VEGF-driven ones.
europmc-pmc2689870:
Mizuno, Kitada, Nakai, and Sarai built in 2009 PrognoScan, a public database for testing whether a gene's activity predicts cancer patients' survival. Public archives held many cancer gene datasets with patient outcomes attached, gold for finding tumor markers, but scattered and hard to analyze without specialist tools. PrognoScan gathers them into one platform.

A user picks a gene, and the system splits patients by its activity level at the cut point that best separates their survival curves, then checks the link's strength. Rather than fixing one arbitrary split, it searches for the most informative one, while guarding against the false patterns such searching can invent. Repeating the test across many datasets acts as a meta-analysis: a gene that predicts outcomes again and again earns trust. The database is free online, aimed at speeding the hunt for markers and drug targets.
europmc-pmc2766070:
Hendrickson and co-authors measured in 2009 how one human microRNA, miR-124, lowers the output of hundreds of target proteins. MicroRNAs pair with messenger RNAs and cut protein production, but whether they act by destroying the message, blocking its translation, or both was unsettled. The team identified direct miR-124 targets by their recruitment to Argonaute proteins, the core of the microRNA machinery.

For more than eight thousand genes they measured message abundance and two gauges of translation, ribosome occupancy and density. A specific microRNA reduced protein synthesis through matching effects on both fronts: target messages fell in abundance and were translated less. The two effects moved together across hundreds of targets. This concordant pattern argues against models in which microRNAs act on translation alone. The scale of the survey is what lets the pattern stand out so clearly.
europmc-pmc2796170:
Stecher and co-authors asked in 2010 what lets a new bacterium settle in the gut, where a dense resident community usually blocks invaders. They worked with mice whose gut communities ranged from simple to full, and challenged them with Salmonella, a germ that causes gut inflammation.

Mice with simple gut communities fell ill easily, while time spent housed with normal mice partly restored their defense. DNA reads showed that richer, more mixed communities resisted better. Surprisingly, mice rich in close kin of an incoming germ were colonized more easily, a pattern the authors call like will to like. The rule may guide both infection control and probiotic design, meaning live germs given for health.
europmc-pmc2815670:
Adams and a large team described PHENIX in 2010, a software system that solves the three-dimensional shapes of large molecules from crystal data. Knowing such shapes drives drug design and basic biology, but the calculations chain many steps that once needed hand file conversion between separate programs.

PHENIX is built around the Python scripting language, with heavy number work handed to compiled C++ modules for speed. That design lets teams in different labs stack their modules into automated pipelines that look uniform from outside. A graphical interface added in recent versions wraps the command-line tools, and the system covers model building, refinement, and validation checks in one place.
europmc-pmc2826370:
Dörr, Vulić, and Lewis found in 2010 how a common antibiotic tricks some E. coli bacteria into a dormant state that shrugs off drugs. These sleeper cells, called persisters, survive treatment without being genetic mutants and help stubborn biofilm infections return. How they form had resisted years of screening.

The antibiotic ciprofloxacin damages bacterial DNA, which switches on the cell's SOS alarm. That alarm raises production of TisB, a tiny protein that pokes into the cell membrane and drains its energy. Drained cells go dormant and tolerate many antibiotics at once. Deleting the tisB gene cut persister formation sharply, giving the first single-gene handle on a mechanism long thought to be fully redundant.
europmc-pmc2853470:
Wolf, Schmidt, Müller-Hannemann, and Neumann built MetFrag in 2010, software that names unknown molecules from their mass spectrometry fingerprints without needing a library of measured examples. Metabolomics machines shatter molecules and weigh the pieces, but reference spectra cover only a sliver of known chemistry. MetFrag instead predicts how each candidate compound from giant libraries like KEGG and PubChem would shatter in theory, then ranks candidates by how well the prediction matches the real fragments.

In tests it placed the correct compound in the top three candidates for most spectra, beating the leading commercial rival. Similar-looking candidates could be clustered to cut redundancy. Each molecule takes under a second to fragment in theory, and full library searches finish within minutes on an ordinary desktop.
europmc-pmc2911870:
Murata and co-authors explored in 2010 whether microRNAs in blood and joint fluid can serve as biomarkers for rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis. MicroRNAs are small gene regulators that circulate stably in blood, raising hopes of a liquid test for joint disease. The team measured five candidate microRNAs in joint fluid and plasma from arthritis patients and in plasma from healthy controls.

The microRNAs proved as stable in joint fluid as in plasma through freezing and thawing, a practical requirement for any test. Joint fluid carried lower levels of four candidates than the same patients' plasma. The two fluids' values did not track each other either. Joint fluid is therefore not just leaked blood. Joint tissues and their cells release microRNAs into culture fluid, supporting a local origin worth mining diagnostically.
europmc-pmc3009670:
Waterland led a team that hunted metastable epialleles in humans in a 2010 study. These are genome spots where chemical marking is set by chance in the early embryo. The team tested whether season of conception in rural Gambia shifts those marks. Gambian nutrition swings hard between seasons.

Their two-tissue screen found candidate spots whose marks matched across tissues from all germ layers yet differed between identical twins, fitting the chance-set pattern. Children conceived in the hungry rainy season carried higher marks at these spots. The finding is first evidence that environment around conception leaves a lasting, body-wide mark.
europmc-pmc3153270:
María Ángeles Argudín and colleagues reviewed food poisoning by a common bacterium in a 2010 paper in Toxins. The germ lives harmlessly on skin and in noses, but strains carrying toxin genes can contaminate handled foods such as processed meats and dairy. The toxins, made in the food before eating, resist cooking and digestion.

Illness strikes within hours, with nausea and violent vomiting, and usually clears in a day or two. One toxin type causes most cases worldwide, though newer toxin types are widespread and their role may be underrated. All these toxins also overstimulate the immune system, and their genes ride on mobile DNA pieces, including the element carrying drug resistance. The review maps the family and its spread.
europmc-pmc3171170:
Kevin Moreau and colleagues found that the cell's recycling sacs must fuse with their own kind before they can mature in a 2011 paper in Cell. Recycling sacs form when small precursor bubbles grow and seal, gathering worn cell contents for breakdown. Where those precursors come from was partly known; how they grow was not.

Precursors carrying a marker protein merge with each other early on, and that merging is essential for building the finished sac. The fusion needs a specific membrane-fusing protein and its partners. Skipping the step leaves precursors the wrong size and stalls their conversion into working sacs. The study couples membrane gathering to sac construction and shows vesicle size at birth shapes the whole recycling pathway.
europmc-pmc3174870:
Saad Noeman, Hala Hamooda, and Amal Baalash measured oxidative stress in the organs of fat-fed rats in a 2011 paper in Diabetology and Metabolic Syndrome. Obesity drives many diseases, and chemical stress from reactive oxygen is a suspected link. Sixty rats were split between a fatty diet and normal chow for sixteen weeks, then liver, heart, and kidney tissues were assayed.

Fat-fed rats ended heavier with disordered blood fats. Damage markers climbed in all three organs, while most protective enzyme activities fell. A key protective chemical dropped in liver and kidney but oddly rose in heart, the one organ where one protective enzyme also held steady. Damage levels tracked the loss of defences closely. The authors conclude diet-driven obesity burdens all three organs with oxidative stress, likely feeding its complications.
europmc-pmc3197470:
Catrine Tudor-Locke and colleagues updated step-count guidance for adults in a 2011 paper in a behavioural nutrition journal. Guidelines speak in minutes and intensity, but step counters speak in steps, and published translations disagreed widely. The review harmonised them against the rule that some activity beats none while keeping focus on brisk effort.

Healthy adults typically log somewhere in the mid thousands to high teens of thousands of steps daily, and ten thousand remains a reasonable target for most. Walking at about a hundred steps a minute marks moderate effort, so half an hour of it adds roughly three thousand purposeful steps above daily routine. Whole-day totals matching the guidelines land in the high thousands to low teens of thousands. Programmes typically add a few thousand steps.
europmc-pmc3234270:
Oksana Subach and colleagues engineered a better blue fluorescent protein in this 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Blue fluorescent tags let biologists watch proteins inside living cells, but the brightest existing one faded chemically over time, its glowing core breaking down into a dark product. The team worked out the chemistry of that breakdown.

Guided by the structure of the degraded core, they redesigned the protein, producing a variant named mTagBFP2. The new tag is about twice as chemically stable, substantially brighter in living cells, and noticeably more resistant to bleaching under both widefield and confocal microscopes. It keeps the parent protein's other virtues, including acid tolerance and fast maturation. In fusion proteins and in energy-transfer experiments with green tags, it outperformed its predecessor, making it the better general-purpose blue marker.
europmc-pmc3312870:
Irwin and colleagues built parent report questionnaires for children's health as part of a national measurement project, describing the work in 2012. Children should ideally report on their own health, but the very young, the very ill, or children with thinking difficulties cannot always do so. A parent or caregiver then answers in their place, which calls for questions tested in that stand in form.

The team converted child questions into parent versions covering movement, mood, friendships, tiredness, pain, and asthma effects. Interviews with twenty five caregivers checked that the wording made sense, though some found judging their child's inner feelings genuinely hard. A large field test then enrolled well over fifteen hundred parent and child pairs to calibrate scoring, giving the project its first parent report item banks.
europmc-pmc3315470:
Dastani led a worldwide genetics effort hunting for gene variants that set levels of a fat tissue hormone, reporting in 2012. The hormone, adiponectin, is made by fat cells, and low levels track with type 2 diabetes and related traits. Levels run in families, so the team combined genome scans from nearly forty six thousand people, mostly of European ancestry, with extra data from African American and Asian groups.

Eight new gene regions linked to hormone levels turned up, plus two already known ones, and the cross ancestry analysis added two more. A score built from level lowering variants also predicted higher diabetes risk, higher blood fats, and worse insulin measures. Tests on human fat cells tied nearby genes to hormone output. The findings name fresh genetic levers on a hormone central to metabolic disease.
europmc-pmc3404070:
Nielsen and colleagues presented a math framework in 2012 for reading genetic variation out of next-generation sequencing data. Such data arrive as noisy short reads, so calling the differences between people is a matter of odds. Their method first estimates the full spread of allele rates in a sample.

A stepwise algorithm does the heavy computing, sped up with exact shortcuts. A second layer then estimates the rate at a single site and supports calling both full genotypes and variant sites. The framework also stretches to cases where gene proportions depart from standard expectations. Tests on simulated and real data checked how the methods behave, offering population geneticists a firmer statistical base.
europmc-pmc3441570:
Tritt, Eisen, Facciotti, and Darling built an all-in-one pipeline in 2012 that assembles a microbe's genome from raw sequencing reads with almost no expert handling. Assembly had been a fiddly, multi-stage craft of cleaning, correcting, assembling, and checking, each stage with its own tools and settings. Their pipeline, called A5, automates the whole chain.

Against a leading assembler, A5 matched quality with no prior knowledge of the genome and no hand-tuning of parameters. Its assemblies also broke far fewer protein-coding genes. It handled a newer library style with very different read patterns, and its appetite for computing is modest: a typical bacterial genome finishes on a desktop in under two hours. The aim is to hand genome assembly to any lab.
europmc-pmc3530470: Mitochondria got a bubble-building study. This 2012 paper rebuilds mitochondria-bubble formation in a test tube. The authors reveal the cargo. Their work guides cell biology. Soubannier's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped mitophagy research.
europmc-pmc3534370: Viral microRNAs got an overview. This 2012 paper surveys virus-made microRNAs and future directions. The authors map the field. Their review guides virology. Kincaid's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped virus research. The review is widely taught.

figuier-primitive-man-1870:
Louis Figuier, a French popularizer of science, published Primitive Man in 1870. An English version carried his account to British and American readers. Engravings of tools, dwellings, and early peoples fill its pages.

Figuier walks readers from the earliest stone tools toward settled life. He writes dramatic scenes that made prehistory feel alive to Victorians. The book became a bestseller and shaped popular ideas of cave life. Its science has aged, sometimes badly. As a record of what the public first imagined about prehistoric people, it endures. Its scenes of mammoth hunts became stock images in classrooms for decades afterward.
frus-1861-d170:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Gabriel Tassara, the Spanish minister in Washington, on 15 July 1861. The letter is document 170 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Tassara spoke for Spain at the capital through the war's first year. Seward's letters to him worked the home end of the Spanish tie. This note, sent the day Schurz reported from Madrid, shows both ends of that tie in motion at once. Spain watched Cuba above all, fearing the war might leap to its island colony. An island colony near the war made Spain a power Seward could not neglect.
frus-1861-d270:
Writing on 29 May 1861, Mr. Brown sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 270 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the opening months of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d70:
A second letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams bears the date 17 August 1861. It is document 70 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward liked to split his orders into short, single point letters. The habit kept each file clean and each order plain. This one belongs to the August push to keep Britain's neutrality strict, while Union arms rebuilt at home. Single point letters let Adams file each order with the talks it governed. Clean files spared later talks the fog that loose records so often breed.
frus-1862-d170:
Filed out of date order as Document 170, this Seward dispatch to Charles Francis Adams in London is dated 21 October 1862. Adams was the American minister to Britain; Seward, as Secretary of State, directed him from Washington.

The printers of the Foreign Relations volumes placed some letters where their enclosures belonged, which breaks the date line. A reader following the London file meets this letter among the late-October papers, though it was written a few days earlier. Its home week was one of active French pressure for joint action on the war, which Britain had yet to accept. Southern agents worked London's clubs and press hard, and the legation tracked their moves.
frus-1862-d270:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, addressed William L. Dayton in Paris on 22 April 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 270 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter shared its date with a Dayton report home.

Seward wrote three days before New Orleans fell, with the expedition's outcome still unknown in Washington. Orders sent at such moments had to hold whether the news broke well or badly. The Paris file is full of this kind of writing: calm on the surface, framed for several futures at once. This dispatch is a clean example of the style. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d370:
Viscount Treilhard wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 August 1862, opening a run of exchanges printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume as Documents 370 through 379. The letters sit in the volume's French section.

Treilhard's correspondence with Seward runs through August and September 1862, the war's most anxious foreign season. The letters traded while Bull Run was lost and Lee invaded Maryland, weeks when French intentions mattered intensely to Washington. This first letter begins a channel the reader can follow almost week by week into the fall. Seward tested what Mercier said against what Dayton reported from Paris, week by week.
frus-1862-d470:
The Chevalier Giuseppe Bertinatti, Italy's minister in Washington, received this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 February 1862. It is Document 470 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Bertinatti represented a kingdom the United States had been quick to recognize and welcome, and dealings between the two governments were warm. A note from Seward to the Italian minister belonged to the friendly routine of recognition, trade, and courtesy between two young national states. Set among the volume's tenser files, the Italian exchange in Washington is a quiet stretch of water. It shows that Civil War diplomacy also included keeping friends close, not only keeping enemies out.
frus-1862-d570:
Dated 12 May 1862, this report from Henry Shelton Sanford in Brussels was printed out of order among the autumn papers of the Belgian file. It is Document 570 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The volume's Belgian papers were gathered by subject, so a May report can rest between September letters. Sanford's spring dispatch belongs to the season of Union advance, when his reports carried improving news and a watchful eye on Confederate agents in Europe. Its placement is a small lesson in reading the printed record: dates, not positions, give the true sequence. Restored to May, the letter fills out the spring half of a file that runs warm and frequent all year.
frus-1862-d670:
Anson Burlingame dated this dispatch 9 January 1862 and sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Burlingame served as the American minister to China, where the United States held treaty rights in a set of open ports. The letter is document 670 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Reports from Peking and the ports kept Washington aware of a vast land in deep unrest. The Taiping revolt tore through China in those years. An envoy's letters mixed court news, trade facts, and the claims of Americans on the ground. This one adds its share to the file that let Seward speak for American stakes in China.
frus-1862-d70:
A letter home from Charles Francis Adams, dated 23 May 1862, landed on Seward's desk. It was printed as Document 70 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d170:
Five letters in the volume bear the date 24 April 1863. This note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams is one of Washington's two. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 170 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward's two sheets of 24 April joined Adams's three of the same date in the printing. Each side wrote from its own last news, ten days stale. This letter opens Washington's half of the peak day. It fed the brief at its spring height: claims, ships, and tone, all pressed at once from a desk in a capital at war.
frus-1863p1-d270:
Writing from London on 21 August 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward; the catalog title misprints the Secretary's first word as 'Air.' The dispatch is document 270 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For historians, this run is a prime source on Britain's choices. It shows how close London came to stepping into the war, and why it never did. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d370:
Writing in Washington on 26 January 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward on British business. The paper is document 370 in the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Lyons knew that harsh words could push the two nations toward a fight neither wanted. His notes are firm on British rights but measured in tone. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d470:
Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington received a letter dated 21 April 1863 from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d570:
Among the day's business on 17 June 1863 was a letter from Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d670:
From the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward: a letter dated 20 November 1863. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. From the London end, the work was pressure and reporting. Adams pushed the British government on Confederate shipbuilding and sent home his reading of British politics and opinion. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d70:
Two letters to London from Secretary of State William H. Seward bear the date 3 February 1863; this is the first of them. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 70 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward's same-day pairs split the London brief into clear parts. One sheet might carry a claim to press; the next, news or a fresh order. This letter opens the pair of 3 February. With its mate, it shows the secretary's desk in a busy week. He fed his envoy the points he would need when he next faced the British foreign office.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d170: American delegation minutes of the tenth regular meeting of the Moscow Conference, held on October 28, 1943, form Document 170 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. By the tenth meeting the ministers were closing their texts, including the joint declaration that made the conference famous. The minutes preserve the order of business and the words used, as the delegation heard them. The volume prints them in full in the Moscow section.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d270:
A Cairo meeting of 25 November 1943 between President Roosevelt and Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek left no official record, and an editorial note in the volume covers it instead. The time and place come from the President's Log, which notes that tea was served, and the editors gather the rest from later accounts.

Elliott Roosevelt says Madame Chiang described her plans for improving China, above all in literacy, and that unity in China, meaning the Chinese Communists, came up again. Stilwell's account says Burma operations were discussed and that Chiang reversed himself on every point of paper C.C.S. 411/2, points he had accepted that same day with Churchill and Mountbatten. The editors judge it was probably here that Roosevelt promised a sizable amphibious operation across the Bay of Bengal.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d370: No official minutes have been found for a Tehran meeting of 30 November 1943, and an editorial note in the volume covers it instead. The editors reconstruct it from four sources: the President's Log, a department historian's 1954 memorandum of a talk with General Hurley, a 1954 letter from Minister Dreyfus, and Elliott Roosevelt's book. From those sources, the note states, the principal subjects discussed at the meeting were Iran's economic problems and the desire of the United States to help solve them. The list of those present is given on the same evidence.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d470:
On December 3, 1943, the United States Chiefs of Staff put their position into a formal memorandum, printed later in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume. The American chiefs were at Cairo between the Tehran meeting and the opening of the Second Cairo Conference. A companion British memorandum bears the same date.

Each side at Cairo wrote down its views before facing the other across the table, and these papers framed the argument of the joint sessions. The American memorandum is one of those founding texts of the debate. Readers who pair it with the British paper and the minutes that followed can watch a strategy dispute being set up on paper.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d570:
Charles W. Taussig, co-chairman of the Anglo-American Caribbean Commission, wrote this memorandum on January 16, 1945. The Commission joined the United States and Britain in overseeing Caribbean colonies and bases acquired during the war. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

The Caribbean was the alliance's backyard: American bases on British islands, colonial economies strained by war, and questions about the islands' future. Taussig, a businessman close to Roosevelt, worked that seam between the two empires. For readers, his memorandum shows a quieter theater of Anglo-American cooperation, where the postwar questions were about colonies and development rather than invasions.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d70: Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on October 29, 1943, amid the same day's heavy traffic between the capitals. The letter is Document 70 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. With Moscow done and Cairo set for late November, the two leaders were shifting from ministers' work to their own. The record gives sender, receiver, and date, and no topic. The letter appears in the Foreign Relations volume in that order of business.
frus-1944-quebec-d170:
No official memoranda of this luncheon meeting were ever found, the editors report, so the note reconstructs it from Canadian Prime Minister Mackenzie King's notes. The conversation at the lunch turned largely on personalities. The three leaders discussed General de Gaulle, Madame Chiang Kai-shek, and Marshal Stalin, among others.

King's notes also record talk of how Roosevelt felt as head of the strongest military power in the world. The table considered what might have happened if Hitler had got into Britain, Roosevelt's chances of reelection, and the length of King's own prime ministership. The note shows the editors preserving even an informal meal in the conference record, on a single witness's evidence.
frus-1944-quebec-d270:
Planning needs a date, and C.C.S. 678, the British Chiefs' paper of September 13, 1944, proposes one for the end of the war against Japan. Redeployment of forces, production planning, and allocation of manpower all had to be related to an estimated date, the British argued. Without one, every department would plan against a different war.

To make due allowance for contingencies, they recommended the Combined Chiefs accept a planning date two years after the defeat of Germany. The proposal was debated the next day. The date finally adopted for production and manpower planning, recorded in the September 15 minutes, was eighteen months after Germany's defeat, to be adjusted as the war developed.
frus-1944-quebec-d70:
Ambassador John Gilbert Winant wrote to Secretary of State Hull on September 14, 1944. He wrote from London while the Quebec Conference sat in Canada. The State Department placed the message in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Winant's reports during the conference carried London's view to Washington. The British leadership was overseas at the time. Britain at home endured the first V-2 rocket attacks. Its leaders bargained in Canada at the same time. For readers, the message shows a third capital speaking. London spoke through its most trusted American listener. Winant was also a close friend of Britain.
frus-1945-50-intel-d170:
On 1 October 1946 the Eighth Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board sat, and the minutes of the session survive here. It stands as document 170 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The war had just ended, and the United States was keeping a central spy service in peace for the first time.

The record runs item by item, the way the meeting itself ran, with each topic closed by the group's choice on it. The brevity is the point: what the group did not settle, the minutes do not claim it did. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d270: "Draft Proposed NSC Directive" bears the date 5 May 1948. Readers meet it as document 270 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. With the Soviet threat in mind, the Council was deciding what secret work the United States should do abroad. The form is stiff because it has to be: each line is a rule that a named office can be held to.
frus-1945-50-intel-d370:
The Chief of the Intelligence Coordinating and Planning Staff (Childs) addressed a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 21 February 1949. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 370, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The first Dulles Report season had begun: an outside team judged the CIA while the agency and its partners answered back.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d70:
Smith wrote to Rosenman, the president's special counsel, on 10 January 1946. The budget director and the president's lawyer were the two staff hands closest to the coming directive. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Legal form mattered: the new intelligence authority would rest on a presidential directive, and its wording had to survive the departments' lawyers. Smith writing to Rosenman shows the Budget Bureau and the White House counsel joining their drafts. Readers tracking how paper becomes power should linger here. Twelve days after this letter, Truman signed the directive the two men's offices had shaped. The National Intelligence Authority and its Central Intelligence Group sprang into being.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d170:
Two pressing problems head the briefing book paper “Principal Hungarian Problems.” Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Both turn on how far Soviet power, holding Hungary under the armistice, will reach.

The first problem is the American share in the Allied Control Commission's work. The second is the size of Hungary's reparation bill. The paper fears Moscow might use its grip on the armistice to meddle in Hungarian home affairs, or to domineer the country outright. A crushing reparation demand would cripple Hungary's economy and slow the recovery of Europe. American and British interests run much the same here, but Washington prefers its own line of approach to the Russians.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d270:
Over seven hundred names stood on the War Crimes Commission's lists, Stettinius reported on 6 January 1945. His memorandum answers the President's request of 3 January. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

The commission has drawn up two lists, one German and one Italian, with Hitler, Goebbels, Goering, Himmler, and Streicher among the names. Its advice runs three ways. Cases should generally be tried in the national courts of the countries wronged. A convention should set up a United Nations court for cases referred to it. Until then, mixed military tribunals should sit. The American representative goes along with all of this, and holds that Hitler and the chief Nazis belong on the lists.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d370:
France would get its own zone of occupation in Germany, under a Soviet proposal tabled by Molotov on February 7, 1945. The paper is short. It states that allotting France a separate zone, to be held by French forces, had been found desirable. It had been decided, the paper adds.

French occupation authorities would run their zone under the general guidance of the Control Council. The text came out of the foreign ministers' meeting that morning. Moscow's support for a French zone surprised some at the table. Read closely, the paper also keeps France under the three-power council's hand, a limit Paris would later resent.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d470:
Release mechanics fill this telegram from Stephen Early to Jonathan Daniels at the White House, sent February 11, 1945. The communiqué text would be dispatched that night, Early wrote. Two declarations had gone ahead: one on Poland, one on liberated Europe. Daniels should disregard earlier instructions and insert these texts where indicated.

One title was to be killed: "Declaration on Poland" would run inside the communiqué without a title. Word-level edits follow, down to changing "it is recognized" to "they recognized that Poland" near the end. A separate statement was to be prepared for release at the same moment, as its own story. The wire is the sound of a news operation landing a summit.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d70:
Alger Hiss sent two draft memoranda toward the President on 27 October 1944, and this covering note explains them. Hiss was special assistant to the director of the Office of Special Political Affairs. He wrote to Harley Notter, chief of the Division of International Security and Organization, in Washington.

The drafts had been prepared at Stettinius's direction. The main one simply lists the items left open at Dumbarton Oaks and asks for a chance to discuss how to settle them. A second memo covers the United States position on voting in the Security Council. Hiss says both drafts went to Dunn, Hackworth, and Wilson for comment, and the voting memo would be cleared with the Joint Chiefs.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d170:
The U.S. Chiefs of Staff accepted the British staff agenda in a memorandum dated June 27, 1945. The paper, C.C.S. 880/2, is document 170 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It approves the British outline and the plan for which side would write which papers.

The Americans add two cautions. The item on control and command against Japan concerns a reorganization of the Southwest Pacific command already under study. They would like it settled before the conference if possible. On Russian participation in the Pacific war, they doubt joint discussion will be needed. They will not be ready to take the matter up until after their own talks with the Russians. They suggest both sides swap papers in advance where they can.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d270:
The Informal Policy Committee on Germany sent the Secretary of State the occupation directive for Austria on June 23, 1945. The covering memorandum and its enclosure form document 270 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The Joint Chiefs of Staff had advised that they had no military objection to the directive.

The enclosed directive, IPCOG 9/2, is addressed to the commander in chief of the American forces of occupation in Austria. It tells him how to act in his two hats: as the American member of the Allied governing body for Austria, and as the ruler of the American zone. It lays out the basic policies for military government after the combined command in Austria ends. Copies went to the War, Navy, and Treasury secretaries and to the Joint Chiefs.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d370:
Writing to the new Secretary of State on July 7, 1945, Pauley sets out the reparations problems he wants Byrnes to grasp before and at the conference. The first is France. Britain urged France's inclusion in the Moscow talks, and Pauley and Harriman supported it, but the Soviets would not accept it. Maisky stood on the Crimea protocol.

Since the question grew out of the Big Three's own Crimea agreement, Pauley argues, only the Big Three could settle it. He also warns against the Soviet attempt to fix a total dollar value on reparations. That road, he fears, leads into the very difficulty the talks had so far avoided.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d470:
Italy is the ninth topic in Dunn's extracts of his July 14, 1945 talk with Sir Alexander Cadogan at Potsdam. Cadogan stated that his government agreed with Washington in wishing to conclude peace with Italy. The Foreign Office, he said, had been working on a draft treaty. He showed no enthusiasm for bringing the Italian treaty before the Council of Foreign Ministers.

He wished first to show the British draft to the Americans. He agreed that early elections were desirable, to be held in 1945 if possible. Cadogan laid emphasis on drawing Italy closer to the West, and on enabling her to rebuild her army enough to keep order at home and resist aggression.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d570:
President Truman answered Marshal Stalin on the Trieste dispute in a top secret letter of June 25, 1945. Sent from Olympia, Washington, it is document 570 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It replies to Stalin's protest of June 21.

Truman says the Trieste talks have ended and a further military accord is signed. Those talks, he stresses, only put the June 9 political deal into effect. The final fate of Venezia Giulia stays reserved for the peace settlement. Yugoslav rule was allowed east of the agreed line, and no one has meddled with it there. In return, the Allied commander must hold full sway west of the line. Truman notes the Yugoslav commander at first refused to grant that sway under article 3.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d670:
Henry Villard, chief of the African Affairs desk, sent the French position on Tangier from Paris on July 6, 1945. His confidential wire is document 670 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. A French official, Meyrier, had handed the U.S. team a formal note the evening before.

The note says the Russian request makes it vital to define the talks' terms precisely first. No answer should go to Moscow until those terms are agreed. France's own aim is stated with care. The state of things at Tangier in 1940, before Spain's military intrusion, must be restored. The statute of 1923, Paris holds, must be brought back into force in place of the Spanish regime. A like note went to the British team the same day.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d70:
Acting Secretary of State Joseph Grew recorded a June 16, 1945 evening meeting with President Truman in the White House study. His memorandum of conversation, printed in extracts, is document 70 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. Grew raised several matters; the printed passage covers the State Department's list of staff for the Berlin trip.

Grew asked whether Truman had approved the recommended list. The President said he had not seen it and pointed to the pile of papers on his desk, where he guessed it lay. He would be satisfied with the Department's choices, he said, and left the matter entirely to the Secretary's judgment. The extract gives a candid look at a new president, two months in office, leaning on his State Department.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1070:
Ambassador Jefferson Caffery cabled Washington from Paris on July 31, 1945. He reports France's formal answer on the Greek elections. A Foreign Office memorandum dated July 30 has now reached his embassy.

Caffery had first reported France's likely acceptance on July 21. The new memorandum confirms that earlier report in writing. The French government, Paris states, accepts readily to take part in four-power control of the elections. The French also share the American view on secrecy. The consultations must stay quiet until all four governments have answered, and the Greek government has been officially informed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1170:
America's military chiefs wrote to President Truman on 20 July 1945, in the middle of the Potsdam Conference. The Joint Chiefs kept a direct line to the commander in chief through the whole summit. Their notes carried the armed forces' view of the questions on the table.

The war against Japan still raged while the peace of Europe was drafted. That fact stood behind every chiefs' message of these weeks. This one brought Truman the uniformed view at the height of the talks. It is the top brass advising in writing, part of the brief the president weighed each day.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1270:
General MacArthur, commanding United States Army forces in the Pacific, wrote to the Joint Chiefs of Staff on 21 July 1945. MacArthur's headquarters was driving toward Japan from the southwest Pacific. His message reached the chiefs while they sat with the president at Potsdam.

A theater commander's word carried the war as it looked from the front. Plans for the final blows against Japan ran through his office. This dispatch fed his view into the summit's counsels. It shows the Pacific war speaking for itself in the record. The voice is its most famous commander's, heard at the talks that would help end that war.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1370:
The chairman of the President's War Relief Control Board wrote to President Truman on 22 July 1945. The board watched over private relief groups raising money and goods for war victims abroad. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Relief rarely shares a page with strategy, yet in 1945 the feeding and housing of millions was a first-order problem. A board chairman writing to the president shows the subject reaching the top. This paper widens the volume's frame: beside the borders and armies, readers meet the men counting bread and medicine for a continent in ruins. They were asking the president to keep their work in view.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-70:
Byrnes described a private talk to the foreign ministers at 4 p.m. on July 23, 1945. An editorial note in volume two ties that missing conversation to one that survives. It is the seventieth unnumbered item following document 710.

Byrnes stated that he had expressed the U.S. views on German reparations to Molotov that morning. He had subsequently informed Eden of this talk as well. No other record of the Byrnes-Eden conversation has been found, the editors note. The morning talk itself can be read in Bohlen's minutes, printed earlier in this sequence. There Byrnes warned that America would not finance German imports. The note thus preserves a link in the day's diplomacy: the warning to Moscow was promptly passed to London, in a conversation no one minuted.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d770:
The British delegation tabled this proposal on July 30, 1945, as document 770. It dates from the conference's final three days. British drafting in the endgame carried the mark of a new government finding its feet. The text joined the second Potsdam volume's closing papers.

Late British texts show London balancing its two partners. Britain needed American support and Soviet restraint at once. Readers can watch that balance being struck on paper. The document also proves the new team's speed: Attlee's men were tabling texts within days of taking office. It adds a British voice to the endgame's chorus.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d870:
The United States delegation tabled this proposal at Babelsberg on July 21, 1945. It is a draft directive from the heads of government to their commanders of occupation forces in Germany. The commanders sat on the Control Council for Germany. The draft tells them which agreed policies to press for in that council.

The orders include ending all military groups, removing active Nazis from posts of power, and arresting war criminals. They also call for a reparations program that destroys Germany's war industry. Further points treat Germany as one economic unit, with central control of finance, farming, trade, and transport. Other clauses cover free press rules and political party activity.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d970: Soviet delegates handed Pauley this draft protocol on July 1, 1945, fixing the Soviet share of German reparations. It claims gold stocks, assets abroad, and securities of German firms in the west. The draft also claims an equal share of industrial equipment in western zones. The American and British members held that a trade had been made. In return for its equipment percentages, the Soviet Union had agreed to drop certain claims. Those claims covered external assets, captured gold, and German company securities in the west.
gao-gaoreports-b-298370: Brian X. Scott doubled his August 2006 protest — two case numbers, one man's fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. He challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Individuals get the same full hearing as the firms. One man's fight got the full process.
gao-gaoreports-b-299370: James C. Trump took his February 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. He said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Individuals get the same full hearing as the corporations.
gao-gaoreports-b-303170: Army procurement dollars for logistics contractors got a fiscal ruling in this April 2005 GAO call, which tests the spending. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the use was legal. The law had the final word. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-310970: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Brian X. Scott. The March 26, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-b-311070: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by North Shore Medical Labs, Inc.; Advanced BioMedical Laboratories, LLC. Decided April 21, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-370: Car crash ratings could get better in 2005, and GAO's report says NHTSA's new-car program had room to improve. The safety stars got a critical eye. The drivers deserved the clearest grades. The program had to be enhanced. The drivers deserved the clearest grades.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-670: SEC and CFTC penalty collections were progressing in 2005, and GAO's report says continued gains were made, though the SEC needed more management attention. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the fines deserved collecting. The attention had to be given.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-870: Wetlands jurisdiction decisions needed better support in 2005, and GAO's report says the Corps had to back its calls on not asserting authority. The findings demand the reasoning. The report warns that the waters deserved honest decisions. The support had to be better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-970: Colombia's drug flight shoot-down program added safeguards in 2005, and GAO's report says new protections were implemented, though effects were unclear. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the traffickers' planes deserved stopping. The safeguards had to work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1070: Security clearances needed White House attention in 2006, and GAO's report says more OMB action was required to fix the process. The findings demand the leadership. The report warns that the vetting line was itself a vulnerability. The clearances had to be cleared faster.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-270: Federal call centers needed better metrics sharing in 2006, and GAO's report says a mechanism for sharing practices and data was needed. The findings demand the system. The report warns that the government's phone lines should learn from each other. The mechanism had to be built.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-470: Commuter rail issues belonged in the Amtrak debate in 2006, and GAO's report says the rail questions should be considered. The findings make the case. The report warns that the morning trains deserved a seat at the table. The issues had to be considered.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-570: Wildfire cost-sharing lacked clear rules in 2006, and GAO's report says the absence of guidance raised concerns about splitting costs. The findings demand the clarity. The report warns that the burning hills' bills should be fairly divided. The guidance had to be clear.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-670: Burned lands' recovery needed better tracking in 2006, and GAO's report says the Forest Service and BLM could benefit from improved information. The findings demand the data. The report warns that the scarred acres deserved honest accounting. The information had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-770: Border-crossing deaths had doubled since 1995, and GAO's 2006 report says the Border Patrol's prevention efforts had grown but the dying continued. The findings count the tragedy. The report warns that the desert should not be a graveyard. The deaths had to stop.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-870: Emergency job grants were getting faster in 2006, and GAO's report says Labor had improved award timeliness and data collection, though more steps were possible. The findings balance credit and prodding. The report shows the rapid aid was getting more rapid. The grants had to keep improving.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-970: Federal financial systems were still broken in 2006, and GAO's report says improvements were underway but serious problems persisted. The findings balance hope and warning. The report cautions that the government's books needed more than patches. The systems had to be fixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-170: International energy talks were useful but limited in 2007, and GAO's report says the forums aided cooperation within constraints. The findings balance hope and realism. The report shows the diplomats talked energy, even when the politics burned. The forums had their place.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-70: Export-control secrets needed better guarding in 2007, and GAO's report says agencies should assess vulnerabilities and improve guidance. The findings target the weak spots. The report warns that the tech that could arm enemies needed tighter lips. The secrets had to stay secret.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-770: Rusty trestles and dark tunnels drew GAO's eye in 2007 — the report asks what Washington owes the safety of railroad bridges. The findings weigh the federal role in watching spans and funding fixes. When a century-old bridge carries hazmat, the report argues, oversight is not optional.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-870: Homeland Security's computers were sitting ducks in 2007 — GAO's report says big weaknesses in support systems needed immediate action. The findings read as a fire alarm for the security department's own networks. The report's irony is sharp: the cyber guardians needed guarding.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-670: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on military Readiness: Joint Policy Needed to Better Manage the Training and Use of Certain Forces to Meet Operational Demands. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-70: This 2007 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at DOD Schools: Additional Reporting Could Improve Accountability for Academic Achievement of Students with Dyslexia. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-770: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at elections: Federal Programs for Accrediting Laboratories That Test Voting Systems Need to Be Better Defined and Implemented. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gertrude-life-and-revelations-1870:
Gertrude of Helfta, a Benedictine nun and scholar of the thirteenth century, recorded her visions in the Legatus Divinae Pietatis, the Herald of Divine Love. Sister M. Frances Clare of Kenmare translated the Life and Revelations into English in 1870. Gertrude died in 1302, and her book is the great record of the Helfta school of visionaries.

Christ speaks to her heart in exchanges of love, and the liturgy of the convent year frames every vision. Her devotion to the heart of Jesus stands here near its source, centuries before it spread through the church. The nuns who loved her finished the book from her notes. It remains a summit of medieval women's writing on prayer.
goethe-faust-part-1-taylor-1870:
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe wrote Faust over much of his long life. Bayard Taylor gave Part One to America in 1870, keeping the original meters. His version made Goethe's masterpiece a classic in English as well as German.

Faust, a scholar sick of book learning, strikes a pact with Mephistopheles. The devil shows him youth, pleasure, and the world beyond his study. Faust woos Gretchen, whose ruin gives the tale its deep pathos and pain. Love, guilt, and striving clash in scenes of song and dread. Taylor's verse keeps the shifts of mood that made Faust famous.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_CH:
In 1970 the CIA ran a plot to block Salvador Allende from taking office in Chile, and it failed. Kissinger Briefed Nixon on Failed 1970 CIA Plot tells how Henry Kissinger reported that failure to President Nixon.

The briefing book, part of the Chile's Coup at 50 series, publishes the records of that briefing and the plot behind it. A kidnapping scheme ended with Chile's army chief murdered, and Allende took office anyway. Three years later a coup succeeded where the plot had not. The documents connect those two attempts in the words of the men who ran the first one.
grimoire-pope-honorius-1670:
