Another group grew used to even-numbered sets, letting the researchers test reactions to sets that cannot split evenly. Both known patterns were successfully reproduced. Showing the two strategies coexist clarifies that young brains use more than one route to quantity.
plos-pone-0350270:
Gizachew Tadele Tiruneh and co-authors evaluated Ethiopia's move to digitize its community health information system, which health workers use to track mothers and children in rural villages. The government rolled out the electronic system in 2018, but its effect on service use was unproven. Their 2026 survey compared households in areas with and without the system, matching similar communities to make the comparison fair.

Areas with the digital system did better on nearly every measure. Contraceptive use, births in facilities, and childhood vaccination coverage all ran higher, with gains of roughly nine to fifteen percentage points after adjustment. The authors call the results evidence that digitizing frontline records can transform maternal and child health, while noting the survey design cannot fully rule out other explanations.
plos-pone-0350670:
Ruby Hornuvo and colleagues held group talks with eighty seven waste workers in Greater Accra, Ghana, and Kisumu, Kenya, comparing plastic only collectors with mixed waste collectors. Informal workers fill huge gaps where city services fall short. Talks sorted barriers, helpers, and fixes for each business type across both cities.

Both groups lacked crushers and trucks, faced harassment, met faecal hazards in waste, and got little public respect. Paths diverged by city: Accra had moved toward rigid plastic sorting, while home sorting in Kisumu stayed low. Fair pay, gear, and recognition for informal collectors are prerequisites, the authors argue, for any clean city plan to work.
plos-pone-0350770:
Eui Jun Lee and co-authors in Korea tested whether a small language model could help sort sick children in an emergency department in 2026. Triage, judging who needs care first, is safety critical, and big models are hard to run inside hospitals.

They trained the model on tens of thousands of past visits, rewarding it for safe choices. It matched the recorded triage level in well over half of test cases and was nearly always within one level. Dangerous under-triage was rare. A model using only structured data scored higher overall, so the authors present the language model as support, not a replacement, for nurses.
plos-pone-0351070:
Kang and colleagues read the full genomes of two scrub typhus bacteria from South Korea in a 2026 study. Scrub typhus is a mite-borne fever common in Asia, and the strain studied matches a Japanese reference type also found in Korea. Two archived patient isolates were sequenced with a mix of long and short reading methods.

Both genomes formed single circular chromosomes packed with repeated stretches, a known trait of this bacterium. Their surface and typing markers matched the Japanese reference exactly, and family trees placed them in its group. Complete local genomes help track how this fever's strains relate across borders and guide future vaccine and test design.
plos-pone-0351170:
Daniel Perez-Garcia de los Salmones and colleagues studied personal ornaments, beads and pendants, from Llonin Cave in Asturias, Spain. Layers span roughly twenty two thousand to eleven thousand years ago, the largest such set in the region. Tests covered animal source, size, wear, and making marks to trace where pieces came from and how they were made and used.

Patterns shifted over time in whether the cave group made ornaments or brought them in, and in what the pieces signalled socially. Shell and material links tie coastal and inland groups together. Ornaments were not mere decoration: they carried identity and mapped movement and alliances among Ice Age hunter groups in northern Iberia.
plos-pone-0351470:
Yong Zhang and Runming Zhao present a vision system tuned to find small faults on power lines from small field computers. Lines cross busy scenes, faults vary hugely in size, and edge gear has little power to spare. Their design guards fine detail early, then uses focused attention to pick out key defects while shuffling channels to keep the model lean.

On a cable inspection data set, the system beat its base model on both correct calls and overall detection scores. Extra tests showed it also handled insulators, dampers, and bolts well. For power firms, a compact detector that stays accurate on tiny faults could mean faster drone patrols and fewer missed risks.
plos-pone-0351670:
Life-threatening complications in pregnancy are rare but telling events for a health system. Ye Xu, Peimin Hua, and Ye Shen analyzed more than one hundred fifty-six thousand deliveries in Wuxi, China, across four years of citywide monitoring, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

About three hundred fifteen critical cases were found, roughly one in five hundred births. The rate held steady for three years, then rose in the final year. Mothers aged thirty-five and older grew to about a quarter of cases, driving much of the increase. Risk group patterns shifted too, from mostly high-risk toward more moderate-risk mothers, a warning the authors send to local planners.
plos-pone-0351870:
Four health problems now show up early and often in Chinese schoolchildren: poor eyesight, obesity, tooth decay, and curved spines. Yun Shao and co-authors built a shared risk checklist covering all four, described in this 2026 PLOS One paper aimed at children aged seven to nineteen.

Guided by national child health plans, the team drafted a three-level framework from past research and expert meetings. Specialists then rated and trimmed the items through two rounds of structured consultation. The result is a single tool meant to flag risky habits and conditions before disease sets in, helping schools and clinics aim prevention where it counts most.
plos-pone-0351970:
Irena Danilovska and three colleagues built a new scale in this 2026 PLOS One study for spotting what sets successful startup founders apart. Most older tools judge the firm, or use broad personality tests made to explain why people start businesses at all. They say little about which founders actually succeed. The team wrote a thirty-one item scale covering six traits, among them resilience, curiosity, bold decision making, and leadership that changes teams.

They tested the scale on more than ten thousand people: proven founders, company managers, and would-be founders. The six traits held together well as a measure. They also separated successful founders from the other two groups by wide margins, far wider than broad personality tests usually manage. Backers and coaches could use such a scale to judge founder potential earlier.
plos-pone-0352170:
Hirsch and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, catalog what neighborhood data exist inside a giant American COVID-19 research alliance. The alliance joins fourteen long-running health cohorts, more than fifty thousand people in all, so their stored addresses can reveal how place shaped pandemic outcomes. The paper is an inventory, meant to make later studies possible.

Together the cohorts cover areas holding about half the United States population, though only about a quarter of its land, since people cluster. Compared with the country, covered areas were more urban and wealthy, with more residents born abroad and fewer cars per household. Twelve cohorts had recorded neighborhood traits, most often local income and education. Food access and walkability were the commonest built-environment measures, while nature data, such as air quality and green space, were rarest. The authors say harmonizing this patchwork is the next step.
plos-pone-0352270:
Gregory Kearney and four colleagues map COVID-19 deaths across North Carolina in this 2026 study. They ask whether the places with the most deaths were also the most socially vulnerable. Vulnerability here covers poverty, age, housing, and similar hardships. The data cover more than twenty-five thousand deaths from March 2020 to April 2022.

Using mapping software, the team located clusters where deaths ran high. Those hot spot areas scored higher on overall social vulnerability than the rest of the state. The gap was real but modest, and clustering patterns were mixed rather than uniform. Vulnerability therefore explains part of the uneven death map, not all of it. The authors offer the approach as a template for fairer responses to future respiratory outbreaks.
plos-pone-0352670:
Sherraine Della-Moretta and six colleagues test what happens when a primary care doctor joins the sickle cell team itself. Their 2026 retrospective study covers adults at one American tertiary centre from 2020 to 2025. Sickle cell disease fragments care badly. Patients see haematologists for crises but miss ordinary prevention. The centre embedded a board-certified generalist inside the comprehensive clinic. She attended its meetings and practised beside the specialists. Of nearly four hundred patients, about one hundred seventy-four received her care.

Prevention gaps closed sharply for her patients. Cervical cancer screening odds were roughly four and a half times higher. Depression screening odds were higher still. Tetanus vaccination and sickle-specific annual checks also improved. Acute care use was tracked alongside. Fragmentation is usually blamed on patients missing appointments. This study relocates the fix: put the missing doctor inside the team the patient already trusts, and the routine care finally happens.
plos-pone-0352870:
Lanjie Wu and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of chronic hepatitis B. Many patients on long-term antiviral pills fully suppress the virus's DNA. Yet their blood still carries viral RNA. That RNA is a sign the virus stays active inside the liver. The team reviewed one hundred fifty-five patients who had liver biopsies before treatment. They hunted for baseline traits that predict the lingering RNA signal.

Just under half the patients cleared the RNA. Two baseline traits predicted persistence on their own. One was higher starting viral DNA. The other was the absence of a viral core protein in the liver sample. The pair predicted better than either trait alone. The authors suggest the pairing could help doctors tailor treatment and monitoring. It suits patients whose virus refuses to go fully quiet.
plos-pone-0352970:
Williams, Riley, and Baxter-Gilbert studied what an invading salamander eats in Newfoundland in a 2026 paper. The island had no native amphibians, yet several introduced kinds now thrive, including this small woodland salamander. The team examined stomach contents and judged which prey were native and which were earlier invaders.

Comparing island diets with mainland diets tested whether broader eating helped the salamander settle. Feeding on prey that arrived earlier as invaders may also have eased its path. Invaders that eat flexibly can slip past competition that stops pickier newcomers. The case shows how one invasion can pave the way for the next.
plos-pone-0353070:
José Miguel Hernández-Agudelo and seven colleagues survey this 2026 PLOS One study of bats living in and around rural homes in southern Chile. Habitat fragmentation pushes some bat species into houses, raising contact with people and pets and the chance of disease spread. The team visited sixty-nine dwellings in two regions, documenting the houses and asking residents about bat contact and perceived risk.

Nearly half the homes reported bats, most houses were wooden, and two-thirds had unsealed openings bats could use. Households with dogs, cats, children, or older residents had significantly more contact. Most residents knew bats can transmit disease, mainly rabies, yet preventive habits were inconsistent and risks to livestock were underappreciated. The authors recommend joined-up education covering people, animals, and environment together.
plos-pone-0353170:
Untracht and colleagues, in a 2026 study, test whether light-based scans plus machine learning can judge how well a cancer drug works in lab-grown tumor balls. Most new drugs fail in human trials, often because early lab tests predict poorly. Three-dimensional tumor models grown with several cell types are more realistic, but fast, standard ways to grade them are scarce.

The team scanned tumor balls treated with three doses of a chemotherapy drug using optical coherence tomography, a method that builds depth images from reflected light. Two reader models were compared: one that views flat slices from many angles, and one that reads the full volume at once. The volume model sorted the dose groups far more accurately. The authors also point to the image features that drove the volume model's choices. Their results support using these scans for fast screening of drugs in realistic tumor models.
plos-pone-0353270:
Burchardi and colleagues set out a mixed-methods study in 2026 on care for post-COVID syndrome in Germany. Many patients manage lasting symptoms with little support. The study blends insurance records from dozens of insurers, a patient survey, interviews, and home visits for the most severely ill.

An expert panel will turn the findings into concrete steps for better care. Routine records show real care paths, while interviews reveal where patients feel abandoned. Combining both views should expose fixable gaps, such as missing referrals or unclear responsibility. The design treats patient experience as evidence alongside billing data.
plos-pone-0353470:
Woo Bin Park and four colleagues track how a dog-infecting bacterium rewires the chemistry of the immune cells it invades, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Brucella canis causes canine brucellosis, a growing concern as pet dogs live ever closer to people. Mouse immune cells in culture were infected and their small-molecule chemistry measured at several time points, with the biggest upheaval a day after infection.

Key building blocks tied to energy, defence chemistry, and cell membranes dropped sharply as infection took hold. The time-ordered map shows which pathways the bacterium bends first. The authors offer the atlas as a guide for future work on how this pathogen survives inside its host — and where it might be vulnerable.
plos-pone-0353570:
Aslan and Yılmaz explored brain signals for imagined swallowing in a 2026 study. Swallowing problems affect many people after illness or injury, and brain-based controls could one day help with therapy. Thirty volunteers wore scalp sensors while picturing swallowing saliva and picturing swallowing water, without actually moving.

Signals were cleaned, measured in many ways, and narrowed to the features that differed most reliably. Tests left one person out at a time, so the system had to read a brand-new person's signals, as a clinic tool must. Checking luck-based results guarded against false success. The work is an early step toward therapy tools that respond to mental practice alone.
plos-pone-0353970:
Mee Hoong See led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of BREAST-E, a low-cost method for measuring breast volume before reconstructive surgery using ordinary photographs alone. Software turns photos into three-dimensional models. The team tuned marker numbers, camera angles, and offsets across four levels of breast droop, then checked the estimates against removed tissue in twelve patients.

Estimates ran somewhat low on average, and accuracy was best for breasts without droop, growing shakier as droop increased. See offers the method for hospitals that cannot afford advanced imaging.
plos-pone-0354170:
Rawand Khasawneh and co-authors survey in 2026 dialysis patients in northern Jordan on skill with online health information, confidence in managing illness, and quality of life. Patients at four hospitals completed Arabic versions of three trusted scales. Chronic kidney disease and its treatment weigh heavily on daily life, so what lifts life quality matters for care design.

Life quality linked in simple checks to both online skill and confidence, yet those links faded once social and medical factors were counted. Holding a graduate degree and having a job predicted higher life quality, while diabetes predicted lower. Support may need to target work and schooling gaps first.
plos-pone-0354270:
Ryosuke Katayose and five colleagues study how patchy oxygen in a Japanese lake reshapes where fish and their prey live, in this 2026 field study. Warming surface water and oxygen-starved depths squeeze cold-water fish such as kokanee salmon and rainbow trout into a narrowing band. The team compared two open-water sites in a small lake whose unusual shape creates uneven oxygen conditions, using environmental DNA to locate the fish.

Kokanee DNA concentrated where oxygen stayed favorable in summer, when heat above and low oxygen below pinched their living space. The authors infer that this crowding changes where the fish feed, which in turn may pattern the zooplankton they hunt. Because the evidence is correlational, they phrase the food web effect as a possibility, but the study shows how invisible oxygen landscapes can quietly reorganize a lake's ecology.
plos-pone-0354370:
Maaidah Algamdi and Ali Alghamdi test whether computer models can predict how intense back pain will feel, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study from a Saudi hospital. Sixty-one patients with severe pain from lumbar disc problems provided personal details, lifestyle answers, and MRI scans of their spines. Two popular machine-learning methods were trained to separate strong pain from very strong pain.

Both models struggled. One missed every case of the strongest pain, while the other caught only a third, largely because most patients clustered in the worst category. The number of damaged disc levels mattered most among the clues. The authors are frank: the tools are not ready for clinic use and need far larger samples.
plos-pone-0354470:
Lama El Haj Sleiman and Linda Abou-Abbas published this 2026 mixed-methods study of screening new mothers for depression in a Lebanese public hospital. Postpartum depression often goes unscreened in Lebanon. Nurses and managers there answered surveys and joined discussion groups about what they know and what routine screening would require.

Most nurses recognized the condition and the baby blues, but few knew the standard screening questionnaires or all the risk factors. The obstacles looked organizational rather than resistant staff. The authors recommend training, clear referral routes, and building screening into routine after-birth care.
plos-pone-0354670:
Maryam Ghadimi led a team of eight authors on this 2026 protocol for a review of preventing a rare but blinding infection after eye injections. Injections into the eye treat many retinal diseases, yet clinics mix prevention steps in varied combinations that past reviews judged one at a time. Their plan uses network meta-analysis to compare whole strategies against each other across trials and observational studies.

Evidence will be graded for certainty using a standard framework. As a protocol, the paper promises a map of which prevention bundles work best, once the review is done.
plos-pone-0354870:
Hamidreza Ahmadasadi leads a team of eight testing whether a hormone passes a mother's diabetes risk to her pups, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Asprosin, a fasting hormone that pushes blood sugar up, was their suspect. Twelve pregnant rats were split into diabetic and healthy groups. Blood was sampled from mothers and, at sixteen weeks of age, from their male offspring, to see whether the hormone tracked sugar and fat problems across the generation.

Diabetic mothers carried clearly higher asprosin, and in them the hormone marched with unhealthy fat patterns and glucose measures. Their pups told a different story. Offspring asprosin levels were nearly identical between the groups, and no meaningful links to sugar or fat measures appeared in the young animals. Whatever carries diabetes risk from mother to child in this model, the authors conclude, it is not a simple inheritance of raised asprosin.
plos-pone-0354970:
Iffath Syed and co-authors investigate in 2026 what stresses workers in long term care homes, where burnout, injury, and quitting are common. In depth interviews and a survey gave both stories and counts. Stress at work can spill into health and family life, so naming its sources is a first step toward fixing them.

Time pressure, the work situation itself, and money worries topped the list. Family duties, personal health problems, and caring for children added more strain. Many workers leaned on friends, family, and colleagues for support, and used prayer or mindfulness to cope. The authors present support networks as a real buffer worth strengthening.
plos-pone-0355170:
Dalong Zhang and seven colleagues published this 2026 teaching study from an emergency department in Zhengzhou, China. Thirty resident doctors rotated through two teaching styles in a crossover plan: standard lectures and an immersive role-play method borrowed from a popular scripted murder-mystery game, where trainees act out clinical cases.

Residents reported higher satisfaction with the role-play lessons, and their hands-on clinical scores improved more than with lectures. Test scores and patient feedback showed no clear gap between the two styles. Because the group was small and from one hospital, Zhang presents the game format as a promising extra, not a replacement, for standard training.
plos-pone-0355370:
Wenhua Pu and coauthors published a 2026 cell study in PLOS ONE on a tiny RNA that may throttle muscle building. The work has implications for the muscle wasting seen in lung disease and cancer. Scanning blood from patients with chronic lung disease, the team had spotted this microRNA sharply changed. In mice healing from a muscle toxin injury, miR-191 and a gene called Wwp1 moved in opposite directions, hinting at a control pair.

Adding extra miR-191 to growing mouse muscle cells blocked their maturation: the master muscle gene and the contractile proteins of mature fibers fell, and a growth pathway's genes quieted. The mechanism proved direct: the microRNA latches onto Wwp1's message and suppresses it. The authors name this axis as a control point in muscle differentiation. If the same axis drives wasting in patients, blocking the microRNA could become a strategy against atrophy, though that is future work.
plos-pone-0355470:
Rinseo Park and co-authors tracked how social ties formed and dissolved among students working together inside virtual reality. Immersive classrooms are spreading, but group dynamics inside them are hard to observe with ordinary surveys. Their 2026 study logged interpersonal distances session by session during a university virtual reality course and modelled tie changes statistically.

Each extra connection a student held cut the odds of forming or keeping another tie by more than half. A shared friend, by contrast, more than doubled those odds. Students drifted toward isolation overall, yet their subgroups persisted. Tie changes also reduced lopsided group identification and raised familiarity within pairs. Park and colleagues offer the framework for studying small-group life in virtual spaces.
plos-pone-0356070:
Cas Goos and colleagues audit how well psychology papers report the quality of their measuring tools. When a study copies a questionnaire or task, readers need to know whether it was reliable and sound, and whether the copying team changed anything. The team reviewed dozens of measures used in a large set of repeat studies and their original papers, then re-checked the tools using open response data.

Full detail on how to reuse a measure appeared in about half of the repeat studies and in only a tiny share of originals. Many tools also passed checks for consistency unevenly across labs. Goos and colleagues urge authors and journals to report measurement quality plainly, since weak reporting can hide weak tools.
plos-pone-0356170:
Md Mahfuz Uddin and three colleagues compare eight machine learning methods for predicting cardiovascular disease in this 2026 study. Working from an open clinical dataset, they ranked risk factors with four different selection techniques and tested each algorithm under several cross-validation schemes, scoring accuracy, sensitivity, and overall discrimination. The goal was a fair head-to-head rather than another single-model claim.

One gradient boosting method, LightGBM, gave the most balanced performance, pairing the best discrimination score with strong sensitivity, while a rival edged it on raw accuracy but missed more true cases. Systolic blood pressure dominated the predictions, with age and cholesterol close behind; every trait except gender differed clearly between groups. The authors are measured: performance was respectable but not clinical-grade, and outside validation is required before any real deployment.
plos-pone-0356270:
Mingze Sun and seven colleagues translated a well-known sleep questionnaire into Chinese and tested whether it still works, reporting their results in 2026. The questionnaire, a short screening tool covering several common sleep problems, had not previously been validated for Chinese-speaking patients. Just over two hundred adults being treated for sleep disorders filled in the eleven-question version.

Statistical checks showed the translated questions hung together sensibly, sorting into four groups linked to sleep apnea, insomnia, restless legs, and unusual sleep behaviors. Scores lined up reasonably well with clinical measures such as the severity of breathing pauses during sleep. The authors also worked out cutoff scores for each problem area. They conclude the Chinese version is reliable enough for evaluating adult patients, giving clinics in China a quick shared screening tool.
plos-pone-0356370:
Andrea Pietravalle, Francesco Cavallin, Giovanni Putoto, and Daniele Trevisanuto used simulated data to test a published shortcut for dating a pregnancy after birth. The shortcut measures the width of a newborn's cerebellum by ultrasound and converts it to gestational age. Their 2026 simulation study was aimed at poor countries, where early prenatal scans are rare. It generated four datasets matching real low-income studies. It scored the equation's bias across pregnancy stages.

The equation wobbled with age. It overestimated in the late second trimester by about six days on average. It underestimated near term. Its error bands everywhere spanned weeks, too wide for decisions that hinge on days. The authors conclude this shortcut, as published, is not accurate enough to replace better dating methods where prematurity care depends on the answer.
plos-pone-0356470:
Jing Yu and four colleagues build and validate a questionnaire measuring what Chinese clinical nurses know, feel, and do about caring for older patients' feet, in this 2026 study. Foot problems in the elderly are common and consequential, yet no tailored instrument existed for nurses. The team drafted items from the literature and nurse interviews, refined them through two rounds of expert consultation, then surveyed more than three hundred nurses at two large hospitals.

The finished tool holds forty-eight items across knowledge, attitude, and practice sections. Statistical testing showed a clean structure, strong agreement among experts on the items' relevance, and high reliability, including when nurses retook it later. The authors offer the questionnaire to nurse educators and managers who need to find specific gaps in geriatric foot care and target training accordingly.
plos-pone-0356770:
Wenyi Qin and colleagues sequenced the gut microbes of twenty papillary thyroid cancer patients. Samples came just before and three days after their thyroid surgery. The microbial census was paired with thyroid hormone levels. Their 2026 paired study used full metagenomic sequencing. It compared diversity and composition across the operation. It also hunted for microbe and hormone correlations.

Surgery clearly reshuffled the gut. Diversity and composition shifted significantly. A Clostridium species stood prominent beforehand. Several Bacteroides species, among others, rose after. The authors frame the gut and thyroid as an axis. Removing the gland and starting hormone treatment changes the terrain microbes live in. Microbes in turn may shape how patients absorb and respond to hormone therapy. Targeting the gut could become part of aftercare.
plos-pone-0356870:
Bing Yang, Jiaying He, and Yuncheng Shen designed a pavement crack mapping network small enough to run on a phone. It still had to be accurate enough for road maintenance crews. Their 2026 paper rebuilds the classic U-Net design with three additions. A feature module exploits skip connections. A multibranch module reads cracks at several scales at once. An aggregation module weights features adaptively before the final outline is drawn.

Across four public crack datasets, the model posted the best overlap scores among rivals. It used a tiny fraction of their computing power. It traded a little recall for precision on some sets, missing faint cracks rather than inventing them. The authors released code and data, aiming at real-time inspection from ordinary mobile devices.
plos-pone-0357070:
The PLOS One Editors issued this Expression of Concern in 2026. It concerns an earlier study of a possible heart treatment. That study tested intravenous injections of extracellular vesicles. These are tiny parcels shed by cells. The target was chronically under-supplied heart muscle. An Expression of Concern is a formal warning. It says questions hang over a published article while the record is sorted out, short of a full retraction.

Editors flagged two figure panels that look alike. They flagged supporting images that do not match the published figures. They also flagged missing details about animal welfare approvals and humane endpoints. The corresponding author acknowledged one panel was wrong and supplied a correction. The approval code, the authors said, is no longer available. Readers should treat the original study's findings as unverified until the journal resolves the case.
plos-pone-0357270:
Mehdi Nourzadeh Hadad and Mojtaba Kordrostami test whether zapping a soil booster with gamma rays makes tomatoes grow better, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Humic acid, a dark organic extract, is widely sold as a plant stimulant, but its structure varies and so do results. The team irradiated the acid at two doses, applied each at two field rates alongside untreated controls, and measured growth, leaf chemistry, antioxidant status, yield, and fruit quality across the season.

One combination stood out on almost every measure: acid irradiated at the moderate dose and applied at the higher rate. Those plants grew tallest, photosynthesized fastest, carried the richest leaf nutrients, and produced the most marketable fruit, with better sugars, vitamin C, and lycopene. Raising the application rate helped unless the acid had taken the stronger radiation dose, which erased the gain. The study gives growers a specific recipe rather than a vague endorsement.
plos-pone-0357370:
William H Livingston, Adam L Putnam, and Erin J Wamsley used the night of the 2024 United States presidential election to study how dreams shape feelings. Older ideas held that dreaming about an upsetting event softens its sting by morning. Nearly a thousand American adults rated their feelings on election day and again the next day, and reported what they had dreamed during the night between.

Dreaming about the election did not soothe anyone in this sample. Instead, those who dreamed of it woke with stronger negative feelings and a darker view of their own future and the country's. The pattern appeared among Democrats and independents but not Republicans. Livingston and colleagues say dreams may amplify fresh emotion at first, at least after a charged public event.
plos-pone-0357470:
Dung Ngoc Nguyen and coauthors published a 2026 systematic review in PLOS ONE on how the Big Five traits shape emotional reactivity. That covers how strongly people respond, how sharply they react, and how long feelings last. Earlier research fixated on neuroticism, leaving the other traits half-mapped. The review gathered thirty records covering thirty-one studies and fifty samples published across a quarter-century, and combined the findings study by study.

Neuroticism showed the most steadily troubled profile: stronger negative affect, sharper sensitivity to stressors, and slower recovery. Extraversion and conscientiousness leaned adaptive, above all in richer positive feeling. Openness looked mixed, with sharper responses and a split between reported feelings and bodily readings. Agreeableness appeared broadly prosocial, though its negative reactions depended on context. Clinicians and researchers should read feeling profiles trait by trait, they say, rather than treating reactivity as one score.
plos-pone-0357570:
Sogand Sarmadi leads a team of seven examining why emergency nurses in Tehran think about quitting, in PLOS ONE in 2026. One hundred eighty nurses at university hospitals answered validated scales covering quality of professional life, sleep, job stress, and intention to leave, during 2025. Emergency work piles psychological demand onto broken sleep, and managers need to know which strain actually pushes nurses out the door.

Intention to leave rose alongside poor sleep, higher stress, burnout, and secondary traumatic stress, the wear of absorbing patients' suffering. It fell as compassion satisfaction, the reward nurses feel from helping, rose. Statistical modeling confirmed those forces as predictors, joined by financial status, patient load per nurse, and shift type. The authors argue retention plans should protect the satisfying side of the job and fix rosters and ratios, not merely counsel nurses to endure more.
plos-pone-0357670:
Kyungsup Kwon and coauthors published a 2026 cohort study in PLOS ONE following Long COVID patients for a year with a standardized symptom score. Long COVID lacks agreed measurement, making its course hard to describe. Adults with confirmed infection answered symptom questionnaires across twelve domains at one, three, six, and twelve months, with Long COVID defined by a score at or above the proposed threshold.

Just over a quarter of the nearly two hundred participants met the definition at some point. The share above threshold drifted down across the year, but not significantly, and within individuals scores barely moved: those with Long COVID stayed high, others stayed low. People drifting across the category line mostly hovered near it. The burden, they conclude, is more stable than headlines suggest, though missed follow-up questionnaires limit what the trend can prove.
plos-pone-0357770:
Guogang Wang, Hongwei Sun, and Zichao Feng improved robot navigation in messy settings, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Mobile robots need routes through complex environments where obstacles move and spaces are tight. The team fused two planning approaches: an improved global planner based on BI-RRT, and an enhanced local method called DWA that handles immediate dodging.

Wang's hybrid plans routes across the whole space yet reacts locally to surprises, combining the strengths of both worlds. Global planning alone is too slow to dodge a walking person; local dodging alone can trap a robot in dead ends. Warehouse, hospital, and delivery robots all face this split problem daily. The fusion approach offers a practical design others can adapt.
plos-pone-0357970:
Tianyu Zhang and colleagues published a 2026 computational study in PLOS ONE on PFOA, a persistent industrial pollutant nicknamed a forever chemical. The study examines its possible role in fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction. The team combined toxicology databases, liver gene datasets, and single-cell data, then ran a machine learning search for genes where the chemical's targets and the disease's genes overlap.

Seventeen shared targets emerged, and the learning models narrowed them to six hub genes that classified the disease with very high accuracy in the data. Single-cell analysis showed those genes switching on in distinct liver cell types. Simulations suggested PFOA binds stably to two of the gene products, and in dish-grown liver cells dosed to mimic the disease, PFOA exposure did shift the hub genes' activity. A mechanism through disturbed fat handling and inflammation is proposed, needing animal and human confirmation.
plos-pone-0358070:
Sean Hartmann led a team of eight authors applying explainable AI to MRI scanning, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. MRI scans are slow and costly, and backlogs delay diagnosis. Instead of a black-box model, the team used rule-learning AI whose advice technicians can read and judge.

Hartmann's approach mined the scanning process for steps that can be trimmed without losing image quality. Readable rules matter in medicine, where staff must defend each change to a clinical workflow. Faster scans mean more patients served on the same machines. The study shows a path where AI improves a hospital process while staying open to human checking, a pattern many clinical settings will demand.
plos-pone-0358570: Lam and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on genes and type 2 diabetes in Vietnam. They looked at two known gene variants, one in IL16 and one in IL1B, both tied to inflammation. The study group was the Kinh, the largest ethnic group in Vietnam. Gene risk can differ between populations, so local data help doctors judge what a variant means for Vietnamese patients.
plos-pone-0358770: Li and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study comparing bone surgeons trained by two routes. The setting was one large general hospital in China. They weighed research output against hands-on clinical skill for surgeons from each pathway. Training reform debates often rest on opinion; a side-by-side count gives hospital leaders firmer ground for judging pathways.
plos-pone-0358870:
Sixin Jiang leads a team of seven testing a different way to train the nurses who sterilize a hospital's instruments, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Staff in the central sterile supply department reprocess surgical tools, and sloppy knowledge there becomes infection risk everywhere. Forty nurses were split by chance into two groups for six months of training: one learned through problem based learning, working from real cases, the other through traditional instruction.

At the end, the problem based group scored higher on every measure the study took. Their theoretical knowledge and practical skills both led, and so did their self directed learning ability, teamwork, and satisfaction with the training itself. All differences cleared the usual bar for statistical significance. The authors recommend the case driven approach for a department whose quiet competence the whole hospital depends on, while noting the single site and small sample.
plos-pone-0358970: Ghasemloo and Moradi published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on making large language models better at forecasting. Their method feeds the model extra background knowledge alongside past data points. The goal is sharper guesses about how a series will move over time. Better forecasts of this kind matter in fields like energy, sales, and health, where plans rest on what comes next.
plos-pone-0359270:
Lluis Lis-López and a large team of collaborators set out the protocol in 2026 for a pilot study of genetic newborn screening in Galicia, Spain. Newborn screening today tests babies for a short list of serious conditions from a heel prick blood spot. Genetic screening could widen that list greatly, catching treatable diseases earlier, but it raises practical and ethical questions.

Their project, called NBGENS, is a pilot: a small, careful run designed to test the workflow, the consent process, and the handling of results before any wider rollout. Publishing the protocol in advance keeps the pilot honest and lets other regions copy the design. Galicia's experience will inform the debate now running across Europe.
plos-pone-0359870: Yang and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on reading planning documents with software. The team built a small, fast transformer model boosted with field knowledge. Its task is to spot land-use conflicts, clashes between what a plan allows and what a site suits. The texts came from territorial spatial planning. Faster conflict spotting could help officials revise plans before disputes reach the ground.
plos-pone-0360070:
Manoel Luis Costa and Claudia Mermelstein wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about Brazil's Atlantic Forest, one of the world's richest and most threatened forests. Their approach joins several ways of watching wildlife and habitat: images, sounds, citizen science, and artificial intelligence, used together to assess biodiversity.

Cameras record animals, microphones catch calls, volunteers add sightings, and AI helps sort the flood of records. Combining sources covers species that any single method would miss. Conservation groups guarding the remaining Atlantic Forest can use an integrated assessment like this to decide where protection money works hardest.
pmc-13194970:
Xingli Xu is first author on a 2026 engineering study of wearable ultrasound imaging patches. Piezoelectric micromachined transducers, tiny ultrasound emitters made with chip technology, suit wearables because they are small and low power. Large arrays, though, perform unevenly, and until now performance could only be checked after fabrication.

The authors model how array cells influence each other to predict each cell's vibration, then arrange cells to raise sensitivity, bandwidth, and uniformity together. A narrow sixty-four element array they built achieved wide bandwidth and clear images of neck and foot arteries and the thyroid in volunteers, in real time. The framework guides design of large wearable ultrasound arrays.
pmc-13197570:
Yao Yu and colleagues review microbes living inside tumors in a 2026 survey. Tumors were long thought sterile, but microbes persist inside cancer cells and nearby tissue. The review asks how those microbes arrive, where they sit, and how they shape cancer growth and therapy.

Microbes can sway DNA stability, cell growth signals, and energy use in cancer cells. They also shape immune and support cells around the tumor. The authors sort claims backed by direct tumor proof from those inferred from gut microbes. New tactics include antibiotics, virus-based hunters, and engineered microbes. Low microbe counts and contamination risk still cloud the field, so tighter methods are a top need.
pmc-13198470:
Virginia Maltese and colleagues report a 2026 clinic study on splitting testosterone gel doses. Men with low testosterone often apply gel once a day, which can cause sharp peaks and troughs in blood levels. The team tested whether splitting the same daily dose into two applications steadies levels.

Twelve men switched from once-daily to twice-daily gel at the same total dose. Peaks fell and troughs rose, so the daily swing shrank. The share of men hitting target levels at peak rose from one third to over four fifths. Safety labs, including prostate and blood thickness markers, showed no worrying change. The small, backward-looking study hints that split dosing may smooth hormone control.
pmc-13199670:
Sofie De Braekeleer and colleagues profile hidden HIV reservoirs with a new sequencing assay in a 2026 study. Even on strong therapy, HIV hides inside a few cells as a reservoir that blocks cure. Reading that reservoir in full could guide cure tactics, so the team applied their long-read assay, HIV-PULSE.

They profiled ninety people whose virus was suppressed by therapy. The assay reads near-full viral genomes from single hidden copies. Profiles combined whether each copy was intact, which cells it targets, its diversity, and stored drug resistance. They also flagged likely response to two immune-based therapies. Each person got a tailored reservoir map. The platform may sharpen future cure trials.
pmc-13200370:
Wiebke Könning and colleagues studied chewing strength, nutrition, and frailty in older patients in a 2026 clinic study. Weak chewing pushes older adults away from fiber-rich foods and toward malnutrition. Yet chewing is rarely checked in geriatric care, so the team measured it in one hundred fifty patients at a German clinic.

Patients averaged about eighty-two years old, and most were frail. Nearly half were malnourished and almost half more were at risk. A two-color gum mixing test scored chewing skill. Lower chewing scores tied to higher frailty and poorer nutrition scores. About twenty-nine percent had no teeth at all. The authors urge brief dental checks in routine elder care to protect overall health.
pmc-13200670:
Hanguang Ruan and colleagues review radiosensitizers, agents that make tumors easier to kill with radiation, in a 2026 article. Radiation cures many cancers, but resistant tumors blunt it. Resistance grows from cell traits and the tumor surroundings acting together, so the team surveyed ways to break it.

Strategies span nanomaterials, natural compounds, targeted drugs, immune modulators, and nucleic acid therapies. Promising routes include boosting dose effects in tumors, blocking DNA repair, and pairing radiation with immune therapy. Lab and animal proof is strong, yet clinic use lags. Delivery, normal tissue harm, tumor variety, and a lack of predictive markers block progress. Smart combined platforms are the way forward, they argue.
pmc-13200770:
Katharina Rump and colleagues set out the CONFUSED study protocol in a 2026 paper. Postoperative delirium is sudden confusion after surgery, common in older patients and tied to longer stays and decline. No reliable early warning markers exist, so the study hunts them across data types.

The study runs at a German university hospital in adults having major surgery under general anesthesia. Enrollment continues until one hundred delirium cases are logged, an expected two to three hundred patients. Blood is drawn at four set times for protein, gene, and epigenetic profiling. Clinical details and delirium checks are logged in parallel. Machine learning will fuse the layers into prediction models. As a protocol, it reports no results yet.
pmc-13201970:
A ruptured dissecting aneurysm in a patient with fragile vessels required a two-part surgery in a 2026 illustrative case authored by Hidenori Ohbuchi. The article presents a 43-year-old woman with fibromuscular dysplasia who suffered a subarachnoid hemorrhage from a torn internal carotid artery inside the skull.

Angiography showed the string-of-beads pattern of fibromuscular dysplasia in both neck vessels, plus another aneurysm in a vertebral artery. Surgeons first built a high-flow bypass using a radial artery graft from the external carotid to the middle cerebral artery. They then trapped the damaged segment, and at three months she had no neurological deficits, backing this approach for carefully selected patients.
pmc-13208470:
Doctors say systems thinking is their job but doubt their own skills, in a 2026 survey headed by Ami L DeWaters of residents and teaching faculty. The cross-sectional survey reached physicians across ten United States health systems in 2021, asking about engagement, responsibility, and ability in systems-based practice, a required training competency since 1999.

About fourteen hundred physicians responded, roughly a fifth of those invited to take part. Most felt engaged and responsible, yet only minorities rated their skills adequate for improving systems, tackling social determinants, or managing population health. Respondents also scored their workplaces low on chances to practice these skills, exposing a training gap the authors want programs to close.
pmc-13241670:
Watson's team at Northwestern compared cutting out torn knee meniscus against fixing it, using a national hospital database. Matching balanced over 36,000 knees, half per procedure. 90-day returns, redo operations, and later osteoarthritis care were tracked. Age subgroups under and over forty were looked at apart.

Returns stayed low and similar for both paths. Repair patients needed redo surgery far less often, roughly two percent against four. Cut-out patients sought arthritis treatment within two years sharply more often. Watson reads the pattern as support for keeping the meniscus across all ages.
pmc-13242370:
Chong's team in Singapore review acute-phase proteins as signs of inflammation in turtle care. Albumin, haptoglobin, fibrinogen, and MRP-126 lead the list of hopefuls. Few studies exist, spread across gel runs, immune tests, and blood chemistry. Mass spectrometry proteomics is a newer, sharper tool.

Known ranges exist for only a handful of turtle species. Tested shop-bought assays are rarer still. Values swing widely between and within species, so each species needs its own range, or each animal its own. The team calls for new marker hunts and test building to serve endangered turtles.
pmc-13242470:
Kara Schick-Makaroff and co-authors gathered qualitative studies of response shift, the way patients change how they judge their own quality of life. Their meta-synthesis appeared in Quality of Life Research in 2026. Response shift can hide real change when people rate their health before and after illness or treatment. The team searched six databases and screened more than a thousand records to find studies that explored the idea through interviews and similar methods.

Fourteen studies qualified, and every one of them found signs of response shift. Patients recalibrated by comparing themselves with their past health or with sicker others. Some shifted their priorities to cope, and some redefined what quality of life meant after their condition changed. The review also catalogs rival explanations, like faulty recall, that researchers must rule out. It ends by urging dialogue across research traditions on how people remake meaning.
pmc-13242670:
Megha Bhardwaj and co-authors built a blood test model that estimates a person's future lung cancer risk from DNA methylation marks. Their paper appeared in BMC Medicine in 2026. Low-dose CT screening saves lives, but choosing exactly who benefits most remains difficult and costly. The model was trained on 2,459 participants in a German population cohort, using methylation sites already linked to lung cancer in earlier genome-wide studies.

In a separate Norwegian cohort, the model kept its accuracy for cases diagnosed up to eighteen years later and for near-term cases alike. Its discrimination scores in external testing matched the strong results from development. Because the model covers never-smokers as well as smokers, it could widen or sharpen screening eligibility beyond smoking history alone. The authors present it as a step toward a practical blood-based risk test.
pmc-13243870:
He Yang, Yi Liu, and Tianyu Zhu used genetic instruments to test whether gut microbes help cause esophageal cancer through blood metabolites. Their Mendelian randomization study appeared in the International Journal of Genomics in 2026. Observational links between the gut and this cancer are plentiful but cannot prove direction. Using gene variants tied to microbe and metabolite levels, the team probed cause and mediation for the cancer and its subtype.

Twenty-five gut taxa linked to esophageal cancer risk, eleven raising it and fourteen lowering it, with fifteen taxa tied to the adenocarcinoma subtype. A handful of blood metabolites also showed causal links in both directions. Mediation analysis found metabolites carrying part of the microbes' effect, completing a gut-metabolite-cancer chain. The authors offer the results as leads for biomarkers and for prevention aimed at the microbiome. Genetic evidence, they note, is a hint, not a clinical verdict.
pmc-13245370:
Hassan, Elawady, Wanas, and co-authors engineered metal nanoparticles wrapped in a natural polymer to attack liver cancer, in this 2026 RSC Advances study. Their nanohybrids combine selenium and silver particles, made by green chemistry using onion extract and vitamin C, locked inside chitosan, a shellfish-derived polymer. The design aims to disturb the tumor's redox balance, its management of oxidative chemistry, more than healthy tissue.

In mice with chemically induced liver cancer, treatment improved survival, shrank tumor burden, and preserved liver structure, with the particles accumulating in the liver far more than the kidneys. Tumor tissue showed restored antioxidant defenses and switched on a mitochondrial self-destruct pathway through p53 and caspase-9, while normal tissue was spared. The authors credit the chitosan cage for metering metal release.
pmc-13246470:
Balkiş and Uysal measured the carbon footprint of growing strawberries in Türkiye's Mediterranean Silifke district, in this 2026 Global Challenges study. Using life cycle assessment from field preparation to the farm gate, they traced emissions for each kilogram of fruit grown in open fields, drawing on standard inventory databases and current climate-impact methods.

The footprint landed at the low end of Mediterranean figures. Cultivation dominated the total, and synthetic fertilizer was the single biggest hotspot, far outweighing irrigation electricity. Cutting fertilizer use by a fifth trimmed the footprint noticeably, while solar-powered irrigation barely moved it. The authors say smarter fertilizer use and stable yields are the real levers for lower-carbon fruit.
pmc-13246970:
Shen, Xia, and Han review why braces sometimes damage tooth roots, in this 2026 Progress in Orthodontics article. Orthodontically induced root resorption, the loss of hard root tissue under sustained force, is frequent and often permanent. Its severity depends on force size, direction, and duration, combined with each patient's biological susceptibility.

The review traces the chain from mechanical pressure to chemistry: ligament and bone cells sense the load and signal osteoclasts, the cells that dissolve hard tissue, to attack the root surface. Hormones, metabolism, genes, and oxidative stress all modulate the process. The authors appraise early-detection methods and prevention ideas, including locally delivered osteoclast blockers and biomaterial carriers, while noting most evidence still comes from rodents and cell cultures.
pmc-13248970:
Cong and co-authors built forecasting models for small liver tumors, in a 2026 study. After curative surgery for hepatocellular carcinoma, some patients relapse within two years and fare poorly. The team balanced a hospital cohort using propensity matching, leaving one hundred sixty-five patients, then tested inflammation and nutrition markers from routine blood work.

Several combined indices, covering inflammation, liver function, and clotting, carried independent prognostic weight. Among a chart-based nomogram and three machine learning approaches, a regularized Cox model performed best for both early relapse and long-term survival. The authors recommend that model to guide how closely each patient is watched after surgery.
pmc-13249170:
Kallio and co-authors mined spinal fluid for early warnings in childhood meningitis, in a 2026 multicountry study. Bacterial meningitis still kills or disables many children, especially where intensive care is scarce. The team pooled one thousand five hundred ninety-eight confirmed cases from Latin America, Angola, and Finland, relating admission spinal fluid values to survival and brain outcome.

Death risk climbed steadily as spinal fluid sugar fell and as protein rose. Children with both the lowest sugar and highest protein fared worst of all. White cell counts added little by comparison. Because these tests are routine everywhere, the authors propose simple combined thresholds to flag children who need the fastest, closest care.
pmc-13250170:
Wang and colleagues trace a brain circuit that links the front of the brain to a stress center in male mice. Their 2026 Cell Discovery paper maps a direct path from the ventromedial prefrontal cortex to hormone cells in the hypothalamus. Those hypothalamic cells release a hormone that starts the body's stress response.

Using virus tracing, cell recordings, and live calcium imaging, the team showed that switching this pathway on spread activity through the local stress cell network. Strong signaling made mice avoid others after social stress and strengthened their fear memories. Blocking the pathway reduced that avoidance behavior. The authors identify the circuit as one driver of stress responses and susceptibility to conditioned fear.
pmc-13250470:
Toshihiko Goto and colleagues report a runaway heart device in this 2026 case report. An 86-year-old woman was receiving a tiny leadless pacemaker for the upper chamber of her heart, after years of device changes driven by infection, battery wear, and worsening heart failure.

During the procedure the new device came loose and drifted backward into a large vein in her left pelvis. The team retrieved it successfully, using a preventive approach they describe in detail. They also explain how the shape of her veins had made the implant difficult in the first place. The case offers guidance for a rare but serious mishap.
pmc-13250870:
Tang and co-authors test whether a simple metabolic score can warn which heart stents will narrow again. Their 2026 Annals of Medicine study reviews eight hundred eighteen patients who had repeat artery imaging for chest pain after stent placement between 2022 and 2025. The score, called METS-IR, estimates insulin resistance from routine body and blood measures.

Patients whose stents had renarrowed carried clearly higher scores, and renarrowing grew steadily more common across the score thirds. The score stayed an independent predictor after other factors were weighed, with the strongest effect on severe renarrowing. A cutoff value separated risk groups with moderate accuracy. The authors present the score as a cheap, practical way to flag patients needing closer follow-up after stenting.
pmc-13251770:
Xiang, Li, and Zhu test expectation-based psychological nursing for women having their womb removed for fibroids. Their 2026 trial in the International Journal of Women's Health randomizes one hundred sixty patients to routine care alone, or routine care plus two structured sessions. The sessions build on the Rosenthal effect, where positive expectations lift outcomes. Self-perceived burden was the main measure.

By three months, the supported group felt less burden and showed better anxiety, self-esteem, confidence, and quality-of-life scores. Stress hormone and heart rhythm markers also improved more in that group of patients. Patients walked sooner, left hospital earlier, reported less pain, and rated nursing higher. The authors present the nurse-led model as a practical way to build expectation-focused support into routine surgical care.
pmc-13251870:
Aikaterini Lampada and colleagues find new brain cells born from bad experiences in this 2026 mouse study. Adult brains keep making neurons in a few spots, a process tied to memory and resilience against depression, and stem cells there answer to life events.

Fear training switched on stem cells in the dorsal septum, a midline brain area sitting near fibres that deliver serotonin, the mood chemical. The antidepressant fluoxetine, which raises serotonin, had the same effect, boosting stem cell division and neuron birth. The new cells were calming interneurons that wired into septal circuits. The authors read this as an adaptive answer to stress in mice.
pmc-13253870:
Wenjin Sun and co-authors set out a future plan for high-altitude medicine in a 2026 review. More people now travel, work, and live where air is thin, raising illness tied to low oxygen. The authors propose one frame, the HSMI spectrum, which treats low-oxygen harm as injury across many organs at once.

Gaps remain in who gets sick and why, in firm tests, and in turning lab finds into care. Their plan pairs large-scale gene and protein data with machine learning, seeks core pathways, and builds fast tests with markers and portable scans. They also urge precise, mechanism-based treatments for groups at special risk.
pmc-13254270:
Jason Hou and co-authors test three-dimensional ultrasound in augmented reality in a 2026 study. Ultrasound users must build a 3D mental picture from flat slices, which makes training slow. Their AR-VIU system streams live 3D ultrasound into a headset at true scale.

Eighteen people, nine novices and nine experts, tried four display setups and did object finding tasks. The augmented reality 3D system gave the highest accuracy and the lowest spread in results. It also nearly erased the gap between novices and experts. The authors offer the set-up as a training and education tool.
pmc-13254370:
Jianfu Zhu and a large team study a chemical tweak to heart scar tissue in a 2026 paper. After a heart attack, collagen in the scar can stiffen the heart. The team found histaminylation, a histamine-based modification made by an enzyme called TGM2, in mouse heart collagen seven days after infarction.

Mice unable to make histamine had more crosslinks and stiffer scars. In lab tests, histaminylated collagen formed fewer crosslinks, stayed softer, and slowed scar-forming cell change. A gel releasing histamine, placed at the injury, restored the modification and reduced heart dysfunction in those mice.
pmc-13255270:
Robert Chen and colleagues present a machine learning tool that ranks drug targets for rare diseases in a 2026 paper. Rare diseases are hard to treat because patients are few and genetic causes often stay unclear. Their framework, RareGPS, blends 11 genetic, clinical, and trial evidence sources, using the full spread of gene variants rather than single cutoffs.

Across 161 disease traits, RareGPS beat existing tools at predicting drug uses and trial progress. Top-ranked targets were 58 times more likely to reach late-stage trials than mid-ranked ones. The team validated the tool in records of two million patients and published predictions for over three million gene-disease pairs.
pmc-13259570:
Emily Richmond and co-authors present a Canadian case of pustular psoriasis flaring around childbirth. This rare pregnancy dermatosis erupts in sterile pustules and can threaten mother and baby alike. Their 2026 CMAJ case follows a thirty-one-year-old patient through recurrence and a postpartum flare.

The key points stress how often the disease returns in later pregnancies, arriving earlier and hitting harder each time. Corticosteroids come first, with cyclosporine or ultraviolet phototherapy behind them. When standard drugs fail or cannot be used, antibody medicines offer another route, especially after delivery. The case doubles as a compact management guide for clinicians.
pmc-13261370:
Groß and co-authors present a 2026 methods study of how solvent lipid extraction affects carbon isotope readings in animal tissue. Whale blubber and skin are rich in fats, which skew isotope ratios used to study diet. Removing lipids with solvents is standard, but extra effects on carbon values were unstudied.

The team tested repeated extractions on four pure proteins and on humpback whale blubber. The solvents, dichloromethane and methanol, did not significantly change the carbon or nitrogen values of pure proteins. Values stayed within 0.5‰ of unextracted samples, matching expected analytical error. Blubber carbon values rose significantly with each extraction cycle, reflecting fat removal itself. Carbon-to-nitrogen ratios matched pure protein, at 2.87, only after three extraction cycles. The authors conclude gentle single extractions are inefficient, and multiple cycles are needed for robust measures.
pmc-13263170:
Yuxia Li and colleagues compare the airway microbes and blood gene patterns of COVID-19 patients on breathing machines versus those not. Sixty-nine very ill patients joined their 2026 study, forty-one of them on machines that breathe for them. Lung fluid and blood told linked stories.

Those patients' airways held far less germ variety. Streptococcus species that ruled in others dwindled sharply on the machine. Their blood switched on programs for swelling and for calling in more cells, including the chemokine CXCL8. The missing streptococci tracked with those rising immune genes. Ventilation itself, the authors suggest, reshapes the lung's microbial and immune balance.
pmc-13263370:
Patrick M. Ryan and co-authors review a 2026 summary of care for ulnar collateral ligament injuries of the elbow. This ligament, on the inner elbow, is often torn in overhead throwing athletes such as baseball pitchers. The review covers anatomy, joint mechanics, diagnosis, and treatment choices, comparing rest-based care with surgery.

Without surgery, eighty to one hundred percent of non-throwing athletes return to sport, but throwers fare far worse with lower tears than upper ones. Reconstruction returns eighty to ninety-seven percent of athletes to play within about a year. Repair reinforced with an internal brace matched that rate with faster recovery, around nine months, in well-chosen patients with fresh tears.
pmc-13264570:
Jessica Michala Jindra and Angela Duff Hogan wrote a 2026 review on bringing new asthma guidance into schools. Since 2019, global guidance has favored a rescue inhaler that pairs a steroid with formoterol, a long-acting opener drug, over the old quick-relief inhaler alone. Schools have been slow to switch.

The authors list the blocks: old-style asthma action plans, gaps in nurse and parent training, and dosing rules that differ from the old inhaler. Their fixes include updated, personal action plans for each child and full training for all parties on the new dosing. They argue schools must adapt plans and teaching so children get the better rescue treatment during the school day.
pmc-13264670:
Koki Takabatake and colleagues published a 2026 benchmarking study on how well large language models talk about multi-cancer early detection tests, blood tests that screen for many cancers at once. Clear talk about such tests matters, and models that sound sure while wrong could mislead. The team set expert-checked questions and graded five models.

The set held 94 multiple choice and 13 free response questions drawn from 19 papers. Each model answered three times and rated its own confidence. All scored high overall, with Gemini on top at 96.3 percent, though its test terms differed. Most errors were wrong recalls of exact numbers. Several models still made errors while claiming high confidence. The authors urge human checks before clinical use.
pmc-13266370:
Md Wahidul Islam and co-authors published a 2026 bioinformatics study of two collagen genes in thyroid cancer, the most common hormone-gland cancer. Collagens shape the tissue around tumors, and these two genes had prior links to the disease. The team mined large cancer databases for gene activity, gene changes, chemical tags, and survival ties.

One gene, COL13A1, was raised in tumors, while the other, COL23A1, was lowered, and both varied by tumor stage and type. Lower levels of the first and higher levels of the second each tied to poorer outlook. Tagging of the second gene's promoter also rose in tumors. Two partner genes stood out as the most co-expressed. Checks in outside data sets supported both genes as markers. The authors propose them for diagnosis and prognosis work in precision care.
pmc-13269970:
Haeyoon Ryu and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on patient experience in an Australian hospital recovery unit. Fifty-one patients in a row filled in a survey across seven areas of care, from shared choices to physical comfort. Their gains in daily function were also scored with two standard tools.

The median age was 68 years, and fifty-four point nine percent were women. Bone and joint problems led at twenty-nine point four percent, followed by stroke at twenty-three point five percent. Support for mood, shared choices, and teaching scored highest, while family input scored lowest. Patients improved a lot in function by discharge on all measures. The authors propose the survey as a quality check beside routine outcome tools.
pmc-13270070:
Fathola Mohamadian and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on aggression, acting without thinking, and thoughts of suicide among teens in a region of Iran. Two hundred secondary school students from four schools, chosen by staged random sampling, filled in standard surveys. Background details were also collected.

Boys reported much higher aggression than girls, while acting without thinking did not differ by sex. Aggression varied across school grades. Aggression moved strongly with thoughts of suicide, at zero point six one, while acting without thinking moved weakly, at zero point one eight. In combined analysis, aggression alone predicted thoughts of suicide. It made up 36 percent of their spread. School results linked to both traits, but parents' schooling and jobs did not. The authors urge early spotting of aggressive teens.
pmc-13270570:
Sanna Mansoob is lead author of a 2026 Perspective paper on RaraSwed, Sweden's national quality registry for rare diseases. A Perspective paper sets out the authors' view and plans rather than a trial result. The registry gathers uniform data on rare disease diagnosis across a very mixed group of illnesses.

The authors describe what helped and what hindered building the registry inside Sweden's public health system, using systems thinking and social innovation ideas. They say RaraSwed supports research and evidence-based care for people with rare diseases, who often face delays and unequal care. Planned additions will record patient- and doctor-reported care, treatment, and daily experience.
pmc-13270870:
Liang Ying is lead author of a 2026 retrospective study, one looking back at treated cases, of telitacicept for IgA nephropathy in children. In this kidney disease, protein leaks into urine, and all ten children in the study also received steroid therapy, with half getting extra immune-suppressing drugs.

After a median follow-up of 3.75 months, eight children reached remission of protein in the urine, four fully and four partly. Six children cut their steroid dose by between a third and almost all of it, and four stopped steroids entirely. Side effects were mild, including two injection-site reactions and single cases of infection, rash, and low white blood cells, with no severe events.
pmc-13271070:
Qing Wang is lead author of a 2026 journal article describing a double-helix patch for holding drainage tubes in place after head and neck surgery. Loose tubes cause pain, skin damage, and extra work, and the standard method uses a bridge of medical tape. The patch uses two spiral strips, an elastic strap, and wide wings to spread pressure.

In a non-randomized trial of 125 patients at one hospital in Shanxi, 61 used the patch and 64 used tape. The patch group had far fewer adverse events, faster fixing time, higher comfort and satisfaction scores, and 43.2 percent lower material costs. Pain from pulling and skin injury rates did not differ between groups.
pmc-13272270:
Malfertheiner and Schulz commented in 2025 on how to keep stomach biopsy tests accurate for Helicobacter pylori when patients cannot stop acid-blocking drugs. Proton pump inhibitors cut the accuracy of nearly every test for this stomach infection, so guidelines ask patients to stop them two weeks before testing, which real practice often cannot manage. The commentary discusses a study of 164 dyspeptic patients that sought a fix while the drugs continued.

Gene-based PCR testing proved most accurate and lost nothing on the drugs, since it needs only traces of bacterial DNA, but cost and availability limit its use. The study's practical trick, pooling paired biopsies from two stomach regions into a single rapid urease test sample, raised the routine test's yield against the PCR standard. The commentators endorse PCR where feasible and the pooled-biopsy workaround elsewhere, so treatable infections are not missed.
pmc-13272670:
Simon Sanwald leads a 2026 matched case-control study of chemical marks on DNA in depression and response to treatment. The marks, called methylation, were measured on three genes linked to stress, serotonin, and oxytocin in blood. Such marks have been proposed as markers of who will improve.

The study followed 66 patients and 66 healthy controls at entry and after two weeks of inpatient care. One gene's marks looked lower in patients at first, but that gap vanished after accounting for blood cell mix. Symptoms improved, yet mark changes in none of the three genes tracked improvement. The authors urge care with confounders in such studies.
pmc-13274170:
Ali Zare and co-authors report a 2026 case report of cells growing on an artificial lens inside the eye after a corneal transplant procedure. The patient was a sixty-one-year-old woman who had already had several eye operations, including cataract surgery. She came in with steadily worsening vision.

Examination found stubborn deposits across the front of her implanted lens, limited to the pupil zone. Laser treatment and surgical polishing both failed to clear them, so the lens was removed and studied under a microscope. It carried a sheet of epithelial skin-like cells, likely strayed from the lens capsule, with no calcium deposits. The authors urge doctors to consider this rare cause when lens clouding resists treatment.
pmc-13274870:
Xia Huang and colleagues present a 2026 journal article measuring stroke knowledge among non-neurology health workers in an underdeveloped county of southwestern China. Outside specialist units, general staff often give the first stroke care, where minutes matter. The team first adapted a standard stroke management questionnaire into Chinese and confirmed it was reliable, then surveyed local staff.

Of 252 completed questionnaires, 225 qualified for analysis, and 69.4 percent of staff reached a good overall score. Knowledge was weakest for the hyperacute phase, the first urgent hours, at 64.7 percent good performance. Nurses scored lower than doctors, and staff in smaller facilities or without a neurologist partner scored lower than peers in full hospitals. The authors target training at those gaps.
pmc-13275770:
Louise Harra and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on what the Sun's outer atmosphere does just before a solar flare. Flares are huge bursts of energy from the Sun. Predicting where and when one will start could help protect satellites and power grids from space weather.

The team studied two large flares from the same active region on two days in March 2024. They used images from two space telescopes that watch the corona, the Sun's glowing outer layer. Spots with high stored magnetic energy also showed frequent tiny flickers in brightness. That flickering peaked at least two minutes before the flare's X-ray burst. The authors say this signal could help pinpoint where a flare is about to begin.
pmc-13276070:
Martin Johansson and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on vision in adults born with extremely low birth weight, meaning at or below one kilogram. Such adults face higher risks of trouble seeing motion. Motion of living things, like a walking person's pattern of movement, matters for social life.

Thirty-eight adults born tiny and twenty-nine full-term controls did eye-tracking tasks with moving dot figures. Some figures formed a walking person; others were scrambled versions of the same dots. Extra visual noise made some rounds harder. The low birth weight group spotted both kinds of motion more slowly overall. They also read the walking figures less accurately when noise was low. Early development scores in toddlerhood hinted at links to adult performance, though those links faded after stricter statistical checks.
pmc-13276270: Yang Gao and co-authors studied cinnamon essential oil packed into tiny capsules to protect a medicinal plant stem from fungi. Their 2026 correction notice addresses errors in one figure of that article. During figure assembly, two pairs of images were duplicated by oversight in separate panels showing fungal growth tests. The notice reprints the original figure and its caption so readers can see the context. The original article has been corrected.
pmc-13276770:
Rebecca Sebastian and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a tool that grabs disease-linked protein seeds right at the synapse. In Alzheimer's and related diseases, clumped proteins like tau spread between connected neurons in a prion-like way. Studying those proteins in their actual synaptic setting has lacked methods.

Their platform, called synCAR, fuses a small antibody fragment to a natural synaptic anchor protein. The antibody arms the synapse to capture chosen proteins in place. Armed with a tau antibody, synapses in mouse and human neuron models caught pathogenic tau species effectively. Expressing the trap actually increased tau clumping, likely by concentrating seeds at the synapse. The authors call it the first published method to isolate and manipulate synaptic proteins in context, useful for research and drug development.
pmc-13276870:
Ahmad Mourad leads a 2026 study of pneumonia testing in patients whose immune systems are weakened. Finding the germ fast matters, yet test success varies a lot between hospitals. The team reviewed 222 patients at ten sites and looked at timing of a lung scope test and a blood DNA test.

Usual testing found a cause in as few as eight percent and as many as fifty-eight percent of cases, by site. A scope test done within three days of an abnormal scan found more causes than one done later. Adding the blood DNA test raised the yield for both early and late groups. Prompt testing, the authors argue, should be the norm for these patients.
pmc-13277570:
Andy Bécue wrote a 2026 Interpol review of research on fingermarks, the residue left by fingertips, covering July 2022 to June 2025. The review was built for forensic work: what fingermarks are made of, and how to make them visible at crime scenes. A total of 761 papers were collected, nearly twice the count in the prior report.

Most collected papers were set aside for weak methods, missed forensic needs, or safety problems, leaving 219 for close discussion. Composition papers were sorted into fields such as aging, donor profiling, and contamination. The author adds personal notes where work departs from good practice. The review aims to give forensic readers a quality-filtered map of a fast-growing field.
pmc-13277770:
Emily C Scheffel leads a 2026 case report of a pregnant patient who needed a cesarean birth and repair of a torn aorta at the same time. The 23-year-old, at thirty-five weeks of pregnancy, had Marfan syndrome, a connective tissue disorder that weakens the aorta, plus sickle cell trait. She arrived with sudden back, belly, and chest pain.

Scans confirmed a tear running from the upper aorta down into the abdomen. Teams delivered the baby, replaced part of the aorta, and rebuilt a heart artery in one operation. Despite a complex course afterward, she had fewer blood-flow complications than earlier similar cases. The authors credit joint planning across specialties and careful heart-lung bypass technique.
pmc-13278370:
