Seong Woo Shin and Sung Hwoan Cho present a 2026 feeding trial that swaps fish meal for duck by-product meal in diets for olive flounder, a farmed flatfish. Fish meal is costly, so cheaper protein matters for fish farming. Four hundred fifty young fish were spread across eighteen tanks and fed six diets for fifty days, with duck meal replacing zero to all of the fish meal.

Fish on the control diet and on diets replacing twenty or forty percent of fish meal grew best and earned the best economic returns. Higher replacement levels cut weight gain and feed intake. Feed use, blood chemistry, and body composition otherwise held steady. Duck by-product meal can replace up to forty percent of fish meal without harming growth or profit, the authors conclude.
pmc-13279170:
Amir Lotfi writes a 2026 letter that critiques surveys of staffing in cardiac intensive care units. Such units care for the sickest heart patients. The surveys, run by a national cardiology group, map how units are staffed and how heart doctors roles shift. Lotfi finds the maps useful for peer comparison, yet urges care in reading them.

Just twenty percent replied, and most came from academic centres, so rates may not fit the whole country. The survey tool was new and not yet validated, meaning not yet proven sound. Terms like high intensity staffing lump unlike models in one group. Cross section data, taken at one time, cannot prove trends over time. Lotfi urges set terms, better sampling and long term follow up.
pmc-13280470:
Haoyan Sun and colleagues report a 2026 study of dung beetle kin diversity along a mountain gradient in a tropical island rainforest in China. Mountains serve as ideal natural laboratories for biodiversity patterns. Scarabaeoidea assemblages, the scarab beetle superfamily, were sampled from March to November 2024 across thirty two plots. Elevation ran from about three hundred seventy to one thousand four hundred seventy metres. Ground and canopy traps caught the beetles.

Species richness showed no significant link with elevation, but rose with litter biomass. Abundance peaked at mid elevation, driven primarily by temperature, reflecting thermal sensitivity of these ectotherms, cold blooded animals. Overall compositional dissimilarity was high and dominated by species turnover, meaning species replacement across sites, not nested loss. Predator assemblage patterns correlated with beetle beta diversity as well. Temperature and food web drivers shape the gradient.
pmc-13280570:
Eeman Ahmad and team report a 2026 study of trends and disparities in lung clot death rates in adults with atrial fibrillation in the United States. Pulmonary embolism, a lung artery clot, is a major cause of cardiovascular death, and fibrillation worsens its outcomes. Long term trends were poorly characterized. The CDC WONDER database from 1999 to 2020 gave deaths with embolism as the underlying cause and fibrillation as a contributing cause.

A total of five thousand four hundred ninety nine deaths were recorded. Overall mortality stayed stable from 1999 to 2009, then rose sharply from 2009 to 2020. The yearly change flipped from slightly negative to a clear positive climb. Males had higher age adjusted mortality than females, with faster rises over time. Non metropolitan areas showed greater mortality than metropolitan areas. Subgroup checks covered the pre, during and post COVID eras.
pmc-13281770:
Yixuan Li and colleagues used gene data to probe clotting and pregnancy blood pressure in a 2026 study. High blood pressure in pregnancy can kill mothers worldwide. Its worst form brings seizures and organ strain. Clotting switches on in that illness, but whether clotting drives it is unclear. The team used genes as natural levers, since genes are fixed before illness. They checked clotting traits and blood proteins against illness risk in large gene datasets.

First passes hinted at links. Higher levels of two clotting factors went with higher risk. Lower levels of a clotting brake went with higher risk too. Extra checks found no wide bias in the data. But when the team applied the strictest error bar, none of the links held firm. A sharing test also gave low odds that the same gene spot drives both traits. The authors call the proof suggestive at best.
pmc-13281870:
Siqi Han and colleagues built a membrane that sorts mirror-image molecules in a 2026 study. Many drugs come in left- and right-handed forms that act unlike in the body. Sorting them with membranes is cheap in energy but hard to make sharp. Weak grip differences wash out under fast flow. The team laced carbon sheets with DNA-wrapped carbon tubes. That built chiral paths, paths that favor one handedness, through the stack.

Each handed form of a test amino acid reshaped the paths in its own way. The reshaping split the energy cost of crossing for the two forms. One form then sped through far faster than the other. The membrane held its sorting for a full week of runs. Stacked passes enriched one form to near-perfect purity. The authors say coupling grip with structure can amplify faint sorting cues.
pmc-13282070:
Jasmine Lee and Alan Kubey describe a 2026 case where a sudden drop in blood sodium pointed to hidden trouble after gallbladder drainage. Sodium is a key salt in blood, and a fast fall can be dangerous. The patient had necrotizing pancreatitis, a severe form where pancreas tissue dies, which had also burst the gallbladder. A drain placed through the skin, called a percutaneous cholecystostomy, was used to empty the gallbladder.

The drain then lost large amounts of bile, the digestive fluid made by the liver. That loss drove the sodium down and, in doing so, revealed a blockage further down the bile path. Fluids given by vein, a stent to hold the duct open, and internal drainage fixed both the sodium level and the symptoms. The authors show how a lab abnormality after drainage can guide a team across specialties toward the real fault.
pmc-13282170:
Fangyi Chen and co-authors describe a 2026 software tool that reads doctors' notes to find when a disease trait first appeared. Knowing that onset time helps doctors diagnose and track illness, but record dates often mark when a note was written, not when symptoms began. Older text methods also struggled with vague time phrases. Their open-source tool, TimeX, uses a large language model called Llama to extract onset times.

TimeX filters out family history, spots traits, handles negated mentions, and then pulls time details. On one hundred two hand-checked notes from a New York medical centre, it reached about eighty-one percent accuracy. That beat five rival methods by a wide margin. In four rare disease groups, note-based onset times proved sharper than record dates. The authors say the tool could support faster, more precise diagnosis at scale.
pmc-13282870:
Community voices shaped mental health research in Pakistan, as Shumaila Hamid and partners recount in their 2026 account. The work sits inside the THE HOPE project on early help for psychosis in young people. It covers work with patients, families, and local communities.

A six-member advisory group with lived experience helped shape study design and topic guides. The team also held 34 community sessions using sermons, posters, leaflets, and direct outreach. Themes included medicine use, service delivery, and the role of healers and primary care. The authors support shared decisions and training that fit local culture and needs.
pmc-13283170:
Memory clinic visitors in Sweden were screened for a treatable brain inflammation mimic in work A Freitas-Huhtamaki's team published in 2026. Autoimmune encephalitis can mimic dementia but can be treated. Wide regional gaps in diagnosis in Sweden hint that cases are missed.

Blood samples from 1,021 clinic visitors were screened for five nerve antibodies. Positive results were checked with added cell and tissue tests for confirmation. Eleven patients were positive in two or more tests in the screen. Chart review suggested true immune or tumor-linked disease in three patients. Four cases lacked enough detail to judge, and three looked like false positives. Screening found few clear cases.
pmc-13283270:
Sixty years of European youth fitness data are stitched into trend lines by Daniel Domingo-del-Val and associates in 2026. Fitness in childhood signals current and future health for young people. Past reviews often used single tests or stopped before the pandemic years.

Data covered 417,362 children and teens aged 6 to 16 years in 20 countries. Studies with repeated measures and full test data were pooled for trends. Scores were standardized so varied tests could be compared fairly. Heart fitness, strength, and speed traits were tracked by sex and age. Some traits fell over time, with shifts that sped or slowed by period. Results can guide school and health policy.
pmc-13284170:
First opioid use and later dependence pull gene activity in opposite ways, argues Ngo Cheung in a 2026 gene study. Many past studies merged both stages into one trait, which may blur distinct biology. The work used gene-based tests on summary data from a large opioid study set.

Risk for first use tied to lower activity in immune and cell pruning genes. Gene sets for star cells and cell aging also trended down for first use. Risk for dependence instead raised activity in energy and fuel sensing paths. Signals for nerve contacts and DNA repair joined that second profile. Some driver genes flipped sign between stages.
pmc-13284470:
Marta Milà-Alomà and colleagues report a 2026 analysis of how fast Alzheimer disease moves from amyloid to tau buildup on PET scans. Data came from two cohorts, ADNI and the Harvard Aging Brain Study, with hundreds of participants who had positive amyloid or tau scans. The team modeled the age at each scan milestone and the gap between them.

The gap length differed a lot from person to person. It ran shorter for women, for people carrying the APOE-ε4 variant, and for those whose amyloid scans turned positive later in life. Carriers and women also reached both milestones younger. A shorter gap after amyloid positivity predicted earlier symptoms. The authors say the timing can help find people at risk of rapid change for early trials and treatment.
pmc-13284870:
Bobur Ataev, Balhen Bolathan, and Weimin Zhang describe a 2026 case of a large hydatid cyst pressing on the heart. Such cysts in the sac around the heart are very rare and can cause tamponade or severe allergy if they burst. A 36-year-old farmer arrived with chest tightness and short breath.

Imaging showed a large mixed cyst inside the pericardium, next to the right heart chambers, squeezing and warping them. Planned surgery removed the cyst under ultrasound guidance through the food pipe, which helped guide exact cutting and limit leftover disease. Recovery went well. The authors urge doctors to suspect hydatid disease when a pericardial mass appears in patients from endemic areas or with animal contact.
pmc-13285370:
What helps or blocks pharmacists when they try to cut unneeded drugs for older patients is the focus of a 2026 focus group study by Sanne Bakker and co-authors. Taking many drugs raises harm risk, and a new guideline with drug fact sheets aimed to aid reviews. Nineteen community pharmacists from a trial arm shared their hands-on experience in online groups.

Coders found twenty-six factors across seven domains. The guideline itself drew few complaints, with praise for its layered build and short summaries. Pharmacists flagged their own skill at spotting cut chances and tracking results. Patient knowledge gaps, mixed patient feelings, and how well family doctors knew the approach also shaped success.
pmc-13285970:
Velina Banda and Deng Gang weigh the place of urodynamic testing in men with urinary symptoms in a 2026 narrative review. Pressure-flow studies long stood as the gold test for telling a blocked outlet from a weak bladder muscle. Newer trial proof and guidelines now question whether every man needs the invasive test before treatment.

Simple tools such as flow rates, leftover urine checks, and ultrasound measures can sort many men well enough for first steps. The invasive test still earns its place when the picture stays cloudy: young men with stubborn symptoms, suspected weak muscle, nerve-based bladder trouble, or symptoms that persist after surgery. Test quality varies between operators, which limits trust in borderline calls. The authors favor a stepwise path that saves the full study for cases where its answer would change care.
pmc-13286370:
Elena Corujo-Simon and co-authors mimic the embryo's physical cradle to grow a missing cell type in a 2026 stem cell study. Lab-made embryo models need early endoderm cells, the layer that becomes yolk sac and gut lining, but older cell lines had already aged past that stage. The team copied the inner cell mass's softness and grip chemistry to coax fresh precursor cells out of mouse blastocysts.

Inner cells were settled on gels of differing stiffness dressed with chosen matrix proteins. The right mechanical setting let brand-new endoderm precursor lines expand through several rounds of growth. The system stayed short-lived, yet long enough to reveal which supports the young cells demand. Better starter cells should slot more smoothly into blastoids, sharpening a key tool for studying the first days of development.
pmc-13286570:
Bruno Miranda and co-authors listen to single neurons while monkeys choose by two learning styles in a 2026 neuroscience study. Goal-directed choice uses a mental map of how actions lead to rewards, while habit simply repeats what paid before. Electrodes sat in two frontal and two striatal regions as two macaques played a two-step choice game whose surprise transitions expose which style drives each pick.

All four regions tracked rewards and the odds of each transition. The anterior cingulate, though, carried the signature blend of reward, transition, and choice that goal-directed math requires, and its cells priced options the map-based way. Caudate cells even flipped their value estimates after a rare transition, exactly as structural knowledge demands. Striatal cells separately echoed the reward-prediction errors of habit learning, sketching a division of labor across the circuit.
pmc-13286870:
Zahra Hatami Asl and colleagues test group therapy for the mental aftershocks of preeclampsia in a 2026 quasi-experimental study. Women whose pregnancies were complicated by the dangerous blood-pressure disorder face higher risks of depression, anxiety, and stress after delivery, yet postpartum care usually stops at the body. Ninety-five such women at a Kermanshah hospital were split between eight group sessions of transdiagnostic training and routine care alone.

The therapy teaches shared skills for handling negative emotions across disorders rather than treating each symptom separately. Scores for depression, anxiety, and stress all fell clearly in the trained group at one week and again at two months. The routine-care group showed no such movement. The authors recommend folding this kind of group training into standard postpartum protocols after high-risk pregnancies.
pmc-13287270:
Carolina De Toma and co-authors describe in 2026 the setup and early results of ALIGNED, an Italian network for rare diseases of brain blood vessels. Forty-nine centres joined. The network standardises records, surveys local care capacity, and offers virtual specialist input to narrow regional gaps.

The first group held 308 people across five conditions, led by CADASIL with 162 cases and Moyamoya angiopathy with 80 cases. Site surveys showed wide unevenness in testing and care. Early gene and protein profiling in Moyamoya samples pointed to disturbed vessel growth signals. The authors argue that mapping expertise is a first step toward equal access to diagnosis.
pmc-13287370:
Candice Marie Sage wrote a 2026 news and perspectives piece arguing that a short writing-based treatment for posttraumatic stress deserves a far wider place in care. Sage reports as a journal correspondent and draws on her own long wait for publicly funded help in Canada.

In written exposure work, patients write about the traumatic event in a small number of guided sessions. Take-up and completion in everyday services are described as high. Sage notes that global access to trauma care is poor, with few patients receiving adequate therapy. Online delivery is presented as a route to fairer access, especially where trained therapists are scarce.
pmc-13287470:
Ulrik Röijezon and colleagues measured body sway in 2026 in 28 young adults and 25 older adults. Each person stood on a force plate. Each watched a virtual roller-coaster ride five times in a row. A time-frequency method split sway signals into bands to reveal how balance strategy changed.

The first ride raised sway energy at higher frequencies and lowered it at very low frequencies. Older adults leaned more on high-frequency corrections. With repeats, high-frequency energy fell in both groups, showing quick adaptation. Older adults still shifted their patterns more overall. The authors suggest virtual challenges can expose age differences in balance resilience and could serve in balance training.
pmc-13287670: A 2025 study comparing a modified method for preserving donor hearts before transplant with standard methods was retracted in 2026. Scientific Reports issued the notice for the work by Xiaoke Shang and colleagues. After publication, worries arose over mistakes in the statistical work and gaps in the data that could not be reconciled. The team also could not provide ethics approval papers when asked. One author agreed with the retraction wording. The other five authors did not reply to the editors. The notice adds no new clinical findings.
pmc-13287970:
Tingting You and co-authors tracked tumour DNA floating in blood in 2026 in 127 patients starting first treatment for advanced pancreatic cancer. Blood was drawn at the start, at the first response check, and later, and read with deep gene sequencing to follow change over time.

Tumour DNA was found in 78.7% of patients at the start, falling to 55.7% at the first check. High starting levels, and a high share of the strongest mutation signal, meant shorter time before growth and shorter survival. Falling or cleared signals meant better control. In patients whose standard marker stays silent, the DNA signal still carried useful forecasts.
pmc-13288370:
Eda G Christensen and co-authors held two focus groups in May 2025, reported in 2026. Twenty Aymara women took part in Sajama, a remote high town in rural Bolivia. The aim was to learn how they see cancer risk and care. Cancer causes nearly a fifth of deaths in Bolivia, yet remote indigenous views are seldom recorded.

Women described cancer as feared, silent, and usually found too late to cure. Five themes covered risk views, barriers such as distance, cost, and mistrust, and the side-by-side use of traditional and clinic medicine. Daily habits and environmental worries also surfaced. The authors call for teaching and screening shaped with the community itself.
pmc-13288870:
Siying Chen and co-authors audit the modeling behind cost claims for community health worker programs in a 2026 systematic review. Following standard reporting guidance, they searched six databases through June 2025 for full economic evaluations that used a decision-analytic model, then graded quality with the Philips checklist.

Thirty-seven studies qualified, split mainly between decision trees and Markov models, with most set in low- and middle-income countries. Average quality reached sixty-seven percent, and validation plus structural uncertainty checks were the common gaps, while data limits kept poorer-country models simpler. Even so, 84 percent of studies judged worker programs cost-effective in their analyses. Stronger validation and local data would make the policy case firmer.
pmc-13288970:
Anwar Seid Ali and colleagues study how babies are fed in Afar, Ethiopia. Their 2026 study uses in-depth talks. Herding families live in this dry region. The team spoke with 16 mothers. Their babies were 6 to 23 months old. Twenty community leaders joined group talks.

Custom and elder rule shaped first feeds. A rite with early foods delayed breast milk. Most mothers knew breast-only feeding was best. Dry seasons and hard work broke that rule. Solid foods began at six months for most. Food range stayed narrow for many. Drought, distance, and prices all played a part. Women bore most care work alone.
pmc-13289370:
Rutcher Madera Lacaza and Edrei Yambao Udaundo analyzed a 2026 pair of national surveys on e-cigarette awareness and use among Filipino adults. Smoking has fallen over the past decade, yet quitting remains hard and vaping has grown, notably among young adults and smokers seeking options. A new excise tax on e-cigarettes began in 2020 to curb use.

Data came from the Global Adult Tobacco Survey waves of 2015 and 2021, with weighted models for who knows about and who uses vaping products. Awareness was broad, but current use clustered in narrow groups. Young adults, men, and more educated adults were more likely to know about and use e-cigarettes in the data. Use peaked among people who smoke and plan to quit.
pmc-13289470:
Naif Munawir Alotaibi headed a 2026 study building one deep learning system to grade neck bone maturity and jaw relation from side head X-rays at once. Orthodontists use cervical vertebral maturation stages to time growth-based care, and jaw class to plan bite correction. Human grading varies, so the authors tested automated reading against orthodontist judgments.

A total of 720 X-rays from patients aged 8 to 18 were sorted into six maturity stages and three jaw classes. Training used 540 images and testing used 180 images, read independently by two orthodontists for comparison. Human agreement was near perfect in the checks. Agreement between the model and humans was substantial for both tasks, suggesting one tool could support both calls.
pmc-13290670:
An antibody-drug conjugate that lost its approval and won back its future is charted by Giuseppe Bertuglia and colleagues in a 2026 review of multiple myeloma treatment. Belantamab-mafodotin was the first conjugate aimed at BCMA, a marker carried by malignant plasma cells.

The drug worked alone in heavily pretreated patients in the phase II DREAMM-2 trial, but the confirmatory DREAMM-3 trial missed its mark against standard therapy, and regulators temporarily pulled the approval. Newer DREAMM-7 and DREAMM-8 results revived it, showing benefit in earlier treatment lines and in combinations. Bertuglia and colleagues place the drug within today's myeloma landscape and survey rival conjugates aimed at BCMA and other targets, weighing where the class goes next.
pmc-13290870:
Stimulation through the skin really does reach the vagus nerve, Norianne Ingram and colleagues argue in an evidence synthesis from 2026. Cervical non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation is FDA-cleared for headache disorders, yet skeptics doubt that surface electrodes can engage deep vagal fibers rather than nearby neck tissue.

The review lines up four kinds of proof. Anatomy and computer models show clinically used settings recruit mainly large myelinated vagal fibers at measured nerve depths. Brain imaging shows activity shifting in vagal brainstem sites, and electrical recordings confirm signals reaching the brain. Immune studies find repeated suppression of inflammatory cytokines, matching the nerve's known anti-inflammatory reflex, and body markers tilt toward parasympathetic tone. Sham-controlled trials in cluster headache and migraine then show real clinical benefit. The authors call the combined fingerprint hard to explain away as placebo.
pmc-13291070:
Special DNA shapes called G-quadruplexes may point to new drug targets in prostate cancer, according to a 2026 study led by Liu Ge. These structures can switch genes on or off and may shape the immune setting around a tumor, yet their role in prostate cancer had stayed unclear until now.

Mapping in a prostate cancer cell line found 1,289 cancer-linked structures, mostly sitting in gene promoter regions where control happens. Machine learning tools combined with immune pathway analysis singled out one gene, IKBKB, as a central hub tied to later stage and poorer outlook. Lab tests showed the gene drives growth, movement, and genome instability in cancer cells. Drug scoring and computer-designed peptides close the study as first steps toward treatment.
pmc-13291170:
New towns need safe ground, and Ali M. El-Hawary leads a 2026 survey of rocks west of Qasr El-Farafra in Egypt. Air surveys read natural radiation and magnetic signals. The goal was to map risk and the deep rock surface below.

Three radioactive elements were measured in surface rocks. Potassium was most common and most evenly spread. Uranium varied most, hinting at local rich pockets. Thorium sat between the two in pattern. Dose estimates mostly fell below world averages. A few spots ran higher and need care. Strong links among the elements helped build risk maps. Town planners can use these maps before building.
pmc-13291770:
Ben Walker and co-authors describe a 2026 taxonomic paper naming a new deep-water amphipod species, Caeconyx papso, from the Porcupine Abyssal Plain in the Northeast Atlantic. The animal is a scavenger in the family Uristidae. Until now the genus Caeconyx held only one known species, Caeconyx caeculus.

The new species stands apart through a triangular eye lobe, a broadly rounded rear edge on its first epimeron, and shorter, stouter walking-leg segments. The team also supplies DNA sequences for four genes and runs family-level analyses placing the species among relatives in Uristidae and Tryphosidae. Full illustrations accompany the description, along with a key separating the two Caeconyx species.
pmc-13292570:
Azadeh Azizian and co-authors question a 2026 surgical habit in pancreatic head cancer: routinely stripping the nerve and lymph tissue hugging the superior mesenteric artery. Clearing that tissue may complete the cancer operation, but severing splanchnic nerves leaves many patients with severe diarrhea. In a prospective pilot at Göttingen, 66 patients had the semi-circumferential tissue fully embedded and serially sectioned for malignant cells.

Cancer cells turned up beside the artery in just 7.6 percent of cases, five patients, all with ductal adenocarcinoma. Four of those five also had positive resection margins elsewhere. Survival hinged mainly on margin status rather than on the artery tissue result. The authors label the findings hypothesis-generating and ask for bigger cohorts before anyone decides the extra dissection earns its diarrhea risk.
pmc-13292670:
Kavin Wee Keat Siaw and Paul C Hackley write a 2026 methods paper standardizing how to read the faint glow of sedimentary organic matter under a microscope. That fluorescence works as a proxy for thermal maturity in oil and gas basins, but readings drift without discipline. Their standard operating procedure tests a spectrometer married to an epi-fluorescence microscope.

Calibration used halogen light bounced off a PTFE standard, with checks on dark-current correction, warm-up time, light delivery, and how many readings a sample needs for precision. Emission is summarized by the peak wavelength and red-green and blue-green quotients. As rock matures, the signal fades, and the procedure maps exactly where the system stays trustworthy. The authors, working in a US Geological Survey context, aim for reproducible maturity calls across laboratories.
pmc-13293270:
Bana Antonios and colleagues report, in 2026, a case of acute myeloid leukemia that returned only in the skin, a form called leukemia cutis, with no sign in the bone marrow. Skin-only return is hard to spot and can be missed if only marrow is checked.

Gene tests on the skin sample found a rearrangement joining KMT2A and MLLT6, which opened the way to use the targeted drug revumenib as salvage care. The case stresses testing the actual site where disease returns, since marrow tests alone would have missed the clue. Early action matters, as skin return can foreshadow wider relapse.
pmc-13293470:
Qian Li leads a 2026 study building a model to place emergency supply depots where disaster risk argues they are needed most. Sensible depot sites can cut losses when earthquakes or other disasters strike a region.

The model scores each area on four parts of risk: hazard, exposure, weakness, and response capacity, using map and satellite data. Weights blend those scores for both before-disaster planning and after-disaster loss review. Layered depots are then matched to city plans to pick candidate zones. A test case, a major earthquake in western Yunnan, China, gave a workable layout, which the authors take as support for the model.
pmc-13293570:
Byunghun Yun and colleagues run, in a 2026 field study, a 12-week digital training program meant to lift thinking skills in older adults. Dementia rates keep rising, and many older adults quit digital training because the tools feel hard to use.

A total of 133 adults aged 55 to 75 with no dementia diagnosis used a program with an AI chat helper and a group chat for peer contact. Thinking scores improved after the program overall. Frequent users gained more than light users, above all those who started with lower scores. Social support and engagement rose, while low mood eased over the 12 weeks.
pmc-13294270:
Eduardo Cuevas and a large team map clashes between oil work and fishing in the southern Gulf of Mexico for a 2026 risk study. Fleets share water with platforms, pipelines, heavy ship traffic, and spills, in a lopsided and poorly documented pairing. Multi-source maps fed individual and combined vulnerability and risk scores for industrial and small-scale fleets.

Two danger zones stood out. Small boats off eastern Tabasco and western Campeche face steady exposure to big vessels and oil structures, while industrial fleets north of Ciudad del Carmen meet surface oil more often. The maps can guide sea planning near a new protected area.
pmc-13294370:
Yutaro Fukushima and a large team solve the structure of a DNA repair remodeler bound to a nucleosome in a 2026 cryo-microscopy study. Yeast Rad26, kin to human Cockayne syndrome protein B, helps restart copying after damage and shuffles nucleosomes. Frozen snapshots show where the machine grips the DNA spool during transcription-coupled repair.

Rad26 clamps near the spool entry point with its two motor lobes flipped versus other remodelers like Snf2 and Ino80. A lysine-arginine loop proved required for grip and shuffling in mutation and binding tests. The protein's own loose head normally brakes the motor through long-range contacts, released by two leucine changes. Shape explains repair choreography.
pmc-13294470:
Bandar S. Alharbi and Majed M. Aljabri interview Saudi imams about helping with diabetes self-care in a 2026 qualitative study. Type 2 diabetes demands daily habits that faith leaders might reinforce, given their moral standing. Nineteen imams from city and rural posts gave face-to-face interviews in Arabic, analyzed thematically without preset codes.

Five themes arose. Trust and authority give imams real sway, and sermons, short talks, classes, and private counsel offer ready channels, above all when advice is framed in Islamic teaching. Yet role boundaries blur: many doubted that health promotion is truly their job, lacked medical knowledge, and feared losing credibility or pushback from worshippers.
pmc-13294870:
Xiaojing Pan and Ting Luo review single-cell RNA sequencing in preeclampsia research in a 2026 article. Preeclampsia is a pregnancy disorder involving the placenta and body-wide inflammation, yet its cell-level causes stay partly hidden. Reading gene activity cell by cell offers a sharper view than older mixed-tissue methods.

Findings from healthy placenta and lining tissue set a baseline for cell types and for how trophoblast cells mature. In preeclampsia, studies found troubled trophoblast groups, faster cell ageing, and changed immune behaviour at the boundary between mother and fetus. The authors also weigh uses in finding warning markers, building prediction tools, and sorting patients into subtypes.
pmc-13295070:
Rosco Kasujja and co-authors map how lay mental health workers are trained and supervised in East Africa in a 2026 scoping review. Non-specialist workers carry much community mental health care where specialists are scarce. How they are prepared and overseen was poorly documented despite their central role.

Searches of five databases yielded 18 studies from five of the seven countries in the region. Training ranged from short workshops to longer apprenticeship style programmes, and supervision came in senior-led, peer, mixed, and digital forms. Client results and worker skills improved in many reports, yet standard supervision, lasting funding, and worker support stayed weak across settings.
pmc-13295170:
Ailin Wu and colleagues test plant-derived tiny vesicles for bowel disease with mood symptoms in a 2026 study. Inflammatory bowel disease often arrives with anxiety and low mood, yet few treatments address gut and brain together. Honeysuckle vesicles were tried as a natural carrier acting through the gut-brain axis.

Mice with long-lasting chemically induced colitis received the vesicles by mouth. Treated mice behaved less anxiously, kept a tighter gut barrier, and carried a reshaped gut microbe mix. Body-wide and brain inflammation eased, serotonin handling steadied, and a key growth signalling route in the brain switched back on, linking gut calm to better mood.
pmc-13295770:
Bingfei Li and colleagues review cell ageing across muscle, bone, and cartilage diseases in a 2026 article. Senescent cells stop dividing for good yet pour out signals that can help or harm their tissue. How that balance plays out differs sharply between body tissues.

Seven conditions are covered, from muscle injury and wasting to osteoporosis, joint wear, and disc breakdown. Ageing cells vary by disease in their markers, secretions, and weak points open to treatment. Shared pathways sit beside tissue-specific ones, and the authors weigh combined detection methods. The map aims to guide treatments that clear harmful ageing cells while sparing helpful ones.
pmc-13295970:
Caner Özyildirim and colleagues examine meals, diet and stress in 2026 among families of autistic children in Antalya, Türkiye. Feeding problems are common in this group and can harm both nutrition and family wellbeing, so the team survey 111 parents of children averaging about seven years old.

Almost every child scored poorly on diet quality, and difficult mealtime behaviour stood out as the strongest factor tied to worse diets. Making separate special meals also linked to poorer quality, while wider proactive tactics helped. Parents of girls reported more stress and burden than parents of boys, prompting a call for combined feeding and stress support.
pmc-13296770:
In 2026, Katalin Kuffa and co-authors build a fast method to catalogue proteins on the two faces of gut lining cells grown as sheets. Which face a protein sits on matters for bowel cancer markers and drug targets, yet side-by-side maps were scarce.

Tagging each face separately with a chemical label, then reading the catch by mass analysis, placed about twelve hundred surface proteins by side. Hundreds of sugar-attachment sites were also logged. Knocking out one gene shifted several surface markers, proving sensitivity. The authors link the atlas to how these cells lose polarity in cancer spread.
pmc-13297070:
Gary B. Wilkerson and colleagues follow, in 2026, twenty-seven women college soccer players through a season of virtual reality perception training. Eye and body responses to moving targets yielded an efficiency score, and sleep quality was surveyed before the season, with all time-loss injuries logged.

Players with the best decision efficiency and best sleep avoided concussion and leg injuries that sidelined others. Training with rising difficulty appeared to sharpen the efficiency score itself. Poor sleep may drag decision speed down, the authors note, and both may follow earlier injury. They argue subtle decision testing needs hard enough tasks to reveal risk.
pmc-13299070:
A B-cell surface protein called CD22 has become a versatile target across blood cancers and autoimmune disease, review Xin Chen and co-authors in 2026. CD22 sits almost exclusively on B cells, dampens their receptor signaling, and is quickly swallowed into the cell, a combination drug developers prize.

The review tours the arsenal built against it: immunotoxins, radioactive antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates, bispecific antibodies, and CAR T-cell therapies. Single-target treatments already achieve high response rates, and pairing CD22 with CD19 in dual-target CAR T cells reduces the antigen escape that causes relapse. The authors trace the same strategies migrating from oncology into autoimmune care and sketch research priorities.
pmc-13300770:
Healthy-looking wetland grasses in Argentina quietly host fungi that menace cereal crops, Eugenia Cendoya and colleagues report in a 2026 survey. Working in the Chaco wetlands along the Paraná and Paraguay rivers, they identified Fusarium isolates from symptom-free wild grasses using shape and TEF1 gene sequences. Attention centered on the Fusarium fujikuroi species complex.

Fifty-eight isolates belonged to that complex, and fifty of them fell into six known species, including the crop pathogens F. proliferatum and F. verticillioides. Two species had never been recorded in Argentina before. Eight isolates formed a brand-new species, named Fusarium varsavskyanum, whose genome carries the machinery for toxins such as fusaric acid and beauvericin.
pmc-13301070:
Nose jobs live or die on bone thickness, Marcin Jadczak and colleagues quantify in a 2026 imaging study. They rebuilt three-dimensional CT scans from eighty-seven adults, forty-four women and forty-three men, scanned for trauma or dizziness between January 2024 and December 2025. Measurements at fixed points charted the nasal bones and pyramid.

Women's nasal bones measured smaller at every point on both sides. At the upper left landmark, women averaged 6.29 against 8.07 in men, and the gap persisted downward along the bone. Such numbers, the authors argue, let surgeons plan the controlled bone cuts of rhinoseptoplasty with better force judgment, cutting the risk of stray fractures and asymmetry.
pmc-13303570:
Song Wei and co-authors build machine learning tools in a 2026 study to predict a whole-body inflammatory reaction after keyhole kidney stone surgery. Muscle loss, called sarcopenia, and branching staghorn stones were tested as joint risk factors.

Records for 755 patients treated between January 2021 and August 2025 were split into training and validation groups. Six models were compared, and an XGBoost model performed best in validation. Staghorn stones and sarcopenia stood out as the strongest signals, and patients with both faced far higher risk than expected from either alone. A web tool from the model may help teams plan closer watch after surgery.
pmc-13303870:
Sagar Paul leads a 2026 physics study of a gadolinium-based molecular magnet and how shape in quantum paths can block tunneling. Storing quantum information in broad features rather than local details could shield it from noise.

Single crystals of the compound were probed with a combined micro-SQUID and microwave method under sideways magnetic fields. The spin levels for the spin value of seven halves were mapped in detail. Tunneling strength rose and fell in clear waves, a sign of interference between quantum paths. The pattern reveals topology at work in this material and hints at new routes toward fault-tolerant quantum computing.
pmc-13304170:
Chiara De Gregorio, Marina Davila-Ross, and Adriano R Lameira compare laughter rhythm across all living great apes in a 2026 evolution study. Laughter is shared by orangutans, gorillas, bonobos, chimpanzees, and humans, making it a rare window on early voice control.

Recordings were timed and compared across the five species. The shared ancestor's laughter already kept an even beat, the authors infer. Over later evolution the beat grew faster, less steady, and more shaped by social setting. Humans sit furthest along that path, suggesting that flexible rhythm in laughter helped pave the way toward speech.
pmc-13304370:
Maria Timoshina and co-authors run a 2026 split-mouth trial of two filling materials for neck-of-tooth defects in professional ballet dancers. Dancers clench under heavy bite loads, and standard tooth-colored fillings often fail in that spot.

Twenty dancers each received a ceramic-network inlay on one defect and a self-curing bioactive filling on another, then returned over 24 months. Ceramic inlays kept smooth edges far more often and none failed outright, while the other fillings failed in a fifth to a third of cases. Dye leak tests and survival curves also favored the ceramic option for worn, non-decay defects.
pmc-13304970:
Ivan Matevski leads a 2026 survey of sheep and goats in North Macedonia for signs of Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus. The tick-borne illness threatens people, yet animal spread data that map risk zones remain scarce.

Blood from 1,992 small ruminants was tested with a commercial antibody kit, and results were adjusted for test accuracy. About one animal in four had past exposure, with sheep higher than goats and older animals highest. Rates swung widely by region, peaking in the east and the Vardar area. Testing farm animals can flag districts where people need stronger tick precautions.
pmc-13306170:
Michał K. Jastrzębski designed new non-steroidal blockers of a hormone-making enzyme for resistant prostate cancer in a 2026 study. Tumours that survive hormone therapy can make their own androgens through CYP17A1, the target enzyme here.

Compounds in the D2AAK1M series rest on a pyridine and piperidine frame shaped to grip the enzyme's iron centre closely. Computer profiling predicted better solubility and fat balance than the standard drug abiraterone, plus possible entry to the brain. Cell tests favoured killing of hormone-dependent prostate cells, matching the proposed blocking route and supporting further development.
pmc-13309370:
Jéssica Francielle Camargo led a 2026 veterinary study on finding the first lymph node that drains a skin tumor in dogs. The tumors were cutaneous mast cell tumors, a common skin cancer in dogs. Knowing which node drains a tumor guides staging and surgery.

Two mapping methods were tested in 21 dogs with 26 tumors. Blue dye used during surgery found more nodes than oil-based imaging done before surgery, and the pair together matched the expected drainage area best. About one in five tumors drained to a node outside the expected area. The authors present the combined method as a practical way to avoid missing spread.
pmc-13309770:
Zuhal Unalp Cepel authors a 2026 country report on Sweden that traces doubt toward the European Union and the rise of populism there. Sweden joined the Union in 1995, and its older parties still back deeper cooperation. Newer forces have shifted debate toward sovereignty, migration, and security themes.

The rise of the Sweden Democrats anchors the account, from entering parliament in 2010 to a breakthrough in the 2022 elections as the second-largest party. Their support deal with the governing bloc now shapes migration and economic policy. Two futures are sketched: a soft skeptic path tied to environment and rights reform, and a harder populist path. The report serves readers tracking European politics.
pmc-13310070:
Alham Al-Sharman and co-authors compare how symptoms push each other in two brain diseases in a 2026 study. Multiple sclerosis and Parkinson disease both mix movement trouble, low mood, poor sleep, fatigue, and pain. Standard correlation cannot say which symptom drives which, so a directional network method was used.

Records covered 104 people with multiple sclerosis and 54 with Parkinson disease, spanning function, thinking, mood, sleep, pain, and activity. Networks were built with a climbing algorithm and checked across 500 resamples for link strength. The sclerosis network alone held 18 nodes and 27 directed links in the reported build. The authors use the contrast to suggest disease-specific points where care might break symptom chains.
pmc-13310870:
Morteza Golbashirzadeh reviews seaweed toxins and nanotechnology in a 2026 paper that weighs harm against healing use. Toxins from marine algae drive harmful blooms that sicken people and wildlife. The same compounds have rare chemical traits that may serve in drug delivery, sensing, and combined diagnosis and therapy.

Nano sensors can spot toxins with high precision, and nano materials may help curb bloom harm. Toxin loaded nano carriers could target drugs to select cells. Safety and nature concerns must guide any use near living systems. Gaps in proof remain wide, so the review maps where careful tests should go next.
pmc-13311370:
Narges Aberuyi, Soheila Rahgozar, and Melika Katebi present a 2026 study on a small RNA that may restore drug response in childhood leukemia. Drug resistance drives relapse deaths in pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

The team measured miR-326 in 58 fresh bone marrow samples and in paired samples taken at diagnosis and relapse. Low levels of the RNA tracked with relapse and shorter disease-free survival. Adding the RNA back to resistant leukemia cells made them more drug-sensitive and lowered two target genes, ABCA2 and YY1, at RNA and protein level. Reporter tests confirmed direct targeting. The RNA looks like a candidate for beating resistance.
pmc-13311570:
Natasha E Noble and colleagues detail a 2026 interview study on Australian clinicians' views of smart inhalers for children with asthma. The devices log each dose, giving an honest record of use.

Eight family doctors, six child specialists, and nine respiratory nurses took part in semi-structured interviews. Most had never used a smart inhaler. Clinicians liked having firm dose data to guide treatment talks with parents. Uptake, they said, would need proof the devices work, lower costs for families, pay for clinician time, and data that flow into existing record systems. Those terms set the bar for rollout.
pmc-13311770:
Jin Zhou and co-authors offer a 2026 protocol for a large study on spotting biliary atresia before birth. In this rare illness, a baby's bile ducts fail, and early surgery gives the best chance.

At least 92,082 pregnancies having routine ultrasound will be screened for set fetal bile system features. Babies with positive signs, plus a matched sample of negatives, get direct follow-up after birth; the rest are traced through health records. Diagnosis rests on postnatal checks, with surgery and duct imaging where needed. Proof that prenatal signs work could move detection months earlier than today's postnatal screens.
pmc-13312070:
Jared M Wohlgemut and colleagues report a 2026 interview study on how acute care surgeons keep up with new published research. These surgeons treat life-threatening conditions and carry heavy night and weekend call loads, so staying current competes with clinical work for scarce time.

The team interviewed 13 surgeons practicing in the United States, with sessions averaging about 27 minutes, and analyzed the transcripts for themes. Surgeons said they read to solve clinical problems, out of curiosity, and for job performance and satisfaction. Paywalls, lack of time, and information overload stood in the way, while easy interfaces and academic posts helped. All wanted faster ways to find what matters, though many distrusted artificial intelligence tools that might reinforce bias.
pmc-13312470:
Haoyang Hu writes a 2026 commentary on a comparative study of dementia burden in Japan, China, and India from 1990 to 2023, built on Global Burden of Disease 2023 estimates. The three countries sit at different stages of aging, so placing them side by side shows how the burden grows as populations age and risk patterns shift.

Hu praises the underlying study for going past case counts to incidence, deaths, disability years, the drivers behind change, risk factors, and projections. China carried the heaviest load, with the heaviest absolute burden and the highest age-adjusted rates of the three, driven jointly by population aging and rising age-specific disease. The commentary argues China's response should lean on midlife prevention, early cognitive checks, and control of vascular and metabolic risks. The piece frames this as a prevention-first turn for neurology across Asia, not just more geriatric services.
pmc-13312970:
Paola Andrea Ospina-Sánchez and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, a multi-scale system that reads a carrot crop's growth stage and carotenoid content without destroying the plants. Six commercial varieties in orange, yellow, white, and purple were followed in field and laboratory with drone multispectral imagery, detailed light signatures, ordinary photographs, and color measurements feeding one modeling framework.

Random forest models trained on drone data classified growth stages with top scores above 0.90 on the reported metric, leaning on spectral changes as canopies grew and aged. Carotenoid estimation from field spectra was strong, and a laboratory model on high-resolution signatures came near perfection. Explanation analysis credited wavelengths in the green and red-edge bands, and a new color index from photographs estimated carotenoids well on its own. The authors pitch the stack for precision harvest and quality decisions.
pmc-13314570:
Heng-Yuan Hsu and co-workers build a machine learning model to flag early liver cancer return after surgery, in a study dated 2026. Relapse within 24 months of resection drives poor outlook in hepatocellular carcinoma, and no standard add-on therapy rules exist, so sharp risk sorting matters.

The team trained four methods on 1681 patients who had curative surgery at Chang Gung sites from 2007 to 2020, as counted in the report. A separate group of 251 patients from another hospital served for outside checking. Missing data were filled by a nearest-neighbor method, and models were tuned by five-fold cross-checks. Scores were judged by how well they ranked risk, and the winning model was opened up so doctors can see which factors drive each call.
pmc-13314770:
Vrushali Manoj Hadkar and Chinnadurai Immanuel Selvaraj pack a plant flavonoid into tiny carriers to make it work better, in a study from 2026. Hispidulin fights oxidation and cancer in tests, but it dissolves poorly in water and breaks down fast, which caps its medical use.

The team loaded hispidulin into nanoparticles of sodium carboxymethyl cellulose by ionic gelation. A battery of tools, from light spectra to heat tests and microscopy, checked size and makeup, and loading rates were measured. Release in dishes was timed and modeled. The loaded particles were then tested for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory action, metal binding, blood safety, clot busting, and killing of MCF-7 breast cancer cells, among other checks listed in the report. Cell death and energy loss were read by stains, and docking models probed targets such as VEGFR.
pmc-13315070:
Emil Skog, John E Marsh, and Patrik Sörqvist test whether products we reject still color how green our picks look, in a study from 2026. Shoppers often sort goods into a basket and a discard pile before judging the set they keep.

In two experiments, people saw streams of grocery items, some kept and some tossed, then rated how eco-friendly the kept set was. When items vanished after showing, tossed green items dragged the kept set rating down, a contrast effect, while tossed harmful items lifted it. When all items stayed in view, both effects flipped, an assimilation pattern, as the authors report. The flip shows that what we pass over shapes judgment, but memory decides the direction.
pmc-13315170:
Lukas Pollmann and colleagues published a retrospective cohort study in 2026 on acid-suppressing drugs given before major liver surgery. The group looked at patients who had at least four liver segments removed at one center between 2006 and 2024. They compared those already taking proton pump inhibitors with those who were not.

Among 507 patients, the 220 who took these drugs had worse overall complication scores and more bile leaks after surgery, with leakage in 38 percent versus 26 percent of the other group. The link held after matching and adjustment, while germ tests on bile samples showed no clear difference. The authors urge care before routine use.
pmc-13315370:
Tariq M. Aslam writes in 2026 about the human side of eye care at a time when artificial intelligence is advancing fast. He notes that a diagnosis in an eye clinic can change how a patient sees their future, touching independence, identity, and daily life, and that listening and honest reassurance shape what follows.

Anxiety and depression are common in people with lasting vision loss, yet the emotional and personal parts of eye care get little funding or study, he argues. Impressive AI gains in screening and grading should not crowd out the encounter itself. The piece defends clinician skills that no tool can replace.
pmc-13315670: Zhifeng Li and co-authors are the named authors of a breast cancer paper on puerarin, DUSP1, and miR-133a-3p that Molecular Medicine Reports has retracted. Only the retraction notice itself is present for this item. Editors acted after a reader flagged reused blot images, and office checks found blot data shared with several other papers by different groups. Since the disputed data had appeared before submission, the editor withdrew the paper, and no author explanation satisfied the concern.
pmc-13315770:
Zuyi Xia argues in 2026 that the world needs to move from sustainable development toward enduring development, with renewed ecological, social, and human foundations. Industrial growth has brought pollution, ecosystem loss, resource overuse, and lasting inequality, even as the 2030 Agenda gave nations a shared action frame.

Only 35 percent of assessed goal targets are on track or moving ahead at a fair pace. Nearly half move too slowly, and 18 percent have slipped back from the 2015 base. Climate change, biodiversity loss, health pressure, conflict, and split governance make gains fragile. Enduring development builds on the goals' logic rather than replacing it.
pmc-13315970:
Antonio Martínez-Murcia and colleagues write a letter in 2026 urging an update to test specificity for Andes hantavirus, after the World Health Organization confirmed the virus behind a cruise ship respiratory outbreak. They note that no RT-qPCR kits made specifically for this virus could be found.

Available commercial tests mostly aim at the whole hantavirus genus or at pulmonary syndrome types. They often use heavily varied primers to widen coverage, which can weaken matching and sensitivity for one target. Published Andes-specific assays were checked on computer against all public virus sequences. Sharper tests would help labs name this virus quickly and correctly.
pmc-13316170:
Baile Mao and co-authors review in 2026 extracellular vesicles in osteosarcoma, the most common primary bone cancer of the young, linking them to drug resistance, immunity, and clinical use. Survival has barely improved in four decades, staying near 60 to 70 percent for local disease and below 30 percent when spread or resistant.

Tumor vesicles carry signals that spread resistance, reshape the immune surroundings, and aid metastasis. The review covers special lab challenges in bone tumors, such as mineral matrix interference and platelet vesicle contamination. It also weighs vesicles as liquid biopsy markers for drug response, outlook, immune state, and tiny leftover disease.
pmc-13316870:
Qi He, Qianying Guang, Yien Xu, and Jian Zhao mined United States survey data from 2003 to 2014 for a 2026 study on diet variety and gum disease. Eating a wider mix of foods might calm the inflammation behind periodontitis, but the link was unproven.

After full adjustment, each step up in dietary diversity score came with lower odds of gum disease, at an odds ratio of 0.95 in the adjusted model, with a smooth dose pattern and no curve. Five food groups shared the credit almost evenly, hinting at synergy rather than one hero food. Body roundness and a red cell spread measure carried small parts of the effect. Widening the weekly menu, they argue, is a simple prevention lever.
pmc-13317170:
Patrik Karlsson, Mats Ekendahl, and Philip Lindner used Swedish registers in a 2026 study of deaths among young people in specialist drug treatment, a group often missed by research. They tracked patients aged 13 to 25 seen between 2011 and 2021 by the country's largest youth treatment provider.

Among 23,709 patients, 229 died, just under one in a hundred, a death rate far above Swedish youth overall. Risk ran higher for males, for those who had inpatient stays, and for those with convictions, whose hazard was 2.64 times the comparison level in adjusted models. For those with convictions, more outpatient visits tied to lower risk. Migrant background and parental schooling showed no clear effect.
pmc-13317770:
Zhengshan Zhang and colleagues built, in a 2026 study, a machine learning model to predict nerve damage in people with type 2 diabetes, a complication that creeps up silently. Their twist was adding artery stiffness readings from both ankles plus body shape measures to the usual clinical data.

Records for 966 patients, sorted by nerve conduction tests, fed nine competing models after a smart feature hunt found thirteen drivers. A support vector machine won, with accuracy of 0.74 and an AUC of 0.82 in the reported scores. Left-side pulse wave velocity dominated the rankings, far above its right-side twin, an asymmetry the authors flag as new. Wider hips looked protective, while smoking and long disease duration raised risk.
pmc-13318670:
Andrea Adrados and colleagues review, in 2026, ways to make immunotherapy work better in two blood cancers. The diseases are multiple myeloma and chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. First-line treatments often work at first, then resistance grows. New immune treatments show promise but do not last for everyone.

The review covers pairing new immune drugs with standard treatments. Checkpoint inhibitors, CAR T-cells, and bispecific antibodies all feature. It also examines the gut microbiota and its effect on treatment response. Microbe balance may shape disease biology and drug success. The authors close with current challenges and future directions. Their goal is longer, safer responses for more patients.
pmc-13318870:
Yuchen Wang and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of neuroprotective drugs added to clot-removal treatment for acute stroke. Thrombectomy reopens big vessels, yet many patients never regain independence. Reperfusion injury at tissue level is a key reason. Searches covered three databases to January 31, 2026.

Most other outcomes showed no clear benefit. Death, symptomatic bleeding, and serious side effects did not differ. Timing and reperfusion context may shape who benefits. The authors call this a weak, mixed signal needing mechanism-guided trials.
pmc-13319270:
Sahrai Saeed and co-authors wrote a short reply letter in 2026 about how sleep loss was classed in their joint study of poor sleep and paused breathing in sleep. A reader had raised the point that poor sleep comes in distinct forms, and that lumping them may hide links to heart harm and death.

The reply notes that their short scale was built to match the core signs of a sleep disorder, which suits large surveys and quick screening. It also agrees that splitting cases by main complaint, such as trouble falling asleep or early waking, would be worth doing. Future work may test whether those forms carry distinct risks.
pmc-13320070:
Xin Jin and co-authors study a common antioxidant drug in severe COVID lung illness in a 2026 records review from a Shanghai hospital. Severe lung cases of this illness carry high death rates and steep care costs, and the drug had shown hints of faster recovery in past reports. Whether it cuts death or worsening in the worst cases had not been tested.

From 221 patients seen in one winter wave, matched pairs gave 176 people split by whether they took the drug by mouth for at least three days. Drug use tracked with a lower chance of death or worsening while in hospital in the matched counts. Stay length, costs, and heavy care use did not shift clearly. The signal is hopeful but comes from one center.
pmc-13320270:
Nana Li and co-authors review a growth factor that both heals and harms in a 2026 article on amphiregulin. The factor latches onto a well known cell growth switch and steers cell growth, change, repair, and immune replies. First found in fluid from a breast cancer line, it can slow some tumor cells while urging healthy cells to grow, a two faced pattern that still draws study.

Proof from cell and animal work is weighed across heart, lung, gut, cancer, and infection settings. In many of them the factor guards tissue after harm yet also drives disease when its signal runs too long or too strong. Turning that balance into safe drugs will need exact control of dose, place, and timing, the review argues.
pmc-13320470:
Aili Wang and colleagues present a 2026 mouse and cell study on fine dust in the air and asthma. The team asked how a lung protein called CC16 guards airway cells against a type of cell death linked to iron and fat damage. Dust exposure is known to worsen asthma and harm the lining of the airways.

pmc-13321070:
Dimitri Breda and co-authors build a data driven method to forecast vector borne disease in a 2026 study. Illnesses spread by ticks and other vectors pose growing risks, yet records are sparse and transmission involves long delays. Past infection and exposure shape later cases, so memory effects matter for any honest forecast.

The framework learns hidden transmission dynamics with memory straight from time series, using only a few basis functions in a sparse discovery step. Tick borne risk to humans is the test case, where tick numbers, weather, and human contact are all uncertain. Checks are reported to back the method's reliability and steadiness under scarce data. Better forecasts could guide early public health action.
pmc-13321370:
Claudius Jelgersma and co-authors compare one stage and two stage spine correction in older patients in a 2026 study. Pedicle subtraction osteotomy is a demanding fix for stiff spinal deformity, with high risk in old age. Splitting surgery into two sittings has been proposed to ease the burden, but proof in older patients was thin.

Records for 51 patients treated from 2014 to 2023 were compared, with median ages near 70 in both groups. Total operating time was far shorter in one stage care, at 431 minutes against 653 minutes on average in the study. Blood loss, hospital stay, and complication rates within 90 days did not differ clearly. Overall surgical load, not staging, seemed decisive.
pmc-13322970:
Xinyu Liu, Wei Meng and Xun Huang comment on a newly found mitochondrial carrier in a 2026 article about fat storage. They discuss work by Yamamuro and others, published in Cell, that names SLC25A35 as the long-sought carrier moving phosphoenolpyruvate out of mitochondria.

That export supplies the glycerol backbone needed to build triglycerides and related fats in liver and fat tissue, a process called glyceroneogenesis. Fatty acid control has drawn far more attention than backbone supply, the authors note. Linking this carrier to triglyceride formation and fatty liver gives a fresh target for metabolic research, and the commentary sets out why the finding matters for energy balance.
pmc-13325070:
Jéssica Alves Bonamichi and colleagues compare how packaged forms of the herbicide clomazone move through soil, corn residue, and soybean plants in a 2026 study. Clomazone suits no-till farming but can evaporate or wash away before it works.

Two microencapsulated and two standard concentrate products were tracked under controlled conditions. The encapsulated forms leaked slowly at first, then reached 42.3 and 36.9 percent leaching by day 30 of the trial. Standard forms leaked fast on day one, near 20 percent, yet lost less overall. Encapsulated products clung to corn residue and kept over 90 percent of the dose on leaf surfaces. No form harmed the soybean plants.
pmc-13325370:
Yunus Emre Toprak and co-authors make glowing carbon dots from pine cone waste to sense copper in water in a 2026 study. Trace copper threatens both ecosystems and health, and field tests need to be fast and cheap.

Dots cooked from pine cone lignin and doped with lysine changed brightness in step with copper levels. The working range spanned 2.81 × 10^-7 to 5.87 × 10^-5 mol per liter, with a detection limit of 2.8 × 10^-8 mol per liter. Trials on drinking water, seawater, and wastewater standards gave recoveries of 98.9 to 104.4 percent. Results matched the standard absorption method at 95 percent confidence. Real lake and tap samples also read cleanly.
pmc-13327870:
Yanyan Zhang and colleagues gather diagnostic clues for liver amyloidosis in a 2026 review of ten confirmed cases. AL amyloidosis deposits abnormal protein in the liver and is rare enough to be missed. The team re-read clinical notes plus CT and MRI scans for shared patterns.

Every patient had an enlarged liver and low blood albumin, and all showed sharply raised alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase with near-normal other liver enzymes. Scans showed delayed contrast uptake, narrowed or poorly seen main liver veins, and fluid around portal veins in all cases, while bile ducts stayed open. Belly swelling affected 90 percent of patients, so the full pattern should prompt early biopsy thinking.
pmc-13328170:
Seon-Chil Kim and colleagues test personalized digital therapy for children with ADHD in a 2026 study. Forty children aged 5 to 12 were split evenly between a standard digital training program and one tuned to each child's first-week performance profile. Training volume was held equal, and attention tests plus a Korean ADHD rating scale bracketed the four weeks.

Profiling showed performance decline tied more to commission errors, the impulsive kind, than to missed targets. The personalized arm then adjusted content mix, difficulty, and feedback to each child's error pattern during weeks two to four, while controls followed the fixed plan. Data-driven tuning of digital practice may beat one-size programs, the design sets out to show.
pmc-13328270:
Hao Kang and Xiaofen Cao review stroboscopic visual training for basketball in a 2026 narrative review. Training under flickering eyewear is meant to sharpen how athletes take in a fast game, but basketball-specific studies are scarce. The pair gathered work from comparable open-skill sports published between 1997 and 2026.

Across sports, the training improved three markers tied to information processing: reaction time, decision accuracy, and motor control. They sort training settings into a three-phase frame matched to processing stages and to basketball-specific measures. Every suggested setting, though, rests on cross-sport trends, so the framework stands as a hypothesis until basketball trials test the numbers directly.
pmc-13328370:
Jianbo Song and co-authors review sound-based pain relief in a 2026 narrative review. Pain affects over 30 percent of the world's people, and drug or surgical routes carry misuse and complication risks. The authors gather evidence on acoustic stimulation, from music and natural sounds to vibroacoustic therapy and immersive sound systems.

Sound seems to work through several brain routes at once: retuning cortex-thalamus loops, switching on the body's own descending pain brakes, and shifting neurochemical messengers. Clinical reports back music, natural sound, and vibration-sound mixes as add-ons for both sudden and lasting pain. The review argues sound deserves a planned seat in multimodal pain care, with dosing standards still to settle.
pmc-13332370:
Ruoyu Zhang and colleagues developed a 2026 method for spotting social media posts that quietly offer prescription drugs for private sale in Japan. Such one-to-one dealing bypasses pharmacies, risks unsafe use, and is hard for regulators to track by hand.

Working from the hashtag “#Okusuri mogumogu,” tied to trading psychiatric drugs, the team crawled 7,499 posts from 2022 and 6,461 from early 2023, then labeled which ones truly offered private transactions. Of 3,228 distinct words, 452 were significantly tied to dealing posts, with terms meaning request, transfer, and direct message among the strongest signals. A decision tree trained on 2022 data reached 82.31 percent accuracy on the 2023 set, with area under the curve values around 0.83 to 0.84. The authors suggest the approach can help monitors flag risky drug trading automatically.
pmc-13332970:
Begonya Nafria and colleagues audited children's trial protocols across Europe in a 2026 study of whether language rules quietly shut families out. Europe has 32 official languages, children with rare diseases may find their only treatment option abroad, and some patients report being turned away over language.

The team searched the eligibility text of 1,754 pediatric protocols run in Europe between 2007 and 2024 on ClinicalTrials.gov. Most, 95.2 percent, never mentioned language at all. Among the 85 protocols that did set language requirements, only 23, or 27.1 percent, offered a scientific justification such as testing that must be done in a shared language or questionnaires validated in few tongues. English at 20 percent and French at 16.5 percent were the most demanded languages. The authors urge ethics committees to demand reasons for language criteria and protocols to plan translation and travel support.
pmc-13333370:
Liming Yang and co-authors engineered a swallowable nanoparticle in 2026 to rescue celastrol, a plant compound with strong promise against fatty liver disease but poor absorption and a narrow safety margin. Their target was nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, the inflamed stage of fatty liver that can march toward cirrhosis.

Instead of loading the drug into a carrier, they let it self-assemble with natural polysaccharides, building 42 candidate assemblies and screening them for the best partner. Chondroitin sulfate won. The winning mix raised total body exposure 3.12-fold over free celastrol, and tracer studies suggested it crosses gut cells through several uptake routes with partial escape from digestive compartments. In a mouse model of the disease, the particles calmed liver inflammation and cut fat buildup while softening the free drug's toxicity. The authors present the design as a platform that widens celastrol's usable window for oral liver therapy.
pmc-13333470:
Shi-Ning Luo and colleagues test two inflammation markers against angiogram-proven coronary disease severity in a 2026 retrospective study. High-sensitivity C-reactive protein is a familiar inflammation gauge, while Lp-PLA2 comes from the vessel wall, and the authors asked how each lines up with how blocked a patient's arteries are.

The Henan cohort covered 438 patients scoped between April 2023 and April 2024, split into 329 with at least half-blocked coronary arteries and 109 controls below that bar. Both markers rose with lesion burden, though in different patterns. Lp-PLA2 climbed to its peak in three-vessel disease, while hs-CRP topped out in two-vessel disease. Both ran higher in heart attack patients than in angina patients. Lp-PLA2 separated coronary disease with an AUC of 0.900 and severe lesions at 0.952; adding hs-CRP barely moved the curve. The authors favour the pair, saying the signals carry complementary information for risk stratification.
pmc-13334270: Jiashun Li and co-authors issued this 2026 correction notice. It concerns their systematic review and meta-analysis of CD3 bispecific antibodies targeting BCMA or GPRC5D in relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. The notice itself carries no study results; it only replaces the article's funding statement, which had been published with errors. The corrected statement lists the supporting grants. They include Xinjiang regional health and medical research projects, a National Natural Science Foundation of China award, and Xinjiang Medical University programs.
pmc-13336970:
Sicong Ren and colleagues design a blood-derived gel that rebuilds gum lining in a 2026 study. Keratinized mucosa, the tough gum tissue around teeth and implants, is hard to regrow. The mouth is wet, moving, and hostile to grafts. Their double-network gel blends treated platelet-rich fibrin, sticky alginate, and microspheres carrying plant compounds.

Two interlocked networks give strong wet grip and fatigue resistance, so the gel stays put under chewing stress. Slow release of growth factors and plant compounds boosts blood vessel growth and steers neutrophils toward a germ-eating state. The gel's stiffness also instructs gum fibroblasts to rebuild matrix faster. Animal tests confirmed strong regeneration of the gum lining.
pmc-13337770:
Regina Idu Ejemot-Nwadiaro leads a 2026 survey of job stress among university teachers in Nigeria. Academic stress in sub-Saharan Africa has had little study that mixes questionnaires with body measures. The setting was the University of Calabar, with staff drawn from all 15 faculties.

A total of 401 permanent staff completed the ASSET stress tool alongside height, weight, and body measurements. Stress proved widespread, with 84.3 percent of respondents falling in stressed ranges in the reported summary. Sources of pressure and links to habits and health factors were tested with standard comparisons. Results underline a heavy strain burden that university policy has yet to address well.
pmc-13339770:
Qingyu Zhang, Yat-Long Cheng, and Ying-Yeung Yeung convert ethers into acetals without a catalyst in a 2026 study. Acetals serve as drug parts, materials, fragrances, and protecting groups. A bromoamide reagent called DBDMH mediated direct editing beside the ether oxygen.

Common ethers such as THF and diethyl ether plus varied alcohols gave acetals in high yields under mild conditions as reported. The method built two commercial fragrances, Cyanophyll and Efetaal, proving practical reach. Trace bromine and acid impurities in the reagent proved crucial to speed, an honest detail that helps others reproduce the reaction.
pmc-13341270:
Canhada and colleagues charted weight gain across adult life in 2026 using the ELSA-Brasil study, a long-running cohort of Brazilian adults followed from 2008 to 2024. The 11,611 participants, aged 35 to 74 at entry, had repeated measures of weight, waist, and body fat and muscle, with weight at age 20 recalled at the start. The team modeled how each measure changed with age.

Adults gained an average of 15 kilograms between ages 20 and 60, when weight peaked, and half of that gain arrived before age 35. Yearly gains were steepest up to the early forties, then slowed, held steady in the late fifties and sixties, and fell in older age. Waist size kept rising to about age 75 even as weight leveled. The authors argue that curbing gain in young adulthood could do the most to cut later obesity burden.
pmc-13341570:
Europe's heart and diabetes prevention needs a life-course reset, argues Sarah Cuschieri in a 2026 policy analysis. Cardiovascular disease and diabetes remain the top causes of early death in Europe despite decades of pledges and cheap, proven preventive tools.

Cuschieri points to early-life risk exposure, patchy surveillance, and care systems built around late treatment rather than prevention. Priority moves include weaving prevention across the lifespan, strengthening front-line and community services, funding equity-focused data, and scaling joint efforts such as JACARDI and JA PreventNCD. Accountability, she concludes, is the missing muscle behind existing ambition.
pmc-13341870:
Digital skills help diabetic foot patients manage their condition, mostly through confidence, in a 2026 survey by Jianxia Yao and colleagues. The cross-sectional study enrolled 328 patients with diabetes-related foot disease in a tertiary endocrinology department between February 2024 and December 2025.

Digital health literacy correlated moderately with self-management behavior (r = 0.42), while self-efficacy correlated strongly (r = 0.53). Mediation analysis showed self-efficacy carried 41.8% of the literacy effect, with an effect size of 0.23, even after adjusting for age, disease duration, and ulcer grade. Teaching patients to find information may fail unless programs also build belief they can act on it.
pmc-13342170:
Research on childhood adversity and personality disorders is mapped bibliometrically by Liuyin Jin's team in the 2026 analysis. Records from three sources through December 2025 were screened and deduplicated to 5,084 publications, analyzed with network and burst-detection tools.

Output grew year by year with a marked climb after 2000. The United States dominated publications, citations, and collaborations; Canada, Germany, the Netherlands, Australia, and the United Kingdom also carried weight. Harvard, the University of London, and Heidelberg led institutions, and authors such as Zanarini and Fonagy anchored the field. The maps expose core themes and emerging fronts for new readers to explore.
pmc-13347670:
Tinyiko P. Hlungwani, Pheagane M.W. Nkoana, and Velibanti N. Sukati survey satisfaction with private eye care in South Africa, in a 2026 study. Questionnaires shared through social media drew 283 users across all nine provinces, with a mean age of 36.3 years. Visits most often aimed at renewing glasses or lenses, routine checks, or blurred vision.

Overall satisfaction averaged 4.38 out of 5 in the reported score, with cleanliness, facilities, and staff conduct rated highest by patients. Waiting time and cost scored lowest, and among patients who had switched provider, moves were led by relocation while 17.9 percent cited poor service. Shorter waits and clearer pricing are the clear fixes.
pmc-13347770:
Husin F. Khizar and colleagues pilot manual therapy against strength training for runner knee pain from the iliotibial band, in a study from 2026. Thirty-four runners were split evenly, with one group getting friction massage, stretching, and soft tissue work. The other following a set hip and knee strengthening plan over six weeks, scored for pain and leg function.

Both groups improved clearly on pain and function by the end of the program in the reported tests, with strong statistical signals in each arm. No loser emerged from this small pilot. So the authors offer both routes as workable starting care and call for larger head-to-head work that also tracks return of symptoms over time.
pmc-13348070:
Tripti Raghavendra and Sarita G. Bhat report the genome of a sea bacterium that eats naphthalene, in an announcement from 2026.
