The genome spans 5,754,741 base pairs with 5,306 genes and a G plus C share of 70.34 percent in the reported assembly. Gene notes flag many pollutant-breaking enzymes plus routes to useful by-products, making the strain a candidate for cleaning tar-like pollution at ports.
pmc-13349770:
Siqi Wang and colleagues review ear-point therapy as an add-on for childhood attention disorder, in a scoping review published in 2026. Seven databases to July 2025 gave 21 controlled trials with 2,270 children, checked with standard bias tools, tabulated by design. Pooled where outcomes allowed, covering parent ratings, anxiety and mood scales, and life quality scores.

Add-on ear therapy improved parent ratings, anxiety and mood scores. Life quality in the pooled results, each clearing the set significance bar, while overall success rate only trended upward. No serious harms appeared, yet bias grades left evidence at low to moderate certainty, so the authors back longer, tighter trials before firm clinic advice.
pmc-13351570:
Lingzhao Min and colleagues report a 2026 case series on children who have both craniosynostosis and hydrocephalus. Seven children had syndromic forms and eight had raised pressure inside the skull. All had cranioplasty, fluid leaked in two cases, and five later needed a ventriculoperitoneal shunt for lasting hydrocephalus. Over follow-up averaging 53.6 months, skull shape and symptoms improved in eight children. The authors favour cranioplasty first, with shunting held for cases that persist.
pmc-13353170:
Merve Acun Pınar leads a 2026 clinical study of coal workers' pneumoconiosis and related lung scarring. Long coal dust exposure scars the lungs and can also drive airway disease. All 100 patients were male, with mean age of 61.7 years. Large opacities appeared in 37 percent, while restrictive and obstructive lung patterns hit 35 percent and 38 percent. Bituminous miners fared worse than lignite miners on both opacity and lung function. Interstitial changes showed in 63 percent and frank interstitial disease in 42 percent, linked in models to longer exposure.
pmc-13355370:
Joice Carla Dorneles Zanin and co-authors ran a 2026 trial in Brazil on a coffee-flavored carbohydrate drink given before surgery. Drinkers reported feeling fuller and less thirsty and anxious than fasters, and they liked the taste. Those who began very anxious felt the drink helped calm them. No harms were seen, though the trial was too small to catch rare events. The authors call for larger studies on wider outcomes and safety.
pmc-13358370:
Fröhlich and colleagues probe how the calcium channel Orai1 opens in cell walls. The channel lets calcium into cells. A sensor protein, STIM1, tells it when to open. The right mix keeps the channel shut at rest. It also lets in enough calcium when the cell calls for it. Too loose a mix lets in too much. The work shows how fine tuning guards cell health.
pmc-13359370:
Yiqun Xu and co-authors simulate how porous materials form in a 2026 study. Their simulations show particles change how the mix separates, slowing pore growth and yielding finer pores. As the mix evolves, the pore size pattern shifts from one hump to two. More of the soap-like ingredient and neutral particle surfaces refine the structure further. The model can guide recipes for filters and lightweight solids.
pmc-13359970:
Tzong-Yueh Chen and co-authors measure what a super typhoon did to ocean life in a 2026 study. Typhoons are often credited with boosting ocean productivity by stirring up nutrients. Surface readings barely changed, likely because sampling came after the brief surface signal faded. Deeper totals told a fuller story: nutrients and plant plankton rose through the water column, though the bloom lasted only about a week, cut short by grazing and falling nutrient supply. Bacteria did not grow in mass, but their growth rates rose, showing a subtler microbial response.
pmc-13360170:
Hao Zhang and co-authors report a 2026 study from two hospitals on stage III lung cancer that surgery cannot remove. All 170 patients first had chemo with immune drugs, then radiation, and reached control of their disease. After that, 65 patients went on to extra immune drug treatment, while 105 did not. The team tracked both groups for a median of 33 months.

Extra checks suggested the benefit showed most in the early months, around 8 to 10 months in. The authors say the added treatment looks worth it, while noting the study looked back at past care.
pmc-13361070:
Shirong Dong and co-authors studied how salts shape protein threads from whey in a 2026 food science paper. When heated in acid, whey protein forms tiny fibrils that can thicken or stabilize foods. Sulfate salts also gave shorter, clustered threads compared with chloride salts. The results give food makers a guide to which salts to pick when they want protein fibrils with set traits.
pmc-13361370:
Jasna Kalanj and co-authors assessed heart ultrasound measures in young patients with thickened heart muscle in a 2026 study. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy makes the heart wall grow too thick. These were set against MRI measures of heart mass, wall thickness, and scarring, and against major bad events over time. Length-wise measures can catch early weakness that the usual pump score misses. Finding which measures warn of trouble could sharpen watch and care for these young patients.
pmc-13362570:
Hong-Tao Li and colleagues present a 2026 computer study of a lead-free perovskite solar cell design. Two layer materials, WS2 and SnO2, worked best in the model. With a tuned absorber about 900 nanometers thick and very low defect levels, the simulated cell reached about 23 percent efficiency. Nothing was built in a lab, yet the numbers give makers a clear recipe to try for safer, high-output solar cells.
pmc-13362770:
Camilo Andrés Cabarcas Castro and colleagues present a 2026 study on turning drinking water sludge into a usable soil material. Water plants produce sludge that usually goes to landfill. The team stiffened it with lime, comparing store-bought lime with lime made from waste eggshells, baked and slaked in the lab. Store lime reached the top strength at its highest dose and longest cure. Eggshell lime peaked earlier, at a mid dose and one week, and stayed competitive at mid and high doses, which marks it as a workable green swap. Adding strong alkali mostly weakened the eggshell mixes. Grain images helped explain the strength patterns.
pmc-13363170:
Xin Liu and colleagues report a 2026 study comparing diets and blood health in 356 adults in northeast China. pmc-13366770:
Mordenti and colleagues described in 2026 how patients and professionals together built transition care plans for young people with rare bone diseases in Italy. Patients and caregivers shaped every step, from design to final approval, rather than being consulted at the end. The authors present the model as a structured yet flexible way to build shared, realistic plans that both clinics and families will back.
pmc-13373270:
Michael Galvin and co-authors linked past trauma to sad mood in parents in Haiti in a 2026 study. Haiti faces years of unrest, quakes, storms, and hard times. Parent mood shapes child growth, so the stakes run across kin lines.

The team used data from a trial of 480 parent and baby pairs in Cap-Haitien. Trauma was logged with a set event list, and sad mood with a local scale. More trauma went with a clear rise in sad mood risk, even when cash and home facts were held in the math. The team calls for mind care built into child health work in Haiti.
pmc-13373670:
Salima Serroukh and co-authors report three eye cases after kidney swaps in a 2026 paper. Fluid built up under the center of the eye's back wall, which blurred sight. The ill is tied to stress and to long use of steroid drugs, a mainstay after a swap.

Eye exams and dye tests proved the ill in all three. A slow cut in steroid dose brought clear gains in sight. Eye checks should be part of swap follow-up.
pmc-13374170:
Raquel Sánchez-Ruano and co-authors heard nurses on shared care words in Spain in a 2026 study. Shared word sets name health needs, care steps, and results in one tongue for all staff. The study sat with 33 nurses who work in care, teaching, leads, and research.

Three group talks and 14 deep chats were read for shared themes in 2024. One theme prized the shared tongue as a path to more say in care calls. Blocks and boosters to daily use were also mapped. Frail health in old age was the test case. The finds can help clinics weave the word sets into real work with less strain.
pmc-13374270:
Zhao Yue and co-authors listed a gene family that moves plant food in hemp in a 2026 study. The family helps roots take in and spread nitrogen, the key food for growth. Good use of it can cut farm waste and cost.

The team found 66 such genes in the hemp code and split them in eight kin groups. Gene reads in roots of two hemp types, fed high and low nitrogen, showed wide spread in acts. Two lead genes stood out in lab checks for their part in food use. The list and leads give breeders fresh aims to raise hemp that needs less feed.
pmc-13378770:
Hojjatollah Sadeqi and co-authors published a 2026 study on why thinking comes and goes in Lewy body dementia. They compared patients with the dementia, patients with Parkinson's disease without dementia, and healthy controls. A modelling method split the recordings into brief brain states that come and go. Patients with Lewy body dementia spent more time in one state and far less in another, unlike the more even pattern in Parkinson's disease. pmc-13381070:

Teresa of Avila wrote her Life at the command of her confessors, who wanted proof that her visions were sound. Lewis's 1870 translation gives English readers her spiritual autobiography in full. The book became the foundation of Carmelite mysticism, the prayer tradition of her order.

Teresa tells of a lax convent youth, long illness, and a slow turn to mental prayer in middle age. She compares the soul to a garden watered four ways, each way a deeper kind of prayer. Her frank, funny, practical voice still startles readers who expect saints to sound remote. Few saints have written about themselves with such unguarded honesty.
the-hound-of-the-baskervilles-pg3070: Arthur Conan Doyle's Hound of the Baskervilles: the spectral hound of Dartmoor. Holmes's most famous case, the detective story supreme. The immortal classic. The hound on the moor, holmes supreme, Holmes supreme, the detective story supreme.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Volume twenty of Casanova's memoirs: the adventurer in his prime. The great life's high summer. Casanova at his most Casanova. Twentieth volume: high summer of adventure, casanova at his peak, Casanova at his peak, high summer of adventure.
theophrastus-characters-jebb-1870:
Theophrastus ran the Athens school of Aristotle after the master's death and wrote on plants, stones, and human nature. His Characters gives thirty short sketches of flawed types met in daily life. R. C. Jebb's 1870 edition pairs the Greek text with his English translation, an introduction, and notes.

Meet the flatterer, the gossip, the boor, the skinflint, and the man who is always late with bad news. Each sketch lists small acts until a whole person stands in front of you. The book founded the character sketch as a form, and its types walk through later European prose. It also shows street life in old Athens in sharp detail.
tob-0170:
Lady Charlotte Guest, cataloged also as Lady Charlotte Schreiber, translated the Welsh Mabinogion into English in the nineteenth century and opened it to the world. Pwyll's otherworldly bargains, Branwen's tragedy, Culhwch's impossible tasks, and an Arthur older and stranger than the French romances fill the tales. Guest's notes and illustrations enriched her edition.

The Four Branches and the native tales preserve a Welsh storytelling world of magic, honor, and shape-shifting, committed to parchment in the Middle Ages from older oral stock. Guest's translation became the founding presentation of Welsh literature in English and a cornerstone of Celtic myth studies. Modern versions exist, but hers made the field.
tob-10070:
Evelyn Underhill addressed Practical Mysticism, by its subtitle, to normal people rather than scholars or monks. Her claim is plain: mystical awareness is not a rare gift for saints. It is a capacity ordinary readers can practice, starting with truly paying attention to the world around them.

Short chapters use art, nature, and everyday moments to show what contemplation looks like in a working life. Underhill strips away technical language and treats attention, love, and self-forgetting as learnable habits. Readers who suspect mysticism belongs only in monasteries are her target audience, and she writes as a calm, plainspoken guide for them.
tob-13570:
Abraham Ortelius, a Flemish mapmaker, published the Theatrum Orbis Terrarum at Antwerp in 1570. Its name means Theatre of the World. He gathered the best maps of his day, cut to one size and bound as a single book.

Seventy maps show the whole known world and its regions, built from the work of many mapmakers whom Ortelius credits. Merchants, rulers, and scholars could now see the earth in one ordered set of pictures. Historians call it the first modern atlas, and it taught Europe what the world looked like for generations.
tob-4170:
Thomas Bulfinch retold the legends of chivalry for American readers in The Age of Chivalry, the medieval volume of Bulfinch's Mythology. King Arthur and the Round Table, the quest for the Holy Grail, Lancelot and Guenevere, and Charlemagne with his paladins fill its pages. Bulfinch drew on Malory and the romances, smoothing them for family reading.

Victorian storytelling at its most earnest, the volume aimed to let readers enjoy poetry and romance whose allusions filled English literature. Generations of Americans met the knights first through Bulfinch, before facing the older texts themselves. As an introduction that assumes no Latin and no prior knowledge, it did its work superbly and remains in print.
tob-4270:
Volume thirty-nine of the Sacred Books of the East, part one, presents Legge's Texts of Taoism in a further copy of the 1891 translation. Lao Tzu's Tao Te Ching opens the volume: eighty-one short chapters on the Way that can be spoken and the power of doing nothing by force.

Chuang Tzu follows, with parables of useless trees, happy fish, and a man who dreamed he was a butterfly. Legge's introductions and notes frame both for Western readers with care and respect. Verified from the 1919 edition, the volume opened the Taoist canon to the English-speaking world and still serves as its classic gate.
un-ga-res-2070:
Gibraltar, the small British-held port at the mouth of the Mediterranean Sea, is the subject of Resolution 2070, passed by the UN General Assembly in 1964. The Assembly had read the reports of its decolonization team and heard the case in committee debate.

Spain and the United Kingdom are invited to open talks at once, as the team's agreed text of 16 October 1964 had urged. Both states must then report the outcome to the team and to the Assembly at its next session. The short text opened a dispute over Gibraltar that the UN is still seized of today.
un-ga-res-a-69-70: Three regional hubs for peace and disarmament work get a nod in Resolution A/69/70, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The hubs serve Africa, Asia and the Pacific, and Latin America and the Caribbean. The text also recalls the UN Disarmament Information Programme. Set up in 1982, it teaches the public about arms control and builds support for the UN's aims in that field.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 2070 (XX), from the twentieth session in 1965, concerned Gibraltar. The Assembly studied the decolonization committee's reports on the territory and heard debate. It then invited the governments of Spain and the United Kingdom to begin talks without delay. The talks were those foreseen in the committee's agreed statement of 16 October 1964. The two governments were to report the outcome to the committee and the Assembly at the next session.

Resolution 69/70 of the General Assembly, adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, deals with the three United Nations regional centres for peace and disarmament. They serve Africa, Asia and the Pacific, and Latin America and the Caribbean. It stresses maintaining and revitalizing the centres. It appeals to states and other donors for the voluntary contributions they depend on. It asks the Secretary-General to keep supporting them within existing resources.
un-sc-res-1270:
The question of Sierra Leone came to a vote in Resolution 1270, adopted on 22 October 1999. The Lomé Peace Agreement of July 1999 had ended the fighting on paper. Rebels had lately seized hostages, including children and United Nations staff. Aid could not reach parts of the country at all.

The Council sets up the United Nations Mission in Sierra Leone, UNAMSIL, for six months. Up to 6,000 troops, including 260 observers, will help carry out the peace deal. The mission will aid disarmament of some 45,000 fighters and watch the cease-fire. Under Chapter VII it may protect civilians facing direct attack. The older observer mission ends at once, and reports are due every 45 days.
un-sc-res-1370: Bearing number 1370, this resolution of the Security Council is dated 2000 in the catalog. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1470:
UNAMSIL was extended as Liberia's war pressed on Sierra Leone on 28 March 2003. The Secretary-General's report of 17 March described fresh strains on security. Fighting in Liberia spilled refugees across the Mano River region. Sierra Leone's own police and army still lacked the means to hold the country alone. The Special Court and the truth commission carried the work on impunity and reconciliation.

The Council extended UNAMSIL's mandate for six months from 30 March 2003. Troop and police contributors won its thanks. The mission's progress in reshaping its size and deployment was praised. UNAMSIL was urged, as Sierra Leone's own forces grew able, to plan its drawdown in step with the threat. The Secretary-General owed detailed plans for the rest of the drawdown once its third phase was running. The funding gap in the disarmament trust fund caused concern. Building Freetown's administrative reach stayed the Council's core demand.
un-sc-res-1570: Resolution 1570, a 2004 act of the Security Council, survives here as a Wikisource transcription of the UN's record. The Council speaks for world peace and security, and a resolution is its strongest written instrument. This entry keeps the instrument intact: preamble, numbered decisions, and the reporting duties that usually close such a text.
un-sc-res-1670:
One month of grace was all the Council granted UNMEE on 13 April 2006. Eritrea's tight limits on the mission had cut its working capacity sharply. Both parties had agreed to accept the Boundary Commission's rulings as final and binding, yet the border stayed unmarked. The witnesses to the Algiers Agreements had met in New York in February.

The Council extended UNMEE's mandate for a single month. It demanded that both parties comply fully with resolution 1640 (2005). That text required Eritrea to lift its restrictions on the mission and Ethiopia to accept the border ruling. Member states were called to keep supporting UNMEE and the peace process with funds. The Council said plainly that if it found the parties had not complied within the month, it would review the mission's future, its shape, and its mandate. The short leash showed how close the mission had come to collapse.
un-sc-res-1770:
Iraq's UN mission gained a wider job under Resolution 1770, adopted in 2007. The mission, UNAMI, had advised Iraq since 2003, but violence and political deadlock were deepening. The Council expanded what its staff could do across the country.

The text asks UNAMI to push talks among Iraq's rival groups, support elections and a review of the constitution, and help refugees return home. It also covers aid coordination and human rights reporting. For readers, the resolution maps the civilian side of the Iraq effort, run beside a war fought by others. Readers can see the mission's full task list set out in one place.
un-sc-res-1870:
Voting on 30 April 2009, the Council adopted Resolution 1870 on Sudan. The 2005 peace deal that ended the long north-south war was entering its final stretch. National elections were due in 2010, and a southern referendum in 2011. The disputed Abyei area still lacked a funded administration, which fed local tension.

The Council extends the United Nations Mission in the Sudan, called UNMIS, until 30 April 2010. The mission should back credible elections with the United Nations Development Programme. It should also get ready to help with the 2011 referendum if asked. More staff should go to Abyei to calm clashes and guard civilians. Both parties must honor the Abyei ruling and the peace deal in full.
un-sc-res-270:
Villages in southern Lebanon came under Israeli air attack in August 1969. On 26 August 1969 the Security Council condemned the raid. Lebanon and Israel had both addressed the Council. The members voiced grief at the loss of civilian life and property. They also recalled the Council's earlier warning after the Beirut airport raid.

The resolution deplores all breaches of the ceasefire. It deplores the spread of the fighting to new areas. It declares that military reprisals of this kind cannot be tolerated. If they went on, the Council said, it would weigh stronger steps under the Charter. The aim was to stop the raids from starting again.
un-sc-res-370:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was renewed during the Vienna talks on 13 June 1975. The Secretary-General's report of 9 June held that the force was still needed to keep the cease-fire. Talks between the two communities had opened in Vienna under resolution 367 (1975). He urged that the talks be kept up and quickened. Both parties had agreed to six more months of the force.

The Council restated resolution 186 (1964), which created the force, and its backing of the General Assembly's settlement terms. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint. They had to press on with determined, cooperative efforts toward the Council's goals. The stationing of the force was extended for six months, to 15 December 1975. All parties were again asked to give the force their full cooperation. The Secretary-General would continue his good offices mission and keep the Council informed of the talks' progress.
un-sc-res-570: This library holds Resolution 570 as an official Council record, dated 1985 in its catalog. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-670:
Iraq's sanctions net was closed over the skies on 25 September 1990. Baghdad still held Kuwait and claimed to annex it. Foreign nationals were kept against their will, and Kuwaitis faced forced removal and abuse. States reported steady attempts to evade the trade embargo of resolution 661 (1990).

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council confirmed that the embargo covered all transport, aircraft included. Every state had to bar aircraft from taking off if they carried cargo for Iraq or Kuwait beyond medical supplies and food in humanitarian need. Planes bound for Iraq had to land for inspection as directed. Flights between a state's territory and Iraq or Kuwait had to be reported to the sanctions committee. Iraqi ships used in breach of the embargo were to be detained in port. Iraq's Decree No. 377 and all acts against the Council's resolutions were declared null and void.
un-sc-res-70: Help from one UN body to another is arranged in Security Council Resolution 70, passed on 7 March 1949. Article 83 of the Charter lets the Council draw on the Trusteeship Council for its work in strategic trust areas. The Council now asks that body, where trust deals allow and where safety lets, to do the tasks of Articles 87 and 88 for such areas on the Council's behalf. Those tasks cover the study of reports and the hearing of pleas from the lands.
un-sc-res-870: Entry number 870 in the Council's official sequence is a resolution the catalog dates to 1993. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-970:
Sanctions relief for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was extended by the Security Council on 12 January 1995. Belgrade had sealed its border with Bosnia and Herzegovina against all goods except food, medicine, and clothing for basic humanitarian needs. Monitors of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia watched the closure. The Council said keeping that border shut was a condition of the relief.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council suspended the restrictions named in resolution 943 (1994) for a further one hundred days. The rules guarding the Bosnian protected areas stayed in force. Every thirty days the Secretary-General had to report whether the conference co-chairmen certified that the border stayed effectively closed. If he reported a failure, the suspension would end within days. The Council kept the question under close review, ready to take further steps on the measures against Belgrade.
un-sc-res-un-security-council-meeting-82:
Eastern Ukraine is the subject of the Security Council's 8270th meeting, held in 2018 and preserved in this official record. The Council had not taken up the conflict for fifteen months. Briefers told members the war in the Donbass was still alive, with tens of thousands of ceasefire breaches recorded that year and about 1.6 million people driven from their homes.

Senior officials from the United Nations and the OSCE, the European security body that monitored the front line, gave the briefings. Member states then stated their positions on the fighting and on the stalled Minsk peace deals. The record shows a Council divided over blame and next steps.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Sierra Leone gets a full UN peacekeeping mission in Resolution 1270, adopted on 22 October 1999. The Lomé Peace Agreement of 7 July 1999 had ended the civil war on paper, and rebel leaders had returned to Freetown. Disarmament of ex-combatants was being prepared. Hostage-taking of UN and ECOMOG personnel by rebel groups had drawn condemnation.

The Council establishes the United Nations Mission in Sierra Leone, UNAMSIL, at once for six months, with up to 6,000 military personnel including 260 observers. UNAMSIL takes over from the observer mission UNOMSIL and must help carry out the peace agreement and the disarmament plan, deploy at disarmament centres, watch the ceasefire, and support elections. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes UNAMSIL to protect its own freedom of movement and, within its means, civilians under imminent threat of violence. It calls on all armed groups to disband and surrender their weapons without delay.

Sierra Leone's peace process was moving forward when this text passed on 18 September 2001, and UNAMSIL, the United Nations mission backing it, is renewed. The mission's mandate is extended for six months from 30 September 2001. Fighting in nearby Liberia and the wider Mano River region still kept life fragile for civilians and refugees.

The Council praised the mission's role in advancing peace and asked for regular reports on how its operations were working. It backed steps toward state authority across the country, open elections, and turning the Revolutionary United Front into a political party. Helping refugees and displaced people return home, where the mission was deployed, also remained part of its work.

Sierra Leone's uneasy peace is the concern of Resolution 1470, adopted on 28 March 2003. The UN Mission in Sierra Leone, UNAMSIL, was helping the government hold the country together. War in nearby Liberia threatened the Mano River region, refugees were many, and Sierra Leone's own police and army were not yet strong enough to keep order alone.

The Council extends UNAMSIL for six months from 30 March 2003 and backs its phased drawdown plan. It urges faster work to restore state authority, above all in the diamond fields, and better control of diamond mining. It voices worry about the funding gap for settling ex-fighters back into civilian life. It also backs the Special Court and the new Truth and Reconciliation Commission, and demands an end to illegal crossings from Liberia.

Western Sahara's referendum mission, MINURSO, is extended until 30 April 2005 in this text of 28 October 2004. The dispute remained at an impasse. The aim of a just, lasting, and mutually acceptable political solution that provides for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara is repeated.

Alongside the extension, a mid-term report is asked for within three months on how the situation is evolving. That report is also to address the mission's size and way of working, including options for cutting staff. Member states are called on to fund confidence-building measures, such as family visits, that increase contact between people divided by the long conflict.

Resolution 1670, adopted on 13 April 2006, warns Ethiopia and Eritrea that their peace is fraying. Eritrea had banned UN helicopter flights in October 2005 and tightened restrictions on the UN mission, UNMEE, which the Council said gravely hampered the mission's work and staff safety. Ethiopia, for its part, had still not accepted the boundary commission's ruling in full.

The Council kept UNMEE in place and demanded that both parties let it move freely throughout its area of operations. It stressed that lasting peace required full marking of the border on the ground, which could not happen while the mission was hobbled. Both governments were reminded that they had agreed to accept the commission's decision as final and binding.

Some lists call this a Sierra Leone text. It is not. The land in question lay in East Africa. It had been run by Britain for the UN since the war. On 9 December 1961 it became free, led by Julius Nyerere. Resolution 170 passed five days later, with no votes against.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Tanganyika. The Assembly did so the same day. Three years on, the state merged with Zanzibar. The union took the name Tanzania. It kept the same UN seat. Under Nyerere, the capital became a haven for groups fighting to free the rest of southern Africa from white rule.

Iraq's assistance mission, UNAMI, is extended and widened for twelve months on 10 August 2007. Iraq now had an elected, constitutional government, yet sectarian violence threatened its unity. All communities, it is underscored, need to join an inclusive political dialogue and national reconciliation.

The renewed mandate gives the mission a more active role. As conditions permit, its head is to advise and support Iraq on political talks, elections, constitutional review, and settling internal boundary disputes, and to promote regional dialogue. The mission would also back aid delivery, refugee returns, and human rights work. Member states are called on to keep funding and staffing the mission's expanded tasks.

Sudan's mission is extended as the peace deal nears its decisive tests in Resolution 1870, adopted on 30 April 2009. The Comprehensive Peace Agreement had reached a critical stage. The Abyei Interim Administration was unfunded, census results were delayed, national elections were planned for February 2010, and the 2011 referendum was approaching.

The Council extends the United Nations Mission in Sudan, UNMIS, until 30 April 2010. It welcomes the parties' agreement to send the Abyei boundary dispute to arbitration at the Permanent Court of Arbitration. It calls on them to implement the ruling and fund the interim administration. UNMIS must support the National Elections Commission toward February 2010 elections and prepare to assist the 2011 referendum if asked. It must protect civilians under imminent threat, including from the Lord's Resistance Army, and help demarcate the 1956 north-south border. The Secretary-General must develop benchmarks for measuring the mission's progress.

Villages in south Lebanon bombed from the air brought this Council rebuke of 1969. On 26 August, it adopted Resolution 270. Lebanon had laid the attack before the Council in a letter. The text voices grief at the loss of civilian life and goods. It recalls the 1949 armistice deal between the two states.

The Council condemns the planned air attack by Israel. It deplores all violent breaches of the ceasefire. It also deplores the spread of the fighting zone. Reprisal raids and grave truce breaches cannot be stood for, it declares. If such acts recur, the Council warns, it will weigh stronger steps under the Charter.

Resolution 370, adopted on 13 June 1975 by fourteen votes to none, keeps the Cyprus force for six more months of uneasy calm. The Secretary-General's June report said the force was still needed to hold the ceasefire and help the search for a settlement. He also reported on Vienna talks between the two communities' representatives, judging that negotiations should continue and speed up, and that success would demand flexibility and reciprocal gestures from everyone.

UNFICYP's stationing was extended for a further six months, as Cyprus's government agreed was necessary. The long line of Cyprus resolutions since 1964 was reaffirmed. The extension came less than a year after the coup and invasion that had split the island in two.

A judge of the International Court of Justice resigned in the summer of 1985, leaving a seat to fill. Judge Platon D. Morozov, named in the text, had resigned on 23 August 1985. The rest of his term still had to be served by someone. Resolution 570 was adopted unanimously on 12 September 1985.

Under Article 14 of the Court's Statute, the Security Council fixes the date of the election for such a vacancy. The Council set the election for 9 December 1985. It would be held at a meeting of the Security Council. A meeting of the General Assembly, during its fortieth session, would vote on the same day. The step is a short, routine one. It keeps the Court, the main court of the United Nations, at full strength.

Resolution 670, adopted on 25 September 1990 by fourteen votes to one, with Cuba against, closes the skies in the sanctions on Iraq. Iraq still occupied Kuwait, refused to free detained foreigners, and was mistreating Kuwaitis, the Council charged. States reported persistent attempts to evade the trade embargo imposed in August, and several had already cut down Iraq's diplomatic presence.

To seal the leaks, the Council confirmed that the embargo covered all means of transport, aircraft included. States were called on to stop cargo flights to and from Iraq and occupied Kuwait, except approved humanitarian shipments, and to detain Iraqi aircraft that violated the rules. It also warned that Iraqi decrees defying the Council's decisions were null and void.

Strategic trust territories were the Council's own responsibility in 1949, but another United Nations body could help with the work. Under Article 83 of the Charter, the Council keeps control of security questions in those areas. For other matters, it may use the help of the Trusteeship Council. Resolution 70 was adopted on 7 March 1949.

The Council asked the Trusteeship Council to carry out part of the work on its behalf. The Trusteeship Council would examine the reports and petitions that came in for the strategic areas. It would send the Security Council its findings and advice. Political, economic, social, and educational matters were all covered. Its questionnaires and reports were to be shared with the Council in advance. The arrangement let the Council keep its legal control while drawing on the other body's daily experience with trust territories.

Four extra days for the United Nations force in the former Yugoslavia came on 1 October 1993. The force, called UNPROFOR, worked in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Resolution 870 repeats the Council's determination to keep the force safe and free to move for all its missions. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended UNPROFOR's mandate for a short added period ending on 5 October 1993. It also decided to remain actively seized of the matter. The tiny extension was a bridge while the Council argued over its future.

Resolution 970, adopted on 12 January 1995 by fourteen votes to none with Russia abstaining, rewards Belgrade for sealing a border. Belgrade's authorities had shut their frontier with Bosnia to all goods except food, medicine, and clothing for essential humanitarian needs. Monitors from the international conference on the former Yugoslavia had verified the closure, which an earlier resolution made the price of relief.

Because that condition was met, the Council extended the partial suspension of sanctions against Serbia and Montenegro for a further fixed period. It stressed that the closure had to stay effective, urged prosecution of violators, and praised the monitors' work. Sanctions relief, the structure implies, lasts only as long as cooperation does.
verne-twenty-thousand-leagues-1870:
Jules Verne published Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas in 1870, a novel of travel beneath the oceans. Professor Aronnax joins a hunt for a sea monster that has attacked ships. He and his companions end up aboard the Nautilus, a submarine run by Captain Nemo. Nemo refuses to let them leave.

The voyage crosses every ocean and reaches the South Pole under the ice. Readers meet giant squid, lost cities, and vast schools of fish. Nemo aids oppressed peoples yet sinks ships without mercy. The book mixes science, wonder, and moral doubt. It helped create modern science fiction as a popular form.
villars-comte-de-gabalis-1670:
The Abbé de Villars published Le Comte de Gabalis at Paris in 1670, the original French text of the famous dialogues. A German count instructs a young abbé in the secret sciences across five conversations. The book fixed the Rosicrucian image in French letters and bridges the manifestos and the French occult revival of the next century.

Sylphs, gnomes, undines, and salamanders people the elements in the count's teaching. The wit sparkles; Villars seems to laugh while he reveals. Church authority banned the book, which only spread it further. French readers took its elementals into their permanent imagination. The 1670 Gabalis is the source from which the English Count of 1680 and all later elemental lore descend.
wallace-contributions-natural-selection-:
Alfred Russel Wallace reached the theory of natural selection on his own, in the Malay Archipelago. He gathered his key essays in Contributions to the Theory of Natural Selection in 1870. Wallace was Darwin's co-discoverer and loyal ally. The collection is a founding document of evolutionary anthropology.

The essays cover mimicry, protective color, island life, and the limits of selection. In the closing essay he breaks with Darwin: natural selection, he argues, cannot explain the human mind, which needed some higher power. Darwin was dismayed; the essay fed debate for decades. The volume shows Wallace thinking for himself inside the theory he helped to found.
